What an insolvency practitioner does, and how to choose one
[IMAGE - Hero] none, or the on-brand Mackintosh vector panel. This page answers a question, so it should open on text.

Certain roles in an insolvency can only be held by someone the law has licensed to hold them. Liquidator, administrator, administrative receiver, monitor of a moratorium, nominee and supervisor of a company voluntary arrangement, and in Scotland trustee in a sequestration or under a protected trust deed: each of those is a formal appointment, and each is closed to anyone without a licence. Taking one without being qualified is a criminal offence under section 389 of the Insolvency Act 1986.

What is not restricted is advice. Anyone may set up offering debt advice, and many do. The line falls at the point of appointment, which is worth knowing when you are working out who you are actually speaking to and what they are able to do for you.

If you are reading this because your company is in trouble, the useful question is not really what an insolvency practitioner is. It is whether you need one yet, and how to find one who will tell you the truth.

Most people arrive at this page somewhere in the middle of financial distress rather than at the end of it. The pressure has been building for a while, the finance options have narrowed, and someone has mentioned that you should speak to an insolvency practitioner. Whether that is the right next step depends entirely on how far things have gone, and that is worth establishing before you appoint anyone.

What they actually do

An insolvency practitioner's job changes depending on the appointment. Across all of them, they take control of a situation that has become too serious to resolve informally, and they owe duties to creditors as a whole rather than to whoever hired them. If you are on the other side of that, owed money by a company that has gone into a procedure, our creditor guides [link to /creditor-services/creditor-guides] set out what you can expect and what you can ask for.

Liquidator in a creditors' voluntary liquidation, members' voluntary liquidation or compulsory liquidation [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition], realising assets and distributing proceeds to creditors. The general shape of the process is covered on our company liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] page

Administrator, taking control of a company to rescue it, sell it, or achieve a better outcome for creditors than an immediate liquidation. Where a sale is arranged in advance, that is a pre-pack administration
Nominee and then supervisor of a company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva], putting the proposal to creditors and then policing it

Trustee in a sequestration [link to /debt-help-scotland/sequestration] or trustee under a protected trust deed [link to /debt-help-scotland/trust-deeds], on the personal side. Elsewhere in the UK the equivalent personal procedures are bankruptcy and Individual Voluntary Arrangements

Administrative receiver under a floating charge, an appointment now largely closed off for charges created since September 2003. Fixed charge receivership over property, including LPA receivership [link to /insolvency/lpa-receivership], is an English procedure and does not require an insolvency practitioner; in Scotland a lender enforces a standard security by calling up instead
Investigating director conduct and reporting on it to the Secretary of State within three months, which is a statutory duty on a liquidator, administrator or administrative receiver

They also take in and check the Statement of Affairs, which the directors themselves have to prepare, deal with employees and the Redundancy Payments Service, advertise appointments in the Edinburgh Gazette, and file at Companies House. In a Scottish compulsory liquidation there is no Official Receiver: the court appoints an interim liquidator when it makes the winding up order, and creditors are then asked to choose the liquidator. That differs from England and Wales, where the Official Receiver acts first.
How they are licensed and regulated
This matters more than most people realise, because it is the thing you can actually check.

A licence means sitting the exams set by the Joint Insolvency Examination Board, the JIEB, and then securing authorisation from a recognised professional body. There are three: ICAS, the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Scotland, ICAEW, the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, and the Insolvency Practitioners Association. All three authorise practitioners across Great Britain, so a Scottish practitioner may hold a licence from any of them. They must also have security in place, which in Scotland is called caution, and follow the Insolvency Code of Ethics and the Statements of Insolvency Practice, which set out how particular procedures should be conducted.

Insolvency law in the UK sits mainly in the Insolvency Act 1986, with separate Scottish rules for court procedure and a separate statute again for personal insolvency in Scotland. An insolvency practitioner has to work within all of it, and the licence is the state's way of confirming they can.

The Insolvency Service maintains a public register on its website, and it takes a minute to check. As the regulator of last resort it oversees the recognised professional bodies, each of which acts as the direct regulator for its own licence holders, and complaints about any practitioner are routed through a single complaints gateway. Professionals who fall short can lose their licence.

For guidance on choosing and on what to expect, R3, the trade body for the profession, publishes free material, as does the Insolvency Service. Neither will give you advice about your own company, but both are a reasonable place to start reading.
The part nobody in this industry likes to say out loud
An insolvency practitioner is paid from the appointment. The fee comes out of the estate, and the appointment only exists if a formal procedure happens.

That does not make practitioners dishonest. Most are careful, regulated professionals doing a difficult job well. But it does mean that when you ask someone whose income depends on formal appointments whether you need a formal appointment, you are asking a question they have an interest in the answer to.

Lancefield does not take appointments. Nobody here becomes your liquidator, administrator or trustee, so we earn nothing from recommending one. That is deliberate, and it is the reason clients and professional contacts come to us first. Where a formal appointment genuinely is needed, we bring in a licensed practitioner we know and trust, and we stay alongside you through it.
What it costs

Fees depend on the procedure and the complexity of the estate. In most insolvent appointments the practitioner is paid from company assets rather than by the directors personally, so where a company has assets to realise, the process may cost you nothing directly.

Where a company has no assets, someone has to fund the work, and directors are often asked to. Fees must be approved by creditors, or by a committee, or failing that determined by the auditor of the court. Professional standards require a practitioner to explain the basis of their remuneration and, where they are charging on time costs, to give a fee estimate before drawing anything. If you are given a number without that explanation, ask for it.
Do you need one yet?

Often, not yet. An insolvency practitioner is required for a formal procedure. A great many situations are resolved before that point, and the earlier you look at it, the more of those options remain open.

The distinction that matters is between financial distress and formal insolvency. Distress is a cash flow problem: late payments, stretched credit, a lender getting nervous. Insolvency is a legal state, either being unable to pay debts as they fall due or having liabilities that exceed assets. Plenty of businesses in real distress are not yet insolvent, and for those the answer is finance, restructuring or a hard look at the numbers, not an appointment. Bringing in an insolvency practitioner at that stage can foreclose options that were still available.
You probably need advice, not an appointment

If creditor pressure is building but nothing formal has started, if you are weighing whether the business is viable, or if you want to understand your exposure as a director, that is advisory work. It does not require an appointment. Support at this stage might mean turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] work, debt restructuring [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring], an independent review [link to /restructuring/independent-business-review] to establish where the business actually stands, or simply getting the legal position clear. Acting before you are forced to is what contingency planning [link to /restructuring/contingency-planning] is for.
You probably do need a practitioner

If a winding up petition has been advertised, if you have decided to close an insolvent company, or if you want to place the business into administration, a licensed insolvency practitioner has to be appointed to carry it out. At that point the insolvency process is under way and the question is who runs it, not whether.

One further benefit of asking early is that it involves the other stakeholders on your terms rather than theirs. Lenders, landlords and HMRC all respond better to a director who approaches them with a plan than to one who has stopped answering the phone, and finance options that exist in month one are frequently gone by month four. Debts do not improve with silence.

Every option below has consequences, and we explain each honestly so you can choose with your eyes open.

If a creditor has already moved against you, start with winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition], because that is the situation with the shortest fuse.
Choosing well, in Scotland

Scotland has its own insolvency regime for individuals and its own court procedure for companies. Sequestration, protected trust deeds and the Debt Arrangement Scheme have no direct English equivalents, and Scottish corporate matters run through the Court of Session or, where a company's paid up share capital is £120,000 or less, which covers most owner managed companies, the sheriff court for the area of its registered office. Either way, not the English courts. A national firm working from English precedent will get some of this wrong.

When you are choosing, ask three things. Is the person who will actually handle your case licensed, and with which body. What are the realistic alternatives to the procedure being recommended. And what happens to your personal position, including any personal guarantees, under each option. A good practitioner will answer all three without hesitating.

That third question is the one directors most often leave until it is too late. If you have signed a personal guarantee, the company procedure and your own finances are two halves of the same problem, and they need to be looked at together. Our Debt Help Scotland [link to /debt-help-scotland] section covers the personal side.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between an insolvency practitioner and an insolvency adviser?

An insolvency practitioner holds a licence and can take formal appointments. An adviser helps you understand your position and your options, and can guide you through the insolvency process, but does not take the appointment. Lancefield is an adviser. We work alongside licensed practitioners when a formal appointment is needed.
When should I contact an insolvency practitioner?

Earlier than most people do. The honest answer is that you should get advice as soon as the position is genuinely uncertain, and that advice does not have to come from someone who takes appointments. If a winding up petition has been served, or you have decided to close an insolvent company, you need a practitioner now. Short of that, an advisory conversation usually tells you whether you do.
Do insolvency practitioners work with accountants?

Routinely, and your own accountant is often the person who suggests the conversation. Accountants generally handle the financial reporting and the tax position but do not take insolvency appointments, so the two roles sit alongside each other rather than overlapping. We work with a client's existing accountants rather than replacing them, and that is usually what everyone wants.
What do you have to do to become one?

The route runs through the JIEB, short for the Joint Insolvency Examination Board, whose exams have a reputation for being among the toughest in the profession. Most people sitting them are already chartered accountants or solicitors. Passing is only the first hurdle. Authorisation from a recognised professional body has to follow, along with a bond, before anyone can accept an appointment.
How do I check someone is licensed?

The Insolvency Service publishes a public register of insolvency practitioners, and each recognised professional body maintains its own list. Ask which body authorises them and check. Anyone genuinely licensed will expect the question.
How much does an insolvency practitioner cost?

It depends on the procedure and the complexity of the case, and fees are usually paid from company assets rather than by directors personally. Under professional standards a practitioner should set out the basis of their remuneration, and give a fee estimate where they are charging on time costs, before drawing fees. The fees themselves have to be approved by creditors or a committee, or determined by the auditor of the court.
Can an insolvency practitioner help me avoid insolvency?

Sometimes, yes, and many will advise on turnaround and restructuring. Bear in mind that their income comes from appointments, which is worth factoring in when weighing the advice. That is precisely why an independent view first is worth having.
Does contacting one make anything official?

No. An initial conversation is confidential and commits you to nothing. Nothing becomes formal until you decide to start a procedure. The belief that asking for advice triggers consequences keeps a lot of directors from acting while they still have options.
Do I need one based in Scotland?

Not strictly, but Scottish procedure and the personal insolvency regime differ from England and Wales, and local court practice matters. Someone who works in the Scottish system every day will not have to learn it on your case.

Company liquidation, explained plainly
[IMAGE - Hero] none required. This page opens on text, since the reader wants an answer quickly. If a visual is wanted, use the on-brand Mackintosh vector panel, not a photo.

When a limited company is liquidated, everything it owns is turned into cash, that cash goes to the people it owes, and the company itself ceases to exist. Companies House removes it from the register and, in all but rare cases, that is the end of it.

That is the mechanical answer. The one you probably want is this: liquidation is not always the right answer, and it is not always necessary. Before you go any further, it is worth knowing whether your company needs to be liquidated at all.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
First, the question most people skip
Directors usually arrive at liquidation having already decided it is the only option left. Often it is. Sometimes it is not.

If the business is still viable underneath the debt, a company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] or a turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] plan may keep it trading. If the pressure is coming from one creditor rather than the whole book, there may be a narrower fix through debt restructuring [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring]. And if the company is solvent and you simply want to close it, you want a members' voluntary liquidation, which is a completely different process with a very different tax outcome.
We do not take appointments. No one here becomes your liquidator, so we earn nothing by telling you to liquidate. That is the point of asking us first.
The three types of liquidation
[IMAGE - Three types section] three teal line icons, one per card (document, coins returning to hand, court building). Vector only.
Which one applies depends on whether the company can pay its debts, and on who starts the process.
Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation (CVL)

The most common route for an insolvent company. The directors start it voluntarily, shareholders pass a resolution, and a licensed insolvency practitioner is appointed as liquidator to wind the company up in an orderly way. Choosing a CVL rather than waiting to be forced into liquidation generally reflects better on the directors' conduct.
[LINK] Read more about CVL
Members' Voluntary Liquidation (MVL)

For solvent companies only. If the company can pay its debts in full and the directors can swear a declaration of solvency, an MVL closes it and returns the remaining funds to shareholders in a tax-efficient way. This is a positive process, usually chosen at retirement, after a sale, or when tidying up a group.
[LINK] Read more about MVL
Compulsory liquidation

This one is done to you rather than by you. A creditor who is owed money petitions the court, and if that winding up petition succeeds the court orders the company to be wound up. In Scotland there is no Official Receiver: the court appoints an interim liquidator at the moment it makes the winding-up order, and the creditors can choose a different liquidator afterwards. By the time a winding up petition has been advertised, your bank account is usually frozen and your options have narrowed sharply. That is exactly why acting earlier matters.
[LINK] Read more about compulsory liquidation
A solvent limited company that simply has no further use has its own route, and it is worth knowing that closing one is a different exercise entirely from closing an insolvent one.

There is also company dissolution, or strike off, which is not liquidation at all. It removes a dormant or unused company from the register without a formal winding up. It is only appropriate where there are no significant debts and no creditor is likely to object. Where a company has assets to distribute, an MVL [link to /insolvency/members-voluntary-liquidation-mvl] is almost always the better route.

Not sure which applies? Compare CVL [link to /insolvency/creditors-voluntary-liquidation-cvl], MVL [link to /insolvency/members-voluntary-liquidation-mvl] and compulsory liquidation [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition] side by side, or speak to us and we will tell you in one conversation.
Solvent or insolvent? That one question decides everything
Before anything else, establish which side of the line your limited company sits on, because it determines which type of company liquidation is even available to you.

A company is solvent for these purposes if its directors, having made a full inquiry into its affairs, can swear a statutory declaration that it will pay its debts in full with interest within a period they specify. That period cannot exceed twelve months from the start of the winding up. Twelve months is the ceiling, not an automatic term, and swearing the declaration without reasonable grounds is a criminal offence, so it is not a formality. Where that declaration can properly be made you can liquidate through an MVL and take what is left as capital. A company is insolvent if it cannot pay its debts as they fall due, or if what it owes comes to more than everything it owns. Once a company is insolvent, or close to it, or an insolvent liquidation or administration becomes probable, the directors' duties shift: creditors' interests have to be weighed alongside the shareholders', and the deeper the trouble the more weight they carry, until at the point insolvent liquidation is inevitable they come first.

That shift matters more than most directors realise. Trading on while insolvent, taking deposits you cannot fulfil or credit you cannot repay, is what creates personal exposure. The moment you suspect the company is insolvent is the moment to take advice, not the moment to press on and hope.
Solvent

Assets exceed liabilities, and the directors can declare the debts will be paid in full with interest within a stated period of up to twelve months. Route: MVL [link to /insolvency/members-voluntary-liquidation-mvl]. Outcome: funds returned to shareholders, often with a favourable tax treatment.
Insolvent

Cannot pay debts as they fall due, or liabilities exceed assets. Route: CVL [link to /insolvency/creditors-voluntary-liquidation-cvl] if you act, compulsory liquidation [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition] if a creditor acts first. Outcome: assets realised, proceeds distributed to creditors by statutory priority.
If you are genuinely unsure which applies, that is exactly the question a short diagnostic conversation settles.
What creditors can do while you are deciding
The clock is not neutral. While you weigh options, creditors have their own remedies, and the further those actions progress the fewer routes remain open to you.
Chasing and default notices, the informal stage, where most situations are still fully recoverable
Statutory demand, a formal demand for an undisputed debt, giving 21 days to pay before further steps
Court actions for the debt, producing a judgment that can then be enforced. In Scotland enforcement is called diligence and includes arrestment of bank accounts and earnings

Winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition], an application to the courts to wind up the company. Once a winding up petition is advertised, your bank account is likely to be frozen and other creditors can join

Compulsory liquidation, if the courts grant the winding-up order. In a compulsory winding up in Scotland the court appoints an interim liquidator when it makes the order, and the creditors can choose a different licensed practitioner afterwards

Each of these steps narrows what is possible. A company that talks to an insolvency practitioner at the default notice stage has options. The same limited company facing an advertised winding up petition has very few. Nothing about that sequence is unusual or shameful, but it is worth understanding that delay is not a neutral choice, it is a decision to let creditors set the pace.
What actually happens in a liquidation
Once a liquidator is appointed, they take control of the company. Directors' powers cease, though your duties to cooperate do not.
The insolvency practitioner appointed as liquidator takes charge of the company's assets and its bank account
Assets are valued and sold, and the proceeds collected
The company's liabilities are established, including contingent liabilities that may not yet have crystallised, such as leases and guarantees
Employees are made redundant, and can claim statutory payments through the Redundancy Payments Service
Creditors are invited to submit claims and are paid in the statutory order of priority set out in the Insolvency Act 1986
The liquidator investigates the conduct of each director, which is a required part of the job rather than a sign of suspicion
The company is dissolved and removed from the register

Secured creditors are paid first from the assets they hold security over, then preferential creditors including employees for certain claims, then HMRC for specific taxes, and finally unsecured creditors. In most insolvent liquidations, unsecured creditors receive little or nothing. Shareholders come last and usually receive nothing at all.
What it means for you as a director
[IMAGE - Director consequences section] optional single icon per card. Keep restrained, this section should feel serious rather than decorated.
This is the part that keeps people awake, and it deserves a straight answer.

In most cases, liquidating a company does not make a director personally liable for its debts. The limited company structure exists precisely to separate the two, so the company's liabilities stay with the company. There are exceptions, and they matter. An insolvency practitioner acting as liquidator has a statutory duty to review how each director behaved in the period before insolvency, so it is worth understanding where the lines fall.
Personal guarantees

If you signed a personal guarantee, for a bank facility, a lease, or a supplier account, that guarantee survives the liquidation. The creditor can pursue you personally for the amount guaranteed. This is the single most common unpleasant surprise we see, and it is worth establishing exactly what you have signed before anything else happens.
Overdrawn director's loan account
If you have drawn more from the company than you put in, the liquidator will treat the balance as an asset of the company and ask you to repay it.
Wrongful trading

If you continued to trade and take on credit after the point where you knew, or ought to have known, that there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvency, a court can order you to contribute personally. Acting early is the clearest defence available to you.
Director disqualification

The liquidator reports on the conduct of every director. Where conduct has fallen short, a disqualification order can follow, for up to fifteen years, preventing you from acting as a director of any company. Ordinary business failure, honestly handled, does not usually lead to this. Directors who took advice early and kept records are in a considerably better position than those who did not.
What it costs, and what if you cannot afford it

A liquidator's fees are normally paid from the company's assets. Where there are assets to realise, the proceeds cover the cost of the work and the process may cost the directors nothing personally. Fees have to be approved by the creditors, the liquidation committee or the court, and the insolvency practitioner should set out the work they anticipate, what it is expected to cost, and the basis on which they are charging, before that basis is approved.

Where a company has no assets at all, someone has to fund the work, and that is a genuine problem faced by a lot of directors. There are still options, and the honest ones are worth hearing before you decide to simply stop trading and hope the company fades away. Walking away tends to create more personal risk than dealing with it does.

On timing, a straightforward company liquidation usually runs six to twelve months from appointment to closure, though the company stops trading almost immediately. The liquidation procedure itself is set by the Insolvency Act 1986, so the sequence does not vary much between cases; what varies is how long it takes to realise the assets and agree the claims.

One practical point that catches people out: any credit agreements, leases and hire purchase contracts in the company's name do not simply disappear. The liquidator deals with them, and where an agreement was personally guaranteed the lender will still look to the guarantor. Check what you have signed before you assume the company's closure ends the obligation. Cases involving property, disputed claims or an investigation take longer. An MVL for a solvent company can be quicker, particularly where the only real task is to distribute cash.
Who gets paid, and in what order

Once the company assets are realised, the proceeds are distributed in an order set by the Insolvency Act 1986. It is not first come first served, and it is not negotiable by the liquidator. Directors are often surprised by where they and their creditors actually sit.
Secured creditors with a fixed charge are paid from whatever their security is worth, outside the general pot
The costs of the liquidation, including the liquidator's fees, come next
Preferential creditors, where employees rank first for unpaid wages and holiday pay within statutory limits. These preferential payments come ahead of everything below them

HMRC, which since December 2020 ranks as a preferential creditor for VAT, and for the PAYE, employee National Insurance and CIS deductions it holds on the company's behalf. Corporation tax and employer National Insurance are not included and stay in the unsecured pot with everyone else
The prescribed part, a portion of whatever the floating charge assets bring in, which the law sets aside so that ordinary creditors are not left with nothing
Floating charge holders
Unsecured creditors, which is most trade suppliers, and where any remaining HMRC debt sits
Shareholders, only if everything above has been paid in full, which in an insolvent liquidation does not happen

Two consequences matter in practice. HMRC's move up the order in 2020 pushed unsecured creditors further down, so trade suppliers recover less than they once did from the same estate. And a director who has lent money to the company is an unsecured creditor, near the back, which is why director loans are so rarely repaid in an insolvent winding-up.

It also changes how a rescue has to be built. Where HMRC is owed a significant amount of VAT or PAYE, it now holds a stronger position than it did before, and any proposal that depends on HMRC accepting a reduced return has to be realistic about that. If HMRC is your largest creditor, its view of the company assets and of what you are proposing tends to determine the outcome, whichever procedure you choose.
Where does HMRC rank in a liquidation?

Partly preferential and partly unsecured, which catches people out. HMRC is a preferential creditor for VAT, and for the PAYE, employee National Insurance and CIS deductions the company collected on someone else's behalf. For corporation tax and employer National Insurance it ranks as an ordinary unsecured creditor alongside trade suppliers. So a company with a large VAT arrears position and a company with a large corporation tax bill face quite different distributions, even if the total owed to HMRC is the same.
What happens to employees

Employees are usually made redundant when the liquidator is appointed, because the company has stopped trading. They become creditors of the company for what they are owed, and they have preferential status for certain claims, which puts them ahead of ordinary unsecured creditors.

Where the company cannot pay, employees can apply to the Redundancy Payments Service for statutory redundancy pay, unpaid wages, notice pay and accrued holiday pay, which come out of the National Insurance Fund. Each element has its own statutory limit, there is a cap on a week's pay, and statutory redundancy pay requires two years' continuous service. Notice pay is treated as compensation, so it is reduced by anything earned or claimable elsewhere during the notice period. The liquidator provides the reference numbers and the information needed to claim, and dealing with this properly is usually one of the first things a good practitioner does.
If you are a director who is also an employee of the company, you may be able to claim from the Redundancy Payments Service too. It is frequently overlooked, and it is worth asking about.
After the liquidation ends

Once the liquidator has realised the assets, agreed the claims and distributed the proceeds, the company is dissolved and removed from the register at Companies House. It stops existing as a legal entity, and any remaining unpaid debts of the company die with it, apart from anything personally guaranteed.

For you as a director, three things follow. The conduct report goes to the Insolvency Service, and in the great majority of cases nothing further happens. Restrictions apply to reusing the company name, which are strict and carry personal liability if breached. And you are generally free to be a director of another limited company, unless you have been disqualified.
Many directors do go on to start again, and doing so lawfully is entirely possible. Doing it accidentally unlawfully, by reusing a prohibited name, is a trap worth avoiding with one conversation.
Liquidation in Scotland

The corporate insolvency framework in the Insolvency Act 1986 applies across Great Britain, but the process in Scotland differs in ways that matter. Court proceedings run through the Court of Session, or the local Sheriff Court where the company's paid-up share capital does not exceed £120,000, rather than the English courts, and Scottish procedure and terminology are not identical. For individuals, Scotland has its own regime entirely, with sequestration, protected trust deeds and the Debt Arrangement Scheme in place of English bankruptcy and IVAs.
We are based in Glasgow, so this is the system we work in every day.

Alternatives worth considering first
Liquidation is one outcome, not the only one. Depending on where the business actually stands:
Company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] lets a viable company repay creditors over time and keep trading

Administration [link to /insolvency/administration] creates breathing space and holds creditors back while a rescue or sale is arranged, and pre-pack administration allows an immediate sale of the business
Turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] addresses the cause rather than the symptom, where there is still a business worth saving
Debt restructuring [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring] reshapes what the company owes without a formal insolvency procedure
Contingency planning [link to /restructuring/contingency-planning] prepares a fallback before circumstances force the decision for you
Independent business review [link to /restructuring/independent-business-review] gives you and any lender an objective read on whether the business is viable
We will tell you honestly which of these is realistic in your situation, including when the answer is none of them.
Frequently asked questions
Which type of liquidation will apply to my company?

It comes down to solvency and to who moves first. A solvent company that wants to close uses a Members' Voluntary Liquidation. An insolvent company whose directors decide to liquidate uses a Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation. An insolvent company whose creditor petitions the court first ends up in Compulsory Liquidation. The practical difference between the last two is control: in a Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation you choose the timing and have a say in who is appointed, whereas Compulsory Liquidation is imposed on you.
How long does liquidation take?

A straightforward CVL usually takes six to twelve months to complete, though complex cases take longer. The company stops trading almost immediately, but the liquidator's work of realising assets, agreeing claims and reporting continues after that.
How does liquidation differ from administration?

The two have opposite purposes. Administration is protective: it holds creditors back while a rescue, a sale or a better return is put together, on the assumption something is still worth saving. Liquidation starts from the opposite premise, that nothing can be saved, and sets about realising the assets and paying out what it can before the company is struck from the Companies House register.
What happens to employees?

Employees are usually made redundant when the liquidator is appointed. They can claim statutory redundancy pay, notice pay, unpaid wages and holiday pay from the Redundancy Payments Service, each subject to its own statutory limit, and redundancy pay requires two years' continuous service. It is one of the first things a good liquidator deals with.
Will I lose my home?

Not because of the liquidation itself, since the company's debts belong to the company. The risk comes from personal guarantees secured against your home, or from an overdrawn loan account. That is why we look at your personal exposure alongside the company's position rather than treating them separately.
Can I start another company afterwards?

In most cases yes. There are restrictions on reusing the same or a similar company name, and separate consequences if you are disqualified. The rules here are strict and easy to fall foul of by accident, so take advice before registering anything.
Who can act as a liquidator?

Only a licensed insolvency practitioner can be appointed as liquidator. Lancefield does not take appointments. We advise you on whether liquidation is right, and which type fits, and where a formal appointment is needed we bring in a licensed practitioner we know and trust, and stay alongside you through it.
Will the Official Receiver be involved?

Not in Scotland, no. The Official Receiver is an office that exists only in England and Wales, so English guides that mention one are not describing the Scottish process. In a Scottish compulsory winding-up the court appoints an interim liquidator, who must be a licensed insolvency practitioner, when it makes the order.
Is liquidation the same as bankruptcy?

No. Liquidation applies to companies. Bankruptcy applies to individuals, and in Scotland it is called sequestration. They are separate processes under separate rules, though they often arrive together when a director has given personal guarantees.

Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation (CVL)

When an insolvent company is closed by its own directors instead of by a creditor going to court, the procedure used is a creditors' voluntary liquidation. The decision is yours, so is most of the timing, and you have a say in which insolvency practitioner is appointed. Directors rarely appreciate how much that matters until they have lost the option.

It is the most common formal insolvency procedure in the UK, and for a company that genuinely cannot pay its debts it is usually the right answer. What it is not is a way of making the problem disappear discreetly. This is a formal process with real consequences for you as a director, and those consequences are worth understanding before you commit rather than after.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
Is a CVL actually the right answer for you?
We do not take insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes your liquidator, so we earn nothing from telling you to liquidate. That is why this section comes first rather than last.

A creditors' voluntary liquidation is the right answer where the company is insolvent, there is no realistic prospect of trading out of it, and continuing would simply increase the debt. That describes a great many companies, and if it describes yours then the sooner it is dealt with the better your own position will be.
It is the wrong answer, or at least premature, in three situations that come up repeatedly.

The business underneath is viable and the debt is historic. A company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] can bind the whole creditor body and let a working business trade on. Liquidation ends it permanently
One creditor is the problem, not the whole book. Negotiation or debt restructuring [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring] may deal with it without any formal insolvency procedure at all

The company can pay its debts and you just want it closed. That is an MVL [link to /insolvency/members-voluntary-liquidation-mvl], a completely different procedure with a very different tax outcome. Putting a solvent company through a CVL would be an expensive mistake

Ask any adviser who recommends liquidation what the alternatives are and why they were ruled out. If the answer is thin, get a second view. A turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] review or an independent review [link to /restructuring/independent-business-review] will tell you whether there is anything worth saving, and both are cheaper than finding out afterwards.
How the process runs

The liquidation process is set by the Insolvency Act 1986 and does not vary much between cases. What varies is how long each stage takes. The steps below describe the whole liquidation process from first conversation to the company ceasing to exist, so that nothing about it comes as a surprise.
Advice and nomination of a liquidator. The directors instruct a licensed insolvency practitioner, who advises on whether a creditors' voluntary liquidation is appropriate and prepares the paperwork

Statement of Affairs. The directors set out, in a prescribed form, everything the company owns and everything it owes, naming every creditor and the amount due to each. This has to be accurate. It is the document creditors and the liquidator work from, and getting it wrong causes problems later
Shareholders' resolution. The shareholders pass a resolution to wind the company up. This is the moment liquidation formally begins
Creditors' decision. Creditors are given the Statement of Affairs and the opportunity to appoint a liquidator of their own choosing. In most cases they accept the practitioner the directors nominated
Liquidator takes control. Company assets pass into the liquidator's hands. The directors' powers cease
Asset realisation. The liquidator sells what can be sold and collects what is owed to the company
Investigation and reporting. The liquidator reviews the conduct of every director and reports to the Insolvency Service
Distribution and dissolution. Whatever is realised is distributed to creditors in the statutory order, and the company is dissolved and struck from the register at Companies House

From instruction to the shareholders' resolution is often two to three weeks. The liquidation itself usually runs six to twelve months, though cases involving property, disputed creditor claims or an investigation take longer. The company stops trading almost immediately, so the practical end of the business comes right at the start.
Where you sit in the queue

Distribution follows a statutory order that the liquidator cannot vary, and the full waterfall is set out on our company liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] page. What matters here is where a director sits in it, because that is the part people get wrong.

If you lent money to your own company, you are an ordinary unsecured creditor, near the back, behind the liquidation costs, the employees, HMRC's preferential element and any floating charge. Directors regularly assume their loan comes back first because it was their money. It does not, and in most insolvent cases it does not come back at all. Anyone planning around recovering a director's loan should stop planning around it.

The other thing worth saying plainly is what suppliers will get, which is usually very little. Being straight with them about that is better than implying otherwise and being found out during the process.
What it means for you as a director
[IMAGE] "What it means for you as a director": the five cards work as a grid, no icons needed.
This is the part most directors are actually worried about, and the part thin guides skate over. Here is the honest position.
Your conduct is investigated. Always.

The liquidator has a statutory duty to review the conduct of every director and report to the Insolvency Service. This is not a sign that anything is wrong; it happens in every insolvent liquidation without exception. In the great majority of cases nothing further follows. Ordinary business failure, honestly handled and properly documented, is not what the regime is aimed at.
Wrongful trading is the real risk, and it is about timing

Wrongful trading exposure arises where a director carried on trading after the point where insolvent liquidation could no longer realistically be avoided, and the creditors ended up worse off for it. The test is not whether the company failed. It is what you knew, when you knew it, and what you did next. Directors who took advice early and kept records are in a considerably stronger position than those who pressed on and hoped.
Personal guarantees survive the liquidation

If you personally guaranteed company borrowing, a lease or a supplier account, liquidating the company does not extinguish that. The lender will look to you. Company directors are caught by this constantly, and a personal guarantee is the single most important thing to establish before you start rather than after. Dig out what you actually signed: guarantees hide in bank facilities, equipment leases, commercial property leases and supplier credit applications, and directors routinely forget the ones signed years ago. If a personal guarantee is called in and you cannot meet it, that becomes a personal debt problem with its own separate answers.
An overdrawn director's loan account becomes a debt you owe

Where a director's loan account is overdrawn, meaning more has come out over the years than went in, that balance is an asset of the company and the liquidator will pursue it as a debt you owe. Dividends declared when there were insufficient distributable profits can be reclassified this way too. Check this early, because it is often the largest single personal exposure and it is entirely foreseeable.
You can usually be a director again, but mind the name

Unless you are disqualified, you are generally free to be a director of another company. The trap is Section 216 of the Insolvency Act 1986, the restriction on re-use of company names, often called the phoenix company rules. For five years from the start of the liquidation you cannot be involved in a business using the liquidated company's name, or any name so similar it suggests a connection, unless one of the statutory exceptions applies. Breach is a criminal offence and can make you personally liable for the new company's debts. Company directors trip over this because the trading name feels like theirs to carry across. Take advice before registering anything that resembles the old name.

If a personal guarantee or an overdrawn loan account applies to you, the company procedure and your own finances are two halves of one problem. Our Debt Help Scotland [link to /debt-help-scotland] section covers the personal side, including Scottish bankruptcy [link to /debt-help-scotland/sequestration] and trust deeds [link to /debt-help-scotland/trust-deeds].
What your creditors see, and what they can do

A creditors' voluntary liquidation is a public process, and it is worth knowing exactly what becomes visible and when, because directors often imagine it is either more secret or more exposing than it really is.

The appointment is advertised in the Gazette, published as the Edinburgh Gazette for a Scottish company. Credit reference agencies pick it up from the Gazette, and the liquidation is recorded at Companies House against the company's filing history. Suppliers, customers and competitors can all see it. What is not published is the detail of your conduct report, which goes to the Insolvency Service and is not a public document.
As for what creditors can actually do, the answer is narrower than most directors fear.
They submit a claim to the liquidator for what they are owed, and the liquidator adjudicates on it. Creditor claims that are disputed get examined rather than simply accepted
They can vote on the choice of liquidator, and on certain decisions during the liquidation
They can ask questions and request information about the conduct of the liquidation

They deal with the liquidator, not with you. In practice claims are made in the liquidation rather than chased separately, and the liquidator takes over dealing with them. Worth knowing, though, that a creditors' voluntary liquidation carries no automatic court stay the way a compulsory winding up does: existing or new court action is only halted if the liquidator applies to the court for it, and a creditor keeps the right to petition to have the company wound up by the court instead. In practice few bother once a liquidator is in place

They cannot pursue you personally for the company's debts, unless you gave a personal guarantee or there is a separate statutory ground, such as an overdrawn loan account, misfeasance, or trading under a prohibited name

That last pair is the point that gives most directors relief. The chasing stops. Creditor pressure that has been consuming your attention for months transfers to the insolvency practitioner on the day of appointment, and dealing with creditors stops being your job.
Creditors who behave differently
Not every creditor responds the same way, and knowing which one you are dealing with changes what is sensible to do before you liquidate.
HMRC

Frequently the largest creditor in a small limited company, and the one most likely to have petitioned had you not acted. HMRC is a preferential creditor for VAT, PAYE, employee National Insurance and CIS deductions, so it recovers ahead of trade creditors. It also looks closely at whether tax money was used to pay other creditors while the debt to it grew, which is one of the specific conduct issues the Insolvency Service takes an interest in.
A secured lender

A bank with a charge over company assets sits outside the general distribution and is paid from its security. In practice a secured creditor is often relaxed about the liquidation process itself, because its position is protected either way. What it will pursue is any personal guarantee you gave.
Your landlord

Commercial leases are among the most expensive liabilities in a liquidation, and the landlord becomes an unsecured creditor for the remaining rent. Landlords very commonly hold a director's personal guarantee, so check the lease before anything else.
Trade suppliers

Unsecured, at the back of the queue, and usually recovering little. Some will have retention of title clauses letting them reclaim goods they supplied but were never paid for, which is worth identifying early because those goods are not company assets to distribute.
You, as a creditor

If you lent the company money, you are an unsecured creditor too. That ranks behind almost everyone. Directors who expect to recover a loan they made to their own limited company are nearly always disappointed, and it is better to know that at the outset.
None of this changes whether you should liquidate. It changes what you check first, and how surprised you are by what follows.

One point that applies to every creditor equally: once the liquidation process begins, no creditor can improve its position by shouting louder. The order of payment is fixed by statute, and a creditor that has been aggressive gets exactly the same treatment as one that has been patient. Directors carrying months of pressure from a particular creditor sometimes find that the most useful thing about the whole insolvency process.
Telling your staff

Redundancies happen on appointment, and what employees can claim from the Redundancy Payments Service is the same in any insolvent liquidation, so the detail sits on our company liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] page. What is particular to a CVL is that you control the timing, which means you can handle this conversation properly instead of your staff learning about it when the locks change.

Use that. Tell people before the appointment, not after. Have the practitioner's contact details and the claim reference process ready for them on the day, because the first thing anyone asks is how they get paid and when. Directors who manage this badly carry it for years afterwards, and it is one of the few parts of the process where acting early makes a human difference rather than merely a financial one.
One thing directors miss: if you are employed by your own company as well as being a director, you may be able to claim from the Redundancy Payments Service too.
What the directors actually have to do

Directors sometimes picture the liquidation process as something that simply happens to them once an insolvency practitioner is instructed. It is more involved than that, and knowing the obligations up front avoids the impression of reluctance that a conduct report will notice.
Hand over the books and records. All of them, including the accounting system logins, and promptly. Missing or disorganised records are the single most common conduct criticism of company directors

Produce an accurate picture of the assets and the debt. Every creditor named, every asset disclosed, including anything sold or transferred beforehand. The look-back is longer than most directors expect: in Scotland a gift or an undervalue transfer to a connected person can be unwound up to five years back, two years for anyone else, and a payment that favoured one creditor up to six months back

Explain the transactions the liquidator asks about. Payments to connected parties, unusual disposals, and any debt repaid to one creditor ahead of others will be looked at, and a straightforward explanation given early is worth a great deal

Stop trading, and stop using the company's assets. Company assets belong to the estate from the moment of appointment, and continuing to use a vehicle or equipment because it "was always mine in practice" causes real problems
Co-operate with the Insolvency Service if it follows up on the conduct report

None of this is onerous for an insolvent company that has been run honestly. It is only difficult where records are poor, which is why the state of your bookkeeping matters more to your personal position than most directors expect.
What it costs, and what if there is no money

Fees come out of the company's assets, so where there is something to realise a creditors' voluntary liquidation often costs the directors nothing personally. Creditors, the liquidation committee or the court approve those fees, and the practitioner should set out the work they anticipate and what it is expected to cost, and explain the basis on which they are charging, before that basis is approved. Scotland works differently from England here: the fees estimate rule English guides describe does not apply, and the amount is formally determined after each accounting period rather than fixed at the start.

The harder case is a company with no assets, where someone has to fund the work and directors are usually the ones asked. This is the point at which some decide to do nothing and let the company drift instead. That is almost always the worse choice. Left alone, the company is eventually wound up by the court through compulsory liquidation [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition]: a less orderly process, no say in who is appointed, and a conduct report written against a background of inaction rather than cooperation. The fee saved is rarely worth what the loss of control costs.
If funding is the obstacle, say so early. There are options, and they are worth hearing before you decide to walk away.
CVL compared with the alternatives
CVL or compulsory liquidation

Both end the company. The difference is control. In a creditors' voluntary liquidation you choose the timing, you nominate the insolvency practitioner, and the record shows you dealt with the position. In compulsory liquidation a creditor petitions the court, the court picks the interim liquidator, and everything happens on someone else's schedule. If a winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition] has already been served, the window for choosing is closing quickly.
CVL or CVA

A CVA [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] keeps the company alive and repays creditors over time. A CVL closes it. The only question that matters is whether there is a viable business underneath the debt. If there is, a CVA is worth exploring properly. If there is not, a CVA delays the inevitable while adding cost.
CVL or administration

Administration [link to /insolvency/administration] is protective. It creates a moratorium while a rescue, a sale or a better return is arranged, and it makes sense where the business or its assets are worth more sold as a going concern than broken up. Administration is also the route where a sale to a buyer is already in prospect, through a pre-pack administration. Where nothing can be rescued and there is no going concern to sell, a creditors' voluntary liquidation is the more direct answer for an insolvent company, and a cheaper one.
CVL or striking off

Directors sometimes ask whether they can simply apply to strike the company off instead. Where real debts exist, the answer is no in practice: a creditor who objects can block the application, and a company struck off while insolvent can be restored to the register afterwards so that a liquidator can look at it properly. You end up in the same place, later, having appeared to avoid it. Strike off suits a dormant company with nothing owed, which is not the situation this page describes.

Frequently asked questions
How long does a CVL take?

From instruction to the shareholders' resolution is typically two to three weeks. The liquidation itself usually runs six to twelve months, longer where there is property, a dispute or an investigation. Trading stops almost immediately, so the business ends at the start rather than the finish.
Who appoints the liquidator?

The directors nominate an insolvency practitioner and the creditors then have the opportunity to appoint someone else. In most cases creditors accept the nomination. That is one of the practical advantages of acting before a creditor forces a compulsory liquidation, where you have no say at all.
Will I be made personally liable for the company's debts?

Not simply because the company was liquidated. Limited liability holds. The exceptions are personal guarantees, an overdrawn director's loan account, and findings of wrongful or fraudulent trading. Establish which of those apply to you at the outset, because all three are foreseeable and none improves with time.
Can I buy the assets back and start again?

Yes, and it is lawful, but it must be at proper value and handled correctly by the insolvency practitioner, who has a duty to get the best price for creditors. This is what people mean by a phoenix company, and there is nothing inherently wrong with it. What makes it go wrong is Section 216: reuse the old name without falling inside one of the exceptions and you commit a criminal offence and can become personally liable for the new company's debts. Get the name question answered before you buy anything.
What if a winding up petition has already been served?

Then the timetable is no longer yours, and this needs attention today rather than this week. A creditors' voluntary liquidation may still be possible, but the window narrows once the petition is advertised. See winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition] for what happens and how quickly.
Does a CVL affect my credit rating?

The company's liquidation is a matter of public record, but it is the company's record, not yours. Your personal credit file is affected only where you have personal liability, most commonly through a guarantee that is then called in. That is another reason to establish your guarantee position early.
What is a Statement of Affairs?

A formal statement of everything the company owns and everything it owes, prepared by the directors, listing each creditor and the amount due. Creditors receive it, and the liquidator works from it. Accuracy matters. Omitting creditors, whether deliberately or carelessly, causes real problems later.
Can HMRC stop a CVL?

Not directly. HMRC cannot prevent the shareholders from resolving to wind the company up. What it can do is petition to have the company wound up by the court instead, and, as usually the largest creditor, have a decisive say in who is appointed liquidator. It may vote on the choice of liquidator and it will scrutinise the conduct of directors where tax debts are significant, particularly where PAYE or VAT went unpaid while other creditors were being paid.
