Members' Voluntary Liquidation (MVL)

Usually shortened to MVL, a members' voluntary liquidation is how a limited company that can pay everything it owes is closed formally. The company directors declare that the company is solvent, the shareholders vote to wind it up, and a licensed insolvency practitioner is brought in as liquidator to settle any remaining liabilities and distribute the company's assets to the shareholders. The reason for doing it this way rather than a simple strike-off is tax: the money comes out as capital rather than income, which for most owners means a considerably smaller bill.

It is the one liquidation on this site that is good news. No creditors are chasing, nothing is being rescued, and the process exists to finish something properly. That does not make it casual. An MVL is a real liquidation of a solvent company with a signed declaration behind it, and the mistakes people make with it are almost all made before it starts: declaring a position they have not checked, or running a full formal process for a sum that never needed one.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
Is an MVL actually worth it for you?

We do not take insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes your liquidator, so we earn nothing from recommending an MVL, and we will tell you when a strike-off does the job. That is the first question, so it comes first.

The figure everyone has heard is £25,000. It is real, but it is widely misunderstood. Under the Corporation Tax Act 2010, a company heading for strike-off can distribute up to £25,000 in total to its shareholders and have that treated as capital. Go a pound over and the whole distribution, not just the excess, is taxed as income. It is a cliff edge in the tax rules, not a break-even point for an MVL.
So the honest position is this:

Retained profits of £25,000 or less. A strike-off almost always does the job. The distribution is capital anyway, and paying for a formal liquidation would be money wasted. One condition: the company has to be dissolved within two years of the distribution and its debts settled, or HMRC can withdraw the capital treatment and tax the whole amount as income
Retained profits comfortably above £25,000. An MVL is usually worth it. The gap between capital gains tax and dividend tax on a six-figure distribution is normally many times the cost of the process

Somewhere near the line. Do the arithmetic properly with your accountant before deciding. The practitioner's fee, your other gains in the year, and whether you qualify for Business Asset Disposal Relief all move the answer
If you have been told you need an MVL and nobody has shown you that arithmetic, ask for it. It takes ten minutes and it is the whole decision.
Who uses an MVL, and why
The same few situations account for nearly all of them.
Retirement. The business has run its course, there is no buyer or no wish to sell, and the retained profits built up over the years need to come out
After a sale. The trade and assets have been sold, the limited company is a shell holding the proceeds, and the shareholders want the money distributed

Contractors and consultants. A personal service company is no longer needed, often because of a change in working arrangements or a move into employment, and it holds more cash than it is sensible to draw as dividends

Group tidy-ups. Dormant or redundant subsidiaries cost money and carry risk for as long as they exist. Closing them through solvent liquidations is the core of corporate simplification [link to /restructuring/corporate-simplification]

Part of a wider exit. Where a founder is planning their way out of a business over a period of years, the MVL is often the final step in a longer piece of exit planning [link to /restructuring/exit-planning]

What these have in common is that the company has done its job and its shareholders want a clean, final, defensible end to it. An MVL gives them that: a liquidator's final account, a dissolution at Companies House, and no loose ends for creditors or HMRC to pull on later.
The tax position, plainly

This is the reason most people choose a members' voluntary liquidation, so it is worth being exact about what it does and does not do. Your accountant will confirm your own numbers, and we work alongside them rather than instead of them.

Distributions paid out in a winding-up are treated as capital. You are taxed as if you had sold your shares for that amount, so capital gains tax applies rather than income tax on a dividend. For a higher-rate taxpayer that difference alone is substantial.

On top of that, many shareholders qualify for Business Asset Disposal Relief, which cuts the capital gains tax rate on the first £1 million of qualifying gains over a lifetime. The relief has become less generous than it was: the rate rose to 14% in April 2025 and to 18% from 6 April 2026. For a higher-rate shareholder it is still well below the rate on dividend income, though for a distribution small enough to stay inside the basic rate band it may not be, and without the relief the capital gains rate is 24%. Anyone working from the old figure of 10% is working from the wrong number. Qualifying depends on holding at least 5% of the ordinary shares and 5% of the votes, plus a 5% economic entitlement, which can be met either through profits and assets on a winding up or through the proceeds on a sale of the whole company, and on being an officer or employee throughout the two years before the company stops trading. The distributions also have to be made within three years of it ceasing to trade, which is a real trap where an MVL drags on, so check your own eligibility rather than assuming it.
There is one rule that catches people out, and it deserves its own paragraph.
The two-year rule

HMRC has a targeted anti-avoidance rule for exactly this situation. It applies where you held at least 5% of the company and the company was a close company, which covers almost every owner-managed business. If you take a capital distribution from a company in a winding-up and then, inside two years, you are back doing the same kind of work, or something close to it, through another company or as a sole trader, and saving tax was one of the main purposes of the arrangement, HMRC can tax those distributions as income after all. It is aimed at people who close a company, bank the money at capital rates, and start again on Monday.

If your plan genuinely is to retire, to take employment, or to do something different, the rule is not aimed at you. If your plan is to carry on the same business in a new company, say so before the MVL starts, because the tax saving you are counting on may not be there, and there may be a better way to do what you want.
How the MVL process runs
[IMAGE] "How the MVL process runs": numbered flow, vector, navy and teal.

The procedure is set by the Insolvency Act 1986 and, for a Scottish company, the Scottish winding-up rules. The steps are the same in every case. What varies is how much has to be done before the first one.

Get the company ready. Final accounts are prepared, the last corporation tax return is dealt with, and every creditor that can be paid is paid. Directors are usually advised to clear the company's debts before the winding-up starts rather than leaving them unpaid, because creditors are entitled to statutory interest on any debt still owed once it begins

Statutory declaration of solvency. The directors, or a majority of them where there are more than two, make a formal declaration that they have made a full enquiry into the company's affairs and that it will meet every debt in full, with interest, within a period they specify of no more than twelve months from the start of the winding-up. It carries a statement of what the company owns and what it owes, is made before a notary public or a justice of the peace, or in England and Wales a solicitor, and must be made no more than five weeks before the shareholders' resolution. It is the document the whole process rests on

Notice to any floating charge holder, then the resolution. Where the company has given a lender a floating charge that has never been discharged, written notice of the resolution goes to that lender first, and the resolution cannot be passed until five business days later unless the lender consents in writing. The shareholders then pass a special resolution to wind the company up and appoint the liquidator, either at a general meeting or by written resolution. A meeting needs at least fourteen days' notice unless members holding 90% of the voting rights agree to shorter notice; a written resolution avoids the notice period altogether and is how most MVLs are done. The winding-up resolution needs a 75% majority of those voting; the appointment itself needs only a simple majority. The declaration is delivered within 15 days of the resolution, to Companies House for a company registered in England and Wales and to the Accountant in Bankruptcy for one registered in Scotland, and notice of the resolution goes in the Gazette inside 14 days: the London Gazette for a company registered in England and Wales, the Edinburgh Gazette for one registered in Scotland

The practitioner takes over. From appointment, the company's affairs and assets are in the liquidator's hands. The directors' powers cease, though in practice the directors are relied on for information and records
Creditors are invited to claim. Notices invite claims and any liabilities still outstanding are settled. In a well-prepared MVL there is little or nothing left at this stage

Distributions to shareholders. Distributions of cash are usually made in stages. A first payment is often made a few weeks after appointment, with the balance held back until it is clear nothing else is coming in. Distributions go to shareholders according to their rights, which means in proportion to their holdings where there is a single class of shares
HMRC clearance. Confirmation is obtained from HMRC that there is no further tax to pay. This is the step that governs how long the whole thing takes

Final account and dissolution. A final account of the winding-up is prepared and sent to the shareholders and to Companies House, and the dissolution of the company follows three months after it is registered
There is very little for you to do once the appointment is made, provided the preparation was done properly. The work is front-loaded, which is exactly why the preparation matters.
Distributing assets that are not cash

Asset distribution does not have to mean selling everything first. An asset can be handed over as it stands, which is called a distribution in specie, and it is useful more often than people expect. A property, a vehicle, an investment, or a debt owed to the company can all be transferred to a shareholder as part of their entitlement, asset by asset, which saves the cost and delay of a sale and keeps the asset where the owner wants it.

The most common use is a director's loan account. Where a director owes the company money, that debt can be distributed to the director, which cancels it against what the director was due to receive. That is lawful and routine. What it is not is a way of making an overdrawn loan account disappear for tax purposes, and it needs to be handled by the liquidator and your accountant together rather than assumed.
How long it takes, and what slows it down

A straightforward MVL, a company with cash at bank and nothing else, can see most of the money distributed within a few weeks of appointment. The formal end of the process, the final account and dissolution, usually takes longer, and six to twelve months from start to finish is a realistic expectation for most companies.
The things that stretch it are predictable:
Tax clearance. The liquidator will not close the liquidation until HMRC confirms there is nothing further to pay, and HMRC's response times are outside anyone's control
Any asset other than cash. Property has to be sold or transferred to a shareholder, debtors collected, investments realised

Unresolved liabilities. A lease not yet surrendered, a contingent claim, a warranty given on the sale of the trade. Each is a debt or a risk that has to be dealt with or provided for before everything can be distributed
An overdrawn director's loan account that nobody planned for
None of these stops an MVL. All of them are faster to resolve before the declaration of solvency is made than afterwards.
What it costs

The liquidator's fee is agreed at the outset and paid from the company's assets, together with the disbursements of the process: the statutory advertisements, the bond, or caution in Scotland (every appointed insolvency practitioner must be covered by a surety or cautioner against loss caused by their own fraud or dishonesty), and similar costs. For a straightforward solvent company most practitioners quote a fixed fee plus disbursements, and you should expect to be told the figure before you commit to anything.

We do not set that fee and we will not quote a number here that turns out to be wrong for your company. What we will do is tell you what the practitioner we introduce charges before you meet them and, more usefully, show you whether the tax saving clears it by a wide enough margin to make the whole exercise worthwhile.
What if the company is not as solvent as you think?
This is the risk in an MVL, and it is worth taking seriously precisely because the process feels benign.

The declaration of solvency is a statutory declaration. Making it without reasonable grounds for believing the company can meet its debts in full within the stated period is a criminal offence. And if the debts are not in fact paid or provided for within that period, the law presumes the directors did not have reasonable grounds unless they can show otherwise. So "I thought it was fine" is not a comfortable place to be standing.

If the liquidator forms the view that the company will not be able to pay its debts in full within the stated period, the process does not stop. It converts into a creditors' voluntary liquidation, the creditors come in, and the directors' conduct is reported on, as it is in any insolvent winding-up. What began as a tidy closure becomes something else entirely.

The practical protection is simple: before anyone signs anything, be certain. HMRC is always one of the creditors until it confirms otherwise. Corporation tax on the final period, VAT on the final return, PAYE, a director's loan account that has been running the wrong way, a lease, a guarantee given to a customer, a dispute that might turn into a claim. Each of those is a debt until it is settled. If there is any doubt about whether the company is solvent, that is a different conversation, and our company liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] page sets out how the solvent and insolvent routes part company.
MVL compared with the alternatives
[IMAGE] "MVL compared with the alternatives": four cards, no icons needed.
MVL or strike-off

Both end the company. Strike-off is cheaper and simpler, and for small retained profits it is the right answer. Its limits are the £25,000 cap on capital treatment, the fact that any creditor can object, which in practice suspends the striking-off while Companies House considers it, and a strike-off that stalls past two years costs you the capital treatment, and the lack of any formal line drawn under the company's affairs. An MVL costs more and takes longer, and in return gives capital treatment on all distributions, a formal final account, and a clean dissolution.
MVL or CVL

The difference between an MVL and a creditors' voluntary liquidation is solvency. A CVL [link to /insolvency/creditors-voluntary-liquidation-cvl] is for an insolvent company; an MVL is for one that can pay every debt. They are not alternatives you choose between. The company's balance sheet chooses for you, and getting that wrong in either direction is expensive.
MVL or carrying on

Some shareholders keep a company open purely to draw the retained profits as dividends over several years, staying under the higher thresholds. That is legitimate, but it costs accountancy fees and filing obligations for every year it runs, and it only works if you do not need the money sooner. Compare the two on your own numbers rather than by instinct.
MVL or administration

Rarely confused, but worth stating: Company administration [link to /insolvency/administration] is a protective procedure for a company in difficulty. If the business is solvent and simply finished, administration has nothing to offer and an MVL is the right route.
[LINK] Liquidation · CVL · Corporate simplification · Exit planning
MVLs in Scotland

The Insolvency Act 1986 applies across Great Britain, so the declaration of solvency, the 12-month test and the shareholders' resolution are the same for a Scottish company as for an English one. The procedural rules differ. A company registered in Scotland follows the Scottish winding-up rules rather than the England and Wales rules, the notices go in the Edinburgh Gazette, and some filings go somewhere different: the declaration of solvency and the liquidator's notice of appointment are delivered to the Accountant in Bankruptcy rather than Companies House, and the final account goes to both.
None of that changes the decision, but it does mean the practitioner you use should handle Scottish liquidations as a matter of routine rather than occasionally. Ours do; Glasgow is where we work.
Where we fit
Lancefield does not take appointments. Nobody here becomes your liquidator, so we have no financial interest in whether your company goes through an MVL, a strike-off, or nothing at all.

What we do is look at the position honestly first: whether the company really is solvent, whether the sum justifies a formal process, and whether the two-year rule or a wider plan for the group or your own exit changes the answer. Where an MVL is right, we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] we know and trust, and we stay alongside you and your accountant until the dissolution is registered. Where it is part of something bigger, a group restructuring or a founder leaving, it sits inside our restructuring work [link to /restructuring] rather than standing alone.
That independence is why accountants send their clients to us for this, and why they come back.
Frequently asked questions
What is a members' voluntary liquidation?

A formal procedure for closing a solvent company. The directors make a statutory declaration that every debt will be paid in full within a stated period of up to twelve months, the shareholders resolve to wind it up, and a licensed insolvency practitioner is appointed to settle the liabilities and make distributions of the remaining assets to the shareholders as capital. It ends with the company's dissolution.
How long does an MVL take?

The first cash distribution often arrives within a few weeks of the appointment. The whole liquidation process, through to the final account and dissolution, usually takes six to twelve months, with HMRC clearance the step that sets the pace. Companies holding property or other assets take longer.
How much does an MVL cost?

Most practitioners quote a fixed fee for a straightforward solvent company, plus disbursements such as the statutory notices and the bond, or caution in Scotland, and it is paid from the company's funds. We do not publish a figure because we do not set it, but you will know it before you commit, and we will show you whether the tax saving justifies it.
Do I need an insolvency practitioner for an MVL?

Yes. Only a licensed insolvency practitioner can act as liquidator, in a solvent liquidation as in an insolvent one. A strike-off does not need one, which is part of why it is cheaper and part of why it is limited.
Can I start a new company after an MVL?

You can. The restriction on re-using the old company's name applies to insolvent liquidations, not solvent ones. The thing to watch is the tax rule: carry on the same or a similar business within two years of the distribution and HMRC can treat it as income if saving tax was a main purpose of the arrangement. Plan for that before the liquidation, not after.
What happens if creditors turn up after the distributions?

A properly run MVL advertises for claims and provides for every known liability before distributing, so genuine surprises are rare. Where one does arise, it is dealt with from any funds still held. It is one reason the final balance is usually kept back from shareholders until the practitioner is satisfied, and one reason the preparation before the declaration matters so much.
Can shareholders be paid a first instalment quickly?

Usually. Where the company's assets are cash and the liabilities are clear, a substantial first distribution is often made within a few weeks of appointment, with the balance following once HMRC has confirmed the position. Ask the practitioner for a realistic timetable for your company rather than a general one.
Is it worth it if my retained profits are under £25,000?

Almost never. Up to £25,000 in total, a distribution before strike-off is treated as capital anyway, so there is nothing to gain from a formal liquidation over a strike-off, and a fee to lose, provided the company is actually dissolved within two years of the distribution and its debts are settled. Miss that and HMRC taxes the whole distribution as income after all. Above that, the whole distribution is income unless you use an MVL, which is the point at which it starts to pay for itself.
Closing call to action
Is an MVL the right way to close your company?
We take no appointments, so we have no stake in the answer. One conversation will tell you whether it is worth it, what it will cost, and what needs doing before anyone signs anything.

/insolvency/winding-up-petition
Winding up petitions and compulsory liquidation
[IMAGE - Hero] none. This page must load fast and answer immediately. No decorative imagery above the fold.

Compulsory liquidation is the closure of a company by court order, following a petition from someone the company owes money to. It is the one insolvency procedure that is done to a company rather than chosen by it.

If a winding-up petition has been presented against your company, time is now the thing that matters most. The window in which you can still influence the outcome is short, and it effectively closes once the petition is advertised.

A winding up petition is most often presented by HMRC over unpaid VAT, PAYE or Corporation Tax, and by trade creditors and landlords over unpaid invoices and rent. Whether you see it written as a winding up petition or a winding-up petition, it means the same thing.
[BUTTON] Get urgent confidential advice
If you have just been served, read this first
[IMAGE - "If you have just been served" cards] three restrained teal line icons (frozen account, reversed arrow, calendar). Vector only.
Three things are true immediately, and knowing them changes what you do today.
Your bank account will probably be frozen

Once the petition is advertised in the Gazette, banks routinely freeze company accounts. Any payment made after the petition is presented can later be void, so banks protect themselves by stopping everything. Wages, suppliers and rent all stop with it.
Payments you make now can be reversed

Disposals of company property after the presentation of a petition can be set aside unless the court validates them. Paying a favoured creditor at this point can create a personal problem for you later, not just a company one.
Advertisement is the point of no return

In Scotland the court grants a first order that directs intimation, service and advertisement of the petition together, so there is no fixed waiting period between being served and the petition appearing in public. This is one of the places where English guidance will actively mislead you: south of the border there is a set gap, and here there is not. Whatever time you have is a matter of how quickly the order is granted and acted on, which is precisely why the day you are served is the day to take advice. Once the petition is advertised the account freezes, other creditors can support it, and stopping it becomes much harder.

So the single most useful thing you can do is take advice before advertisement, not after. A winding up petition dealt with in week one has options that the same winding up petition does not have in week four.

It is worth being clear about what a winding-up petition actually is, because the language around it is used loosely. It is not a demand and it is not a warning. It is a court action asking the court to end the company's existence and hand its assets to a liquidator to distribute among the creditors. The petitioning creditor is not seeking payment at that point, it is seeking the company's closure, and any payment it receives comes out of that process rather than instead of it. Directors who read a petition as a stronger version of a debt letter tend to respond too slowly, which is the most common and most expensive mistake we see.
How the process runs
[IMAGE - Process section] consider a simple horizontal step diagram in navy and teal showing statutory demand to winding up order. Vector, built from the brand geometry, not a stock graphic.
The chain is fairly predictable, which is what makes early intervention possible.

Statutory demand. A creditor owed more than £750 serves a formal demand. The company then has three weeks to pay, or to secure or compound the debt if the creditor will accept that. Let that pass without paying and the company is deemed unable to pay its debts under section 123 of the Insolvency Act 1986, which is what opens the door to a petition. A creditor does not have to start here, though. In Scotland, letting the days of charge run out on a charge for payment following a decree has the same effect, and a creditor who can simply satisfy the court that the company cannot pay its debts can petition without serving any demand at all, which is why a petition sometimes arrives with no warning shot
Petition presented. If the demand is unmet, the creditor presents a petition to the court to wind up the company, paying the court dues. HMRC is the most common petitioning creditor
Service. Notice of the petition is served at the registered office

Advertisement. For a Scottish company the petition is advertised in the Edinburgh Gazette, and in whatever newspaper the court specifies. Banks act on this. Other creditors can now join as supporting creditors
Petition hearing. The court hears the petition. The company can oppose it, seek an adjournment, or offer terms. Many companies instruct solicitors at this stage
Winding-up order. If the court makes the order, the company is wound up compulsorily. Directors' powers cease immediately

Interim liquidator. In Scotland the court appoints an interim liquidator at the moment it makes the order, and only a licensed insolvency practitioner can take that office. The creditors can choose a different liquidator afterwards

The liquidator then realises assets, agrees creditor claims, distributes any funds in the statutory order of priority under the Insolvency Act 1986, and reports on the conduct of each director. The company is eventually dissolved and removed from the register at Companies House.
How this differs in Scotland

Almost every guide to winding-up petitions online describes the procedure for England and Wales, referring to the High Court and the Companies Court, and to the Insolvency (England and Wales) Rules 2016. That is not how it works here.

In Scotland, a winding-up petition is presented to the Court of Session in Edinburgh, or, where the company's paid-up share capital is £120,000 or less, to the Sheriff Court for the sheriffdom in which its registered office sits. Procedure, terminology and timetables follow Scottish court practice, and notices appear in the Edinburgh Gazette. Enforcement in Scotland is called diligence, not execution, and covers steps such as arrestment and attachment rather than the England and Wales equivalents.

The underlying insolvency legislation is largely common across Great Britain, but the court route, the local practice and the practical timetable are not. If you are being advised by someone working from English precedent, they are working from the wrong map.
What you can still do about it
The options narrow as the process advances, which is exactly why the timing matters.
Pay, or agree terms

If the debt is genuinely owed and the money can be found, paying it or agreeing terms with the petitioning creditor is the cleanest answer. The petitioner can then withdraw or consent to dismissal. Bear in mind that other creditors may have already joined by then.
Dispute the debt

A winding up petition is not a debt recovery tool for disputed debts, and the courts take a dim view of it being used as one. If the debt is genuinely and substantially disputed on real grounds, that is a strong basis to have the petition dismissed, and potentially to recover costs. What matters is that the dispute is real and evidenced: a genuine dispute about whether the work was done, or about what was agreed, is a defence, whereas simply not having the money is not.
Propose a CVA

If the business is viable underneath the debt, a company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] can deal with the whole creditor body rather than just the petitioner. This needs to start early, because building a proposal takes time the petition timetable may not allow.
Enter administration

Administration [link to /insolvency/administration] brings a statutory moratorium that stops creditor action, including the petition, where a rescue or a better outcome for creditors than winding up is realistically achievable. One timing point matters: once a petition has been presented, the quick out-of-court appointment route closes, and administration has to be applied for at court. Where a sale is lined up in advance, that becomes a pre-pack administration.
Choose a CVL instead

Where the company cannot be saved, a directors' own creditors' voluntary liquidation is generally a better outcome than waiting for a compulsory order. A creditors' voluntary liquidation is more orderly, you have some choice over the insolvency practitioner appointed, and conduct handled proactively tends to be viewed more favourably. Once a winding-up petition has been advertised, that choice starts to disappear.
[LINK] Company voluntary arrangement · Administration · Creditors' voluntary liquidation · Liquidation
When the petitioner is HMRC

A large share of winding up petitions in Scotland are presented by HMRC, and a petition from HMRC behaves differently from one brought by a trade creditor. HMRC will usually have written several times before it gets to this, so by the time a winding-up petition lands there is rarely any surprise about the debt itself.

Two things follow from that. HMRC is generally willing to discuss a Time to Pay arrangement, but its appetite falls away sharply once a petition has been presented, and further once it has been advertised. And because HMRC is frequently the largest single unsecured creditor, its position tends to decide whether any rescue proposal succeeds. A CVA [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] that HMRC will not support is not a realistic plan, whatever the other creditors think of it.

If your debts are largely tax debts, the practical route is usually to engage before the petition, not after. That is advisory work, and it does not need an insolvency practitioner appointment to start.
What it costs

A creditor pays court dues to present a winding-up petition, and in practice has to find an insolvency practitioner willing to act as interim liquidator, which is part of why petitions tend to arrive only after other attempts to recover the debt have failed. The deposit English guidance quotes is security for the Official Receiver's fee and does not apply in Scotland. If the order is granted, those costs usually rank as an expense of the liquidation and are paid from whatever the company's assets realise.

For the company, the costs that matter are rarely the court's. Once the petition is advertised the bank account freezes, trading effectively stops, and the value of the business falls quickly. That is the real cost of waiting, and it is why acting in the first days is worth more than any argument you might make later. Directors sometimes ask whether it is cheaper to let the compulsory liquidation run than to fund a CVL [link to /insolvency/creditors-voluntary-liquidation-cvl]. Occasionally it is. More often the loss of control costs considerably more than the fee saved.
What it means for directors
A compulsory winding up brings a mandatory report on the conduct of every director, made by the liquidator to the Secretary of State through the Insolvency Service.

Disqualification. Where a company is wound up by the court and a director is found unfit to be involved in running a company, the court must disqualify them for between two and fifteen years. Many cases are settled by an undertaking given to the Secretary of State rather than at a hearing
Wrongful trading exposure arises where trading continued past the point at which there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvency, and personal contribution can be ordered
Personal guarantees are unaffected by the liquidation and remain enforceable against you personally
Overdrawn director's loan accounts will be pursued by the liquidator as an asset of the company
Reuse of the company name is restricted, with criminal and personal liability consequences for getting it wrong
None of this is meant to alarm. Ordinary business failure, honestly handled and dealt with early, rarely produces these outcomes. Ignoring a petition for six weeks is what produces them.
If you are the creditor

For completeness, because some readers arrive from the other side. A winding-up petition is a powerful remedy, and a blunt one. Your petition requires court dues up front and, in practice, an insolvency practitioner prepared to act as interim liquidator, and it is appropriate where a debt is undisputed, substantial and unpaid, and where you are content for the company to be closed and to share whatever is realised with all other unsecured creditors.

It is not a good tool for a disputed debt, and using it that way can result in the petition being dismissed with a court order for costs against you. Most creditors instruct solicitors before issuing. Winding-up petitions also frequently produce a lower recovery than a negotiated settlement, because unsecured creditors typically receive very little in a compulsory liquidation, and the reputation damage to a customer you might otherwise trade with again is permanent. Take advice on whether it is really the best route to your money.
Where we fit

The liquidator in a Scottish compulsory liquidation is the interim liquidator the court appoints when it makes the order, or whoever the creditors choose in their place. Either way it is a licensed insolvency practitioner, and Lancefield takes neither role.

What we do is look at your position fast, tell you honestly whether the petition can realistically be stopped, and set out what each remaining route actually leads to. Because we are not appointed and do not benefit from any particular outcome, that assessment is not shaped by what pays us. Where a formal appointment is needed, we bring in a licensed practitioner we know and trust, and stay alongside you through it.
Frequently asked questions
How long do I have?

Usually a matter of weeks between service and the court hearing, but the practical deadline is much sooner. Advertisement is when your bank account is likely to freeze and the situation becomes far harder to influence, and in Scotland the court orders service and advertisement together rather than leaving a set gap between them. Treat the day you are served as the deadline, because there is no guaranteed grace period after it.
Can a winding-up petition be stopped?

Yes, in several ways: paying or settling the debt, having it dismissed where the debt is genuinely disputed, or obtaining a moratorium through administration. Each becomes materially harder after advertisement, which is why the first days matter so much. Winding-up petitions are stopped far more often when advice is taken in the first week than in the last.
What is a statutory demand?

A formal written notice demanding payment of an undisputed debt of more than £750. The company has three weeks to respond. It is often the step immediately before a petition, and it is a clear warning that should be acted on rather than filed away. Do not count on getting one: a creditor holding a decree can go straight to a charge for payment, and HMRC often petitions without a demand at all. One caution worth knowing: the procedure for setting a demand aside is an English one. In Scotland a company that disputes the debt challenges the petition itself, so if you believe the debt is wrong, say so early and in writing.
Does a winding-up petition damage our reputation?

Yes. Advertisement in the Gazette is public, credit agencies pick it up, and suppliers and customers often hear quickly. Reputation damage is one of the strongest practical arguments for dealing with the debt before it reaches petition stage.
Will my bank account be frozen?
Very probably, once the petition is advertised. Banks freeze accounts because payments made after presentation of a petition can later be void. Plan for it happening rather than hoping it will not.
Who becomes liquidator when the order is made?

In Scotland the court appoints an interim liquidator at the moment it makes the winding up order, and that person must be a licensed insolvency practitioner. They secure the assets, deal with the employees and report on the conduct of the directors, and the creditors can choose a different liquidator afterwards. There is no Official Receiver in Scotland. That is an England and Wales office, which is why guidance written for England describes a process that will not happen to a Scottish company.
Is compulsory liquidation worse than a CVL for directors?

Generally yes. Both involve an investigation into conduct, but a creditors' voluntary liquidation is a decision taken by the directors, is more orderly, and shows the company dealt with the position rather than waiting to be forced. Where closure is inevitable, choosing it is usually better than having it imposed.
Which court deals with this in Scotland?

The Court of Session in Edinburgh, or, where paid-up share capital is £120,000 or less, the Sheriff Court for the sheriffdom covering the company's registered office. It is not the High Court or the Companies Court, which is what most online guides describe, because those are English courts. What decides it is where the company is registered rather than where it trades, so a Scottish-registered company is dealt with in Scotland even if all of its work is south of the border.
Can a winding up petition be withdrawn?

It can, but not unilaterally by you. The petitioning creditor can withdraw or consent to dismissal, usually where the debt has been paid or terms agreed. The complication is that once a winding up petition has been advertised, other creditors can appear at the hearing and take it over, so settling with the original petitioner no longer ends it. That is the practical reason for moving before advertisement rather than after.
What happens at the court hearing?

At the hearing the court either makes the winding up order or it does not. It will hear the petitioning creditor, the company if it appears, and any supporting or opposing creditors. Where the debt is genuinely disputed, or where the company can show a realistic alternative such as a CVA [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] in progress, the court may dismiss the petition or continue the hearing to allow it. Turning up without representation and without a plan rarely helps, and this is the point at which insolvency solicitors earn their fee.
Can I be disqualified as a director because of this?

Director disqualification does not follow automatically from a compulsory liquidation. The liquidator reports on the conduct of each director, and disqualification follows only where that conduct is found to make someone unfit. Where a company is wound up by the court and a director is found unfit, the disqualification period runs from two to fifteen years. Ordinary business failure, honestly handled and properly documented, is not what this is aimed at.
Can I start a new company afterwards?

Usually yes, unless you have been disqualified. The trap is the restriction on reusing the failed company's name, which is strict and carries personal liability if breached. It catches directors who assume the goodwill in a trading name is theirs to carry across. Take advice before registering anything that resembles the old name.

/insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva
Company Voluntary Arrangement (CVA)
[IMAGE - Hero] none, or the on-brand vector panel.

A company voluntary arrangement is a legally binding deal between an insolvent company and its creditors. The company keeps trading, and instead of paying its historic debt in full, it pays an affordable amount over an agreed period, usually from future profits. Whatever remains unpaid at the end is written off.

CVAs are the main rescue procedure in which the directors stay in control of a limited company that is insolvent but still has a viable business underneath the debt. Directors stay in control throughout, which is the feature that distinguishes CVAs from almost every other formal insolvency procedure. Retailers and hospitality groups have used CVAs to renegotiate rents across a portfolio, but they are just as available to a single owner-managed company.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
How a CVA works
The mechanics matter, because the whole thing turns on one vote.
The directors work with a licensed insolvency practitioner, acting as nominee, to build a proposal setting out what the company can realistically afford to pay and over what period
The nominee reviews it and reports to the court on whether it is viable and worth putting to creditors

Creditors vote through a decision procedure, usually by correspondence or electronic voting rather than at a meeting. The proposal is approved if 75% or more by value of those who respond vote in favour, and exactly 75% is enough. A physical meeting is only held if creditors requisition one

Clearing 75% is not the whole test. A second count is taken of the unconnected creditors only, and if creditors holding more than half of the total admitted unconnected value vote it down, the proposal falls anyway. That count is against all admitted unconnected claims, not only the ones that voted. Unconnected means creditors who are not connected with the company, so money owed to directors, their families or associated companies is stripped out. The purpose is to stop a company approving its own rescue on the strength of debt it owes to itself, and in a small company carrying large director loans this is frequently the test that decides the outcome
Voting is on unsecured debt. The claim of a fully secured creditor counts as nil, and a partly secured claim counts only for the unsecured part

Approval binds every creditor who was entitled to vote, or who would have been entitled had they been given notice, not merely the ones who backed it. A creditor who opposed the proposal, or who ignored the vote entirely, is caught by it just the same. Secured and preferential creditors are bound only on terms that leave their security and their priority intact, unless they agree otherwise
The practitioner becomes supervisor, monitoring the payments and reporting to creditors
The company trades on, pays as agreed, and the balance of the debt is written off at the end

A CVA typically runs for three to five years. Proposals normally provide that interest and charges on the arrangement debts stop, and a creditor bound by the arrangement has no claim to pursue for the compromised debt while the company complies with it, so legal action to recover that debt cannot continue. There is no automatic court moratorium: the protection comes from the terms of the arrangement itself.
Who has to agree, and why HMRC usually decides
In most small and mid-sized company CVAs, HMRC is the largest single creditor, because the debt has built up as unpaid VAT and PAYE. That means HMRC's vote frequently determines the outcome.

There is a further point that changes what a proposal can offer. HMRC has held secondary preferential status since 1 December 2020 for the taxes a company collects on someone else's behalf: VAT, PAYE, employee National Insurance and CIS deductions. Those debts cannot be written down or ranked behind ordinary unsecured creditors without HMRC's agreement, so in a company whose arrears are mostly VAT and PAYE the arrangement is usually structured to pay that element in full over time. Corporation tax and employer's National Insurance remain ordinary unsecured debts and can be compromised in the usual way.

HMRC has a published approach to CVAs and will engage with proposals that are realistic, properly evidenced and honest about what went wrong. It reacts badly to optimistic forecasting and to proposals from directors who have ignored correspondence for a year. This is one of the clearest reasons why acting earlier produces better outcomes than acting later.
A secured creditor sits outside the arrangement unless it agrees to be bound, so a bank with a fixed charge keeps its security. Employees have preferential status for certain claims.
When a CVA is the right answer
[IMAGE - "Right answer" cards] two teal line icons (tick, cross) kept restrained.
It suits you if

The business is profitable, or would be without the historic debt. There is enough cash flow to fund meaningful contributions. The cause of the problem has been identified and fixed, whether that was a bad contract, a failed expansion or a single large loss. And you want to preserve the company, its contracts, its licences and its people.
It does not suit you if

The business loses money at an operating level. The forecasts only work if trading improves substantially. The debt is so large that any affordable contribution would look derisory to creditors. Or you would rather stop than commit to another three to five years.

We will tell you honestly which of these describes your company. If a CVA would only delay a liquidation by two years and cost you more in the meantime, that is worth knowing before you start rather than after.
The honest disadvantages
Pages selling CVAs tend to be light on this section. It deserves proper treatment, because CVAs are demanding and not every company should attempt one.
CVAs are a formal insolvency procedure, publicly recorded, and they affect the company's credit rating and its standing with suppliers and other stakeholders
Some suppliers will move to pro forma terms, and some contracts contain clauses triggered by an insolvency event
It is demanding. Three to five years of committed payments while running a business is not a soft option
If the company defaults, the supervisor can petition to wind it up, and you may end up in liquidation having spent the intervening period paying
Not all CVAs succeed. A meaningful proportion fail, usually because the original forecasts were too optimistic
Personal guarantees are unaffected. A guarantee you have signed remains enforceable against you personally
CVA compared with the alternatives
CVA or administration

Administration [link to /insolvency/administration] gives immediate protection from creditors through a moratorium and puts an administrator in control. It suits a business that needs breathing space right now, or one being prepared for sale, which is where a pre-pack administration comes in. A company voluntary arrangement gives no automatic moratorium in the same way, but directors stay in charge. Sometimes the two insolvency procedures combine, with administration used to stabilise and a CVA to exit.
CVA or liquidation

Liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] closes the company. A CVA keeps it alive. The test is simply whether there is a viable business worth keeping. If there is not, a CVA delays the inevitable at cost, and a CVL [link to /insolvency/creditors-voluntary-liquidation-cvl] deals with it honestly instead.
CVA or informal arrangement

If only one or two creditors are the problem, a negotiated arrangement or debt restructuring [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring] may achieve the same thing without any formal insolvency procedure at all. Where the debt is spread across many unsecured creditors, the binding effect of a CVA is exactly what makes it work. A turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] review will usually tell you which of the two you are actually looking at.
CVA or winding up petition

If a creditor has already presented a winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition], the timetable changes completely. A CVA proposal takes weeks to build and the petition may not wait. It can still be the right answer, but it has to start immediately rather than after the hearing.
[LINK] Administration · Liquidation · Debt restructuring · Winding up petition
What a CVA does not do
Three limits are worth stating plainly, because proposals sometimes get built on assumptions that do not hold.

It does not override security or priority. A bank with a fixed charge, or any other secured creditor, keeps its right to enforce that security unless it agrees otherwise, and a preferential creditor keeps its priority. Only the ordinary unsecured debt can be compromised. That distinction shapes the whole proposal: if most of the debt sits with a secured creditor, a CVA may not reach the part of the problem that actually matters, and a different insolvency procedure will serve you better.

It does not remove personal guarantees. If you have guaranteed company borrowing, the guarantee survives the arrangement, and the lender can still pursue you personally even while the company keeps paying. Directors are regularly caught by this, and where it applies the personal position needs its own answer alongside the company one.

It does not fix a business that does not work. A company voluntary arrangement reschedules debt; it does not create cash flow. If the underlying trading position is loss-making, the arrangement will fail at the first missed payment, and the company will be in a worse position than if it had dealt with matters directly.
How the payments actually work

Most CVAs run on monthly payments out of trading profit, set at a level the business can genuinely sustain rather than the maximum it could manage in a good month. The figure is built from a cash flow forecast, and the forecast is the part creditors scrutinise hardest, because an over-optimistic one is the most common reason arrangements fail. A forecast is only as reliable as the financial reporting systems behind it, so getting monthly management figures in order is part of preparing a credible proposal.

Some proposals also bring in a lump sum, from selling assets the business does not need, or from a third party such as a director or an investor. Where a company has assets that are not central to trading, realising them early tends to make the proposal considerably more attractive to unsecured creditors than a longer schedule of monthly payments would.

If circumstances change, the supervisor can put a variation to creditors. That is worth knowing, because directors often assume the terms are fixed for the full term and stop communicating when trading dips. Missed payments without explanation are what lead to a failed arrangement; a variation proposed early usually does not.
What it costs

There are two elements: the nominee's fee for preparing and reporting on the proposal, and the supervisor's fees for running the arrangement, which are normally drawn from the contributions rather than paid separately. Fees have to be disclosed and approved by creditors, so the arrangement should be transparent about what the practitioner takes.

The relevant comparison is not the fee in isolation. It is what creditors would receive in a liquidation instead, which is usually very little, against what they receive under the arrangement. A proposal that beats the liquidation comparison is the one that passes.
Where we fit

CVAs require a licensed insolvency practitioner to act as nominee and then supervisor, and some firms use a turnaround practitioner alongside them to drive the operational changes. Lancefield does not take those appointments.

What we do is tell you whether a CVA is realistic before you spend money finding out, stress-test the numbers the proposal will stand or fall on, along with the financial reporting systems that produce them, and be straight about whether the business underneath the debt is genuinely viable. Because we are not appointed as supervisor, we do not benefit from you entering an insolvency procedure of any kind. Where a CVA is the right answer, we bring in a licensed practitioner we know and trust and stay alongside you through it.
If a winding-up petition has already been presented, the timetable changes completely and a CVA may no longer be achievable in time. That is worth establishing on day one.
Frequently asked questions
Is a CVA the same as liquidation?

No. Both are insolvency procedures available to an insolvent company, but they are opposites in intent. Liquidation closes the company and distributes what can be realised. A CVA keeps the company trading and repays creditors over time from future income. A CVA only makes sense where there is a business worth saving.
How long does a CVA last?
Usually three to five years. Shorter CVAs exist where a lump sum is introduced, for example from an asset sale or an injection from a third party.
What happens if creditors reject the proposal?

Nothing automatically. The company is not forced into another insolvency procedure by a failed vote, though the company remains insolvent and creditors are free to act, including by serving a statutory demand or presenting a winding up petition. Often a rejected proposal can be revised and put again if the objection was specific. Sometimes rejection is the signal that liquidation or administration is the honest answer.
Can a CVA stop a winding up petition?

Not by itself. A winding up petition follows the court's timetable, and a CVA proposal takes time to build and put to creditors. Where a petition has been presented, a moratorium is usually the tool that buys time. That can be an administration moratorium, or a standalone moratorium under Part A1 of the Insolvency Act 1986, which a company subject to an outstanding petition can apply to the court for and which is designed to lead into a rescue such as a CVA. This is why a CVA works best started before a petition, not after.
Can HMRC block a CVA?

Because approval needs 75% by value of those who respond, any creditor holding more than a quarter of the value voted can block it on their own. HMRC is frequently in exactly that position in a small company CVA, which is why proposals need to be built to withstand its scrutiny from the outset rather than hoping to win the vote without it.
Do directors keep control?

Yes, and this is the main attraction. Directors continue to run the business, subject to the terms of the arrangement and the supervisor's monitoring. Contrast that with administration or liquidation, where control passes to the appointed practitioner.
Does a CVA affect my personal guarantees?

No. A guarantee is a personal contract between you and the creditor, and it survives the arrangement. A creditor can pursue you personally on the guarantee even while the company complies. This needs to be understood before you commit, not afterwards.
Will suppliers and customers find out?

Yes. A CVA is registered at Companies House and creditors are notified as part of the process. Most businesses handle this by getting ahead of it and explaining the plan to key stakeholders, which lands better than letting people discover it.
Closing call to action
Is there a viable business under the debt?
That is the only question that decides whether a CVA is worth pursuing, and we will answer it honestly. Free, confidential, and it commits you to nothing.

/insolvency/administration
Company administration

In company administration a licensed insolvency practitioner takes control of a company as its administrator, under a formal insolvency procedure, and runs it, sells it or winds it down under the protection of a statutory moratorium that stops creditor action while they do. It exists to produce a better outcome than an immediate winding up: sometimes by rescuing the company itself, more often by selling the business as a going concern or realising its assets in a more orderly way.

Going into administration is not the same as going bust, but it is not the rescue that directors hope for either. The directors hand over control, the debts remain, and most administrations end with the business sold, often through a pre-pack administration, and the old company going into liquidation. Understanding that before you start is what separates directors who use the procedure well from those who are surprised by it.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
Is company administration the right answer for you?

This firm takes no insolvency appointments, so nobody here stands to be appointed over your company and we earn nothing by recommending the procedure. It means we can tell you when a cheaper or simpler route does the job, which is why the question leads.
It suits you if

There is a viable business inside the insolvent company, and it needs protection from creditor action while a sale, a restructuring or a repayment proposal is put together. The assets are worth more kept together as a going concern, goodwill included, than sold piecemeal. A creditor is about to petition, a landlord is about to irritate the lease, or a lender is about to enforce, and a short breathing space would change the outcome. And there is funding, from the business, a buyer or a lender, to pay for it.
It does not suit you if

The trade has stopped working and there is nothing to sell, in which case a creditors' voluntary liquidation reaches the same end at a fraction of the cost. The creditors would agree a company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] without any need for protection, which keeps you in control and the business intact. Or there is no money to fund it: administration is expensive, and a business with no assets and no buyer cannot pay for it.

It is a tool for protecting value while something is done with it. If nothing is going to be done, the protection is pointless and the cost is real. A turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] review before any appointment is the cheapest way to find out which side of that line you are on, and the business rescue options are wider the earlier it happens.
What it protects you from, and what it does not
[IMAGE] "What it protects you from": a shield panel would fit the existing vector set.

The moratorium is the reason the procedure exists, so it is worth being exact about it. Once the company is in administration no resolution can be passed to wind it up at all, and no winding up order can be made against it apart from on a petition brought in the public interest or by the financial regulators. A creditor's petition can still be presented, but it cannot be taken through to an order.

Beyond that, and to a large extent from the moment the directors file notice of their intention to appoint where the company has given a lender a qualifying floating charge, a creditor cannot do any of the following without the administrator's consent or the court's permission:
Enforce security over the company's property, which is the restriction secured creditors feel most. No administrative receiver can be appointed at all
Repossess goods held under hire purchase, leasing or retention of title
Irritate a lease, or in England and Wales forfeit it by peaceable re-entry
Start or continue legal action, diligence, execution or other legal process against the company

Suppliers are also restricted, since 2020, from terminating supply contracts simply because a customer has entered an insolvency procedure, which matters to any business that needs to keep trading. In plain terms, the phone stops ringing. Creditor pressure that has consumed the directors' attention for months transfers to the administrator on the day of appointment.

What it does not do is equally important. It does not cancel a single debt. It does not protect you personally: a personal guarantee can still be called, and the creditor holding it can still pursue you. It does not stop a lender with a qualifying floating charge from appointing an administrator of its own choosing. And it does not last: this is a temporary state with a statutory clock on it.
The administrator's job

Administrators are licensed insolvency practitioners and officers of the court. The administrator acts in the interests of the creditors as a whole rather than the directors or any single creditor, and the Insolvency Act 1986 sets three objectives to be worked through in order. Saving the company itself, as a trading business, comes first. Where that cannot realistically be done, or where the creditors as a whole would do better the other way, the aim becomes a return to the general body of creditors that beats what winding the company up straight away would have produced. Only where neither is achievable does the job reduce to selling what is there and paying out the creditors holding security or preferential status.

In practice the first is rarely achieved, because by the time most companies reach this point the corporate entity is not worth saving even where the trade underneath it is. The second is where most administrations live, and the usual way of achieving it is a sale of the business and assets, either after a period of trading or as a pre-packaged sale agreed before the appointment. The realisation of what is left then follows.

From appointment, the directors' powers are suspended. They remain directors, they must cooperate and provide a statement of affairs, but they cannot exercise management powers without the administrator's consent. This is the single biggest difference from a voluntary arrangement, where the directors stay in control, and it is the point most directors have not grasped when they ask for administration.
Who can put a company into administration, and how

The company or its directors, out of court. Where the company has given a lender a qualifying floating charge, that means filing a notice of intention to appoint, which triggers an interim moratorium, and then a notice of appointment within ten business days. Where there is no such lender there is no notice of intention and no interim protection, only the notice of appointment. This is the most common route for an owner-managed company

A lender holding a qualifying floating charge, out of court, usually after the directors have given it notice or after a default. The lender chooses the administrator, and its right of appointment takes priority over the directors' choice

By court order, on the application of the company, its directors or a creditor, where an out-of-court appointment is not available, for example because a winding up petition has already been presented

The out-of-court routes are not open in every case. A company that has recently been in administration, that has a petition outstanding, or that has an administrative receiver in office, may need a court order. For a Scottish company the papers are lodged in the Court of Session, or in the sheriff court for the sheriffdom of the registered office where paid-up share capital is £120,000 or less. A winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition] that has already been served changes the route and shortens the time, which is why that page tells you to act on the day you receive it.

Directors sometimes file a notice of intention purely to obtain the interim protection, with no real intention of appointing. The courts have taken a dim view of that, and so should you: it is a step to take only when an appointment is genuinely in prospect.
How the process runs
[IMAGE] "How the process runs": numbered flow.

Advice and preparation. The directors take advice on whether this is the right route, whether there is a buyer or a rescue plan, and how it will be funded. Where there is time, this is the contingency planning [link to /restructuring/contingency-planning] stage, and it is where the outcome is largely decided
Appointment. By one of the routes above. Notice goes to Companies House, to every creditor and into the Gazette
The protection takes effect. Creditor action stops. The administrator takes control of the company's affairs, property and bank accounts
Statement of affairs. The directors provide a statement of the company's assets and liabilities, as a statutory declaration, within eleven days of the administrator asking for it

Trading, sale or closure decision. The administrator decides whether the business can trade on, whether it should be sold and to whom, or whether it should be closed and asset realisation begun. A pre-pack sale completes at this point if one was arranged

Proposals to creditors. Within eight weeks of the company entering administration the administrator sends the registrar, every creditor and every shareholder a statement of proposals setting out how the objectives will be achieved, and asks the creditors to decide whether to approve them, by a decision procedure or by deemed consent, within ten weeks of the appointment
Implementation. The administrator trades, sells, collects in assets, deals with employees and suppliers, reports on the directors' conduct, and keeps creditors informed with progress reports

Exit. The procedure ends automatically after twelve months unless the creditors or the court extend it. It ends with the company handed back to its directors rescued, or with a voluntary arrangement, or by moving into a creditors' voluntary liquidation, which is how the remaining realisation reaches unsecured creditors because an administrator cannot generally distribute to them without the court's permission, or by dissolution where there is nothing left to distribute
The honest summary is that company administration is usually a twelve-month corridor between a failing company and either a sale or a liquidation. What happens in the first few weeks decides which.
What it means for employees

On appointment, employment continues. The administrator has a short window, fourteen days, in which to decide which staff to keep, and those kept on after that point carry priority for their wages from then on. Where the business is sold, the employees who work in it transfer to the buyer with their continuity of service intact under the TUPE regulations. Where the business, or part of it, is closed, redundancies are made and the affected employees claim what they are owed, within the statutory limits, from the Redundancy Payments Service.
Staff almost always learn about it on the day it happens. What they hear, and from whom, shapes whether the business the administrator is trying to sell still has a workforce the following week.
What it means for you as a director

You lose control. The administrator runs the company. You remain a director, you must cooperate, hand over the books and records and provide a statement of affairs, but you do not manage the business unless the administrator asks you to

Your conduct is investigated. The administrator has a statutory duty to review the conduct of every director and report to the Insolvency Service. This happens in every case; it is not a sign that anything is wrong

Wrongful trading applies. If you carried on past the point where insolvent liquidation or administration could no longer realistically be avoided, and creditors ended up worse off, the court can order you to contribute to the company's assets, usually measured by the extra loss creditors suffered over that period. Your defence is that once you knew there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvency you took every step you ought to have taken to minimise creditors' losses, which is why the advice you took and the record of it matter

Personal guarantees survive. The protection covers the company, not you. A lender or landlord holding your guarantee can call it, and that becomes a personal matter with its own answers in our Debt Help Scotland [link to /debt-help-scotland] section
An overdrawn loan account is a debt you owe. The administrator will pursue it
You can be the buyer. A business owner often buys the business back through a new company, usually by pre-pack. That is lawful, and heavily regulated; the pre-pack page explains the rules
None of this should put an honest director off an administration that is genuinely the best outcome. It should put them off entering one without understanding it.
What it costs, and who pays

This is the most expensive of the formal procedures. The administrator's fees, the legal costs, the agents and valuers, and the costs of any trading all rank ahead of the creditors and come out of the realisation of the company's assets, and trading losses can add to them. Where a secured creditor has appointed, it often funds the process against its security. Where a pre-packaged sale is planned, the buyer's price is usually what funds it.

We do not quote fees here because we do not set them, and because a two-week pre-pack of a single site and a six-month trading administration of a multi-site business are not the same thing. What we will do is tell you what the insolvency practitioners we introduce expect it to cost, and whether a winding up would achieve the same result for less. The creditors' committee fixes the administrator's outlays and remuneration, or the creditors do it by a decision procedure where there is no committee, and the court fixes it if they do not. Creditors are sent the administrator's accounts and remuneration claim with the progress reports, and creditors holding a quarter of the debt by value can ask the court to reduce it, provided they apply within eight weeks of the end of the relevant accounting period.
Administration compared with the alternatives
[IMAGE] "Administration compared with the alternatives": four cards.
Administration or CVA

A voluntary arrangement keeps the directors in control and the company intact, and binds creditors to a repayment plan. It has no protection of its own, so it suits a company that is not under immediate attack. Administration suits a company that needs protection first and a plan second, and the two are sometimes combined.
Administration or liquidation

A winding up ends the company. Administration may end it too, but after a period in which the business could be sold or traded. If there is nothing to sell and nothing to protect, a CVL is quicker, cheaper and reaches the same place; compulsory liquidations, where a creditor petitions, reach it on someone else's timetable. Our liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] page sets out the whole family.
Administration or pre-pack

A pre-pack is a type of administration, not an alternative to it: the sale is agreed before the appointment and completed immediately after. It suits a business that would not survive a visible period in the procedure. A trading administration suits one that would.
Administration or receivership

A receiver is appointed by one lender and deals only with the property charged to it. In England and Wales that is usually an LPA receiver over a single property; in Scotland a heritable creditor enforces its standard security instead, and a floating charge created since 15 September 2003 cannot normally be used to appoint an administrative receiver, outside a short list of statutory exceptions for capital markets and project finance. Administration deals with the whole company, and once it begins a lender needs consent to enforce and the administrator can require a receiver to step aside. See LPA receivership [link to /insolvency/lpa-receivership].

Since 2020 there has also been a standalone moratorium, separate from administration, in which the directors stay in control while a monitor oversees a short breathing space of twenty business days, extendable. It is not the same thing as administration, and it fits far fewer companies than it sounds. A monitor has to be willing to say that rescuing the company as a going concern is likely, and throughout the moratorium the company must keep paying its rent for the period, its wages, any redundancy payments, anything supplied to it during the moratorium, the monitor's fees and its bank debt. A company that has been through another insolvency procedure in the previous twelve months cannot use it at all.
Administration in Scotland

The procedure is governed by the Insolvency Act 1986 across Great Britain, and the protection, the objectives and the twelve-month period are the same for a Scottish company. The detail differs. A company registered in Scotland makes its filings in the Court of Session, or in the sheriff court where paid-up share capital is £120,000 or less, follows the Scottish administration rules rather than the England and Wales rules, and advertises in the Edinburgh Gazette. The Scottish law on transactions that can be challenged, gratuitous alienations and unfair preferences, has its own tests.

None of that changes whether administration is the right answer, but it does mean the insolvency practitioners and solicitors involved should run Scottish cases routinely. Ours are Glasgow people who do.
Where we fit

No appointments means no financial interest in the outcome. Whether your company enters administration, agrees a CVA, goes into a CVL or settles the thing by negotiation, our position is the same, so the recommendation you get is the one the facts support.

What we do is establish where the company actually stands, say honestly which route fits, and set out what it means for you personally before anything formal starts. Where administration is right, we introduce a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] we have worked with and trust, then stay alongside you through the procedure and whatever follows it. Accountants and solicitors send us their clients first for that reason.
Frequently asked questions
What does going into administration mean?

Company administration means that a licensed insolvency practitioner has been appointed to take control of the company under a moratorium that stops legal action by creditors. The directors' powers are suspended, the administrator decides whether the company or its business can be rescued or sold, and it ends within twelve months unless extended, usually with a sale and the company then going into liquidation.
Is going into administration the same as going bust?

No. The company is insolvent, but the point of the procedure is to get a better result than simply closing it. The business is often sold and continues under new ownership. The old company, though, usually does end up being wound up once the administrator has finished.
Who can put a company into administration?

The company or its directors, out of court; a lender holding a qualifying floating charge, out of court; or the court, on application by the company, the directors or a creditor. A lender's appointment takes priority over the directors' choice of administrator, and only licensed insolvency practitioners can take the appointment.
Can a company still trade in administration?

Yes, if the administrator decides that trading preserves value and there is funding for it. That is how a business is kept alive while a buyer is found. Many smaller companies cannot afford it, which is one reason pre-packs are common.
How long does it last?
Up to twelve months, automatically, unless the creditors or the court extend it. The key decisions are usually made in the first few weeks; the rest is implementation and reporting.
What happens to staff when a company goes into administration?

Their employment continues on appointment. If the business is sold they usually transfer to the buyer under TUPE with continuity of service. If it closes, redundancies are made and staff claim what they are owed from the Redundancy Payments Service, subject to statutory limits.
Do directors stay in control?
No. That is the defining difference from a voluntary arrangement. The administrator takes control; the directors must cooperate but cannot manage the company without the administrator's consent.
Closing call to action
Is administration the right answer, or just the one you have been offered?

We take no appointments, so we have no stake in which route you take. One conversation will tell you whether administration, a CVA or a liquidation fits, what it will cost, and what it means for you personally.
