/insolvency/pre-pack-administration
Pre-pack administration
[IMAGE] "How a pre-pack administration works": numbered flow, vector.

The phrase describes an administration where the deal selling an insolvent company's trade and property is struck in advance, then signed the moment an administrator is in office. The company goes into administration, the insolvency practitioner appointed as administrator completes the pre-pack sale, and the business comes out the other side, usually the same day, owned by someone else. Sometimes that someone else is a trade buyer. Very often it is the existing directors, buying through a new company, the NewCo you will see referred to in every guide.

The point of doing it this way is value. The worth of most small businesses sits in things that evaporate the moment the word administration becomes public: customers, contracts, suppliers, staff, goodwill. A pre-pack sale moves the business assets across before that happens, and with them the jobs and the relationships with the stakeholders who matter: customers, suppliers, landlord, staff. The criticism is also about value: unsecured creditors find out afterwards, get little or nothing, and watch the same people carry on trading from the same premises. Both things are true, which is why the rules around pre-pack administration have tightened over the last decade and why the decision deserves more care than it usually gets.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
Is a pre-pack administration actually the right answer?

No one at Lancefield takes insolvency appointments, and we are not paid to find you a buyer. Since nothing we earn depends on a pre-pack administration going ahead, this question comes first rather than last.
A pre-pack administration suits a particular set of facts, and it is worth being honest about whether yours are among them.
It suits you if
[IMAGE] "It suits you if / It does not suit you if": two cards side by side.

The underlying business is viable and the problem is the insolvent company's balance sheet. There is a credible buyer with real money, whether that is a third party or you. The value of the business would be destroyed by a public insolvency procedure: contracts that terminate on insolvency, customers who would walk, staff who would leave. And the secured lender, if there is one, can be brought onside.
It does not suit you if

The trade itself is what has failed, in which case a new owner simply inherits the problem. Nobody can fund the purchase. The creditors would accept a repayment plan, which makes a company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] the better route because the company survives intact. Or the real aim is simply to leave the debts behind, which a pre-pack administration is not designed for and which the rules are specifically built to catch.

If a pre-pack administration is being proposed to you and nobody has asked whether a CVA, a turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] or a straightforward liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] would serve you better, ask. The answer should be reasoned, not assumed. The directors of the insolvent company are the people who will live with it.
How a pre-pack administration works

This is still an administration under the Insolvency Act 1986, so the insolvency practitioner taking the appointment carries the same duties as in any other. They answer to the creditors as a body, and they work through the statutory objectives in sequence: save the company if it can be saved, unless that is not realistically achievable or the creditors as a whole would do better from a sale, in which case the aim becomes beating what a straight winding up would have produced. Our administration [link to /insolvency/administration] page sets those objectives out in full. What marks a pre-pack out is when the deal gets done. In outline:

Advice and viability. The directors take advice, usually from an insolvency practitioner and often through a contingency planning [link to /restructuring/contingency-planning] exercise, on whether the business is viable and whether a sale is realistic. In the Insolvency Act 1986 framework this is the stage at which the directors' own exposure is at its most manageable

Marketing and valuation. An independent valuer puts a market value on the business and its assets, and the business is marketed, or the administrator records why it was not. That valuation is the part that later has to stand up to scrutiny
The buyer and the terms. A buyer is identified, the price and terms are negotiated, and the funds are confirmed. If the buyer is connected to the company, the additional rules below apply

Consents. A secured lender with a fixed charge has to release its security for those assets to be sold, or the court has to sanction the sale over it, and a lender holding a qualifying floating charge has its own right to appoint an administrator, so lenders are consulted before anything is signed

Appointment. The administrator is appointed, usually out of court on the directors' or company's application, or by the floating charge holder. A Scottish company files in the Court of Session or the sheriff court. Notice then goes to Companies House and into the Gazette, which is the point at which the insolvent company's position becomes public

Completion. The pre-pack sale completes, typically on the day of appointment or immediately after. Staff, assets and contracts move to the buyer. The old company is left with its liabilities, and with the unsecured creditors who hold them, and whatever was paid for the business

Disclosure to creditors. The insolvency practitioner has to explain the pre-pack sale to creditors in a formal SIP 16 statement, the professional standard the regulators enforce,, covering the marketing, the valuations, the price and who the buyer is, with the first notification to creditors and normally within seven calendar days of the sale

The rest of the administration. The directors provide a statement of affairs under the Insolvency Act 1986, the administrator sends proposals to creditors within eight weeks of appointment, collects in the sale proceeds and any other assets, reports on the directors' conduct, and in due course the old company usually moves into a creditors' voluntary liquidation or is dissolved. Where a creditors' voluntary liquidation follows, the liquidator completes the distribution to unsecured creditors
The administration itself lasts up to a year, extendable. The pre-pack sale, which is what everyone means by the pre-pack, is over in hours.
What transfers, and what stays behind
[IMAGE] "What transfers, and what stays behind": a two-column vector panel would help.

Directors sometimes picture a pre-pack administration as the company changing hands. It is not. The company stays where it is, in administration. What moves is the business: a defined list of business assets sold by the administrator to the buyer for a price.

Typically that list includes the goodwill and trading name, the customer contracts and order book that can be assigned, the intellectual property, meaning the trade marks, software, designs and know-how the business runs on, the website and domain names, the stock, the plant and equipment, the fixtures and the lease if the landlord agrees, and the employees, who transfer by law. Each of those assets is valued, and the total is the price the administrator has to justify as the best reasonably obtainable for the assets sold.

What stays behind in the old company is everything else: the unsecured debts, the tax liabilities, the pension obligations, any claims against the company, and the directors' loan accounts. The buyer is not taking on the company's liabilities unless the sale agreement says so, and the old company's creditors have no claim against the new one. That separation is the entire mechanism of a pre-pack administration, and it is why the rules insist on a fair price for the assets and full transparency with creditors.
Pre-pack or a trading administration?

In a trading administration the administrator is appointed first and then runs the business while looking for a buyer. It is more transparent, because the marketing happens under the insolvency practitioner's control and creditors and other stakeholders can see it. It is also more expensive and riskier, because the business has to survive being visibly in administration while the process runs. Trading administrations suit larger businesses with enough cash and enough goodwill to withstand it. A pre-pack administration suits the business that would not, where business continuity is the only thing protecting the value.

The administrator's job is to pick the route that produces the better outcome for creditors as a whole, and to be able to show why. Directors do not get to choose a pre-pack administration because it is more convenient for them, and a proposed administrator who behaves as if they do is a warning sign.
Buying the business back yourself

A large share of pre-pack administrations sell the business and its assets to the existing directors through a NewCo. This is lawful and often the best outcome available, because management is frequently the only buyer who understands the business, can move fast, and will keep the staff. It is also the version of a pre-pack administration that creditors most resent, and the rules have been written with that in mind. If you are contemplating it, these are the things that will be examined.

The price. The administrator has to achieve full value for the assets and be able to evidence it. An independent valuer's view of market value is the floor. If a third party would have paid more for the assets, that is a problem for the administrator and, in practice, for you

The evaluator's report. Since 2021, a sale of the business or a substantial part of its assets to a connected person within the first eight weeks of an administration cannot go ahead unless the creditors have approved it or the buyer has obtained a written report from an independent evaluator on whether the case for the sale is reasonable. The evaluator is chosen by the buyer, and must be independent, professionally insured and satisfied they have the knowledge and experience for the job. The report goes to the creditors with the SIP 16 statement, though the administrator may withhold anything they judge confidential or commercially sensitive, which is the point of the transparency the rules demand. A report saying the case is not made does not stop the sale, but it is disclosed alongside the administrator's written reasons for going ahead anyway, and it follows you. The voluntary Pre-Pack Pool that reviewed connected sales before 2021 has been superseded by this requirement, and now offers evaluator reports itself, with no special status under the regulations

Real money. Deferred consideration is common, but the administrator has to be satisfied it will actually be paid, and will usually want security for it. A purchase funded by the cash you took out of the old company invites exactly the scrutiny you do not want

The company name. The Insolvency Act 1986 restricts re-using the name of a company that has gone into insolvent liquidation, and breaching the restriction is a criminal offence that can make you personally answerable for the debts of the new company. There is a specific exception, but only where the business is bought from the insolvent company under arrangements made by the office-holder, not where the directors sold it to themselves beforehand. It needs formal notice to every creditor and an advert in the Edinburgh Gazette, given before you act under the old name. Get this right before you trade, not after

The old debts. Every liability stays with the old company. So do your personal guarantees, and an overdrawn director's loan account, and anything the administrator identifies as a gratuitous alienation or an unfair preference in the run-up, These are the Scottish challenges, and their tests are not the same as the English ones: an unfair preference needs no proof that you wanted to prefer anyone, and on a gratuitous alienation it is for the person defending it to show the company was still solvent afterwards or that full value was paid. Where you were the one who received the value, the claim is pursued against you personally. A pre-pack administration does not launder the past

Done properly, a management pre-pack administration is a legitimate rescue with a full paper trail and SIP 16 transparency. Done badly, it is the case study the regulators have in mind. The difference is preparation, and it is why the work before the appointment matters more than the day itself.
What happens to employees

In most pre-pack administrations the staff transfer to the buyer with the business and its assets under the TUPE regulations, with their continuity of service intact, because TUPE treats the sale of a business as a transfer of the employees who work in it. That is one of the main reasons the procedure exists, and for employees it is the best outcome an insolvency procedure offers. Not every employee transfers: where the buyer is taking part of the business, or genuinely needs fewer people, the administrator makes the redundancies and those employees claim their statutory entitlements through the Redundancy Payments Service in the usual way. TUPE also has specific provisions for transfers out of insolvency under the Insolvency Act 1986 procedures, including which pre-transfer debts the National Insurance Fund meets rather than the buyer, and a buyer who does not understand TUPE before the sale tends to find out about it afterwards.

The thing to get right is communication. Staff usually learn of a pre-pack on the day it completes, which is unavoidable, but what they hear on that day, and from whom, shapes whether the business you have just bought still has a workforce on Monday.
What creditors get, and why they are angry
It is worth understanding the creditors' position, because you will be dealing with their reaction.

The price paid for the business assets goes into the old company, along with anything else the administrator realises from the assets left behind, and is distributed in the statutory order: the fixed-charge lender from the assets it holds security over, then the costs of the administration, then preferential creditors, employees' wage and holiday claims first and HMRC behind them as a secondary preferential creditor for VAT and PAYE, then a prescribed part set aside for unsecured creditors, then the floating charge holder, and finally the unsecured creditors at large. In most pre-packs the unsecured creditors receive little, and HMRC, usually among the largest creditors even after its preferential slice, notices. They find this out after the sale has completed, from a statement written by the administrator, and they see the same business trading on. Their anger is rational.

What they are entitled to is transparency, and SIP 16 exists to deliver it. That disclosure has to tell them how the business was marketed, what it was valued at, who bought it, what was paid, whether the buyer was connected, and why the administrator concluded the sale was the best available outcome. That transparency is the price of being allowed to do the sale without asking them first. Creditors can question the administrator, and if they believe the process was misused they can complain through the Insolvency Service's complaints gateway, which passes the complaint to the administrator's regulator. A well-run pre-pack survives that scrutiny. It is the thin ones that do not.

Suppliers you intend to keep working with, and any other stakeholders whose cooperation the NewCo needs, deserve a phone call, not a statutory notice. Whether they trade with the NewCo is up to them, and how you handle that conversation decides it.
What it means for you as a director

Every duty the Insolvency Act 1986 puts on directors of an insolvent company in an ordinary administration applies here too: the conduct report, wrongful trading, disqualification, an overdrawn loan account, and personal guarantees that the sale leaves completely untouched. Our administration [link to /insolvency/administration] page sets all of that out, and it is worth reading alongside this one. Three things, though, bite harder in a pre-pack administration.

The investigation is sharper when you are also the buyer. The insolvency practitioner writes the conduct report knowing you now own the business, so any assets that left the insolvent company in the months beforehand get a closer look than they otherwise would, and so does the valuation the sale was priced on

The timing question is unavoidable. A pre-pack administration is usually arranged over weeks while the company is already insolvent. That period is precisely the window wrongful trading liability is concerned with under the Insolvency Act 1986, so the advice you took and the records you kept during it matter more here than in an administration that arrives suddenly

Your guarantees follow you into the new company. The old lender or landlord will still call on them, and the NewCo needs its own facilities and its own lease, frequently guaranteed again. Directors end up personally exposed on both sides at once, a liability best identified before the sale rather than after. Our Debt Help Scotland [link to /debt-help-scotland] section deals with the personal half
None of this should put an honest director off a rescue that is genuinely the best outcome available. It should put them off doing it without advice.
What it costs, and how long it takes

A pre-pack administration is more expensive than a liquidation and cheaper than a trading administration. The costs are the administrator's fees, the valuers and agents, the legal work on the sale, and the statutory disbursements, and they are met first from what the buyer pays for the assets and from the old company's other assets. Where the buyer is management, the purchase price and the costs of the process are, in practice, both being found by the same people, which is why funding is the first practical question.

No figure appears here, for two reasons: we do not set these fees, and they end up in the SIP 16 disclosure the administrator makes to creditors, where an invented number would be worse than none. The spread between a simple asset sale and a contested business with property and lenders is too wide for a single answer anyway. Ask us and we will find out what the practitioner expects it to cost before you commit to anything.

On timing, the sale itself can complete within days of the appointment being decided upon, and the whole exercise from first advice to completion is often measured in weeks. The administration that follows runs for up to twelve months unless extended, but by then the business has moved on and your involvement is the director's statutory cooperation rather than the running of a process.
Pre-pack administration in Scotland

The connected-person regulations of 2021 and SIP 16 both reach Scotland, so the scrutiny a management buyer faces is identical. What changes is the machinery around it. A Scottish company's administration is run under the Scottish rules, not the England and Wales ones; the filings go to the Court of Session, or to the local sheriff court where paid-up share capital is £120,000 or less; advertisement is in the Edinburgh Gazette; and the excepted case that lets you keep using the old trading name has its own Scottish rule, though the 28-day deadline is the same.

None of that changes whether a pre-pack administration is the right answer, but it does mean the insolvency practitioner and the solicitors involved should be people who run Scottish administrations routinely. Working out of Glasgow, we deal with them week in, week out.
Where we fit

Because we take no appointments, nobody in this firm stands to be your administrator. That removes the financial interest most advisers have in a pre-pack administration going ahead, and any reason to prefer it over a CVA or a liquidation that would serve you better.

What we do is work out with you, early, whether the business is worth saving and which route saves it at the least cost and risk to you personally. That is restructuring work before it is insolvency work, and our restructuring options [link to /restructuring] section covers the options that stop short of a formal procedure. Where a pre-pack administration is right, we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] we know and trust, we help you prepare for the scrutiny that will follow, and we stay alongside you through the administration [link to /insolvency/administration] and into the new company.
Accountants and solicitors send us their clients before anything is signed for exactly that reason.
Frequently asked questions
What is a pre-pack administration?

An administration where the terms of the sale are agreed in advance, so the deal completes as soon as the administrator takes office. The buyer may be a third party or the existing directors through a new company. Liabilities stay behind with the old company; the trade carries on under its new owner.
Is a pre-pack legal?

Yes. It is a recognised use of the administration procedure under the Insolvency Act 1986, governed also by the 2021 regulations on sales to connected persons and by SIP 16, which sets out what the administrator must disclose. The controversy is about how it is used, not whether it is allowed.
Do the directors choose the pre-pack route?

They start the conversation and they are often the buyer, but the decision to sell, and how, is the administrator's, made on the basis of what produces the best outcome for creditors as a whole. A proposed administrator who simply does what the directors want is not doing the job.
Can I buy my own business back?

Yes, and it is common. Expect the sale to need creditor approval or a report from an independent evaluator if it completes within eight weeks of the administration, expect the price to be tested against an independent valuation, and expect the name-reuse rules to apply. Done properly it is a legitimate rescue; done carelessly it is the thing the Insolvency Act 1986 rules and SIP 16 were written to catch.
How long does a pre-pack take?

The sale of the assets completes on or immediately after the day of appointment. The preparation before that, valuation, marketing, lender consents and the buyer's funding, usually takes weeks. The administration itself then runs for up to a year unless extended.
Do creditors get notice before the sale?

Usually not, unless the sale is one the creditors are asked to approve instead of an evaluator's report. Giving notice would destroy the value in the assets that the procedure exists to protect. Instead, the administrator must send creditors a detailed SIP 16 disclosure explaining the sale shortly after it completes, which is where the transparency comes in, and the creditors can question it and complain if they believe the process was misused.
What happens to staff in a pre-pack?

Most transfer to the buyer with the business under TUPE, keeping their continuity of service. TUPE applies to a pre-pack sale in the same way as to any other business transfer, with some insolvency-specific adjustments. Employees who are made redundant claim what they are owed from the Redundancy Payments Service, subject to statutory limits.
What happens to my personal guarantee?

Nothing, which is the problem. The old company's debts stay with the old company, but your guarantee is a personal promise to the lender or landlord and it survives the administration. Establish what you have guaranteed before any pre-pack is planned, because it is often the largest personal exposure you have.
What was the Pre-Pack Pool?

An independent body set up in 2015 that connected-party buyers could voluntarily ask to review a proposed pre-pack sale. Take-up was low, and the 2021 regulations made an independent evaluator's report effectively mandatory for connected sales inside eight weeks. The Pre-Pack Pool still exists and offers evaluator reports, but the 2021 regulations point connected buyers at no particular provider: any individual who meets the independence, insurance and experience tests can act. A guide that describes referring to it as voluntary is describing the old regime.
What does SIP 16 require?

SIP 16, short for Statement of Insolvency Practice 16, is the professional standard every administrator must follow when a pre-pack sale is made, and the one creditors will quote back at you. It requires a written SIP 16 disclosure to creditors of the marketing, the valuations, the price, the buyer and the reasons for the pre-pack sale, and it is the document creditors and regulators use to judge whether the pre-pack was properly done.
Closing call to action
Is the business worth saving, and is a pre-pack how to do it?
Nothing we earn turns on which route you take. One conversation will tell you whether a pre-pack, a CVA or a liquidation fits the facts, and what has to be in place before anyone is appointed.

LPA receivership

An LPA receiver is someone a lender appoints to take control of a property it holds a fixed charge over, usually to collect the rental income and, in most cases, to sell it. The power comes from the Law of Property Act 1925, which is where the name comes from: this has nothing to do with a lasting power of attorney, which is a different thing with the same initials. You will also see the role called a fixed charge receiver. Fixed charge receivership and LPA receivership are the same thing.

Two things set it apart from everything else in this section. It is not an insolvency procedure: no court is involved, nobody is made bankrupt or wound up, and the rest of the business is untouched. And it is an England and Wales remedy. Property in Scotland is enforced under a different statute, with different steps, covered below.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
If a receiver has just been appointed over your property
This is the version most people arrive here with, so it comes first.

From the day of appointment the receiver controls the asset, and everything they do is aimed at clearing the secured debt from it. Tenants are told to pay their rent to the receiver, who manages and insures the building and, in nearly every modern case, can sell it too, because the loan documents extend the statutory powers that far. You still own the property until it is sold and, as borrower, you still owe the debt. The costs of the receivership process are added to what you owe, and if the eventual sale does not clear the secured loan, the shortfall remains yours.

The part that surprises people is that the receiver is, in law, your agent. The 1925 Act makes the receiver the borrower's agent rather than the lender's, so you carry responsibility for what the receiver does while the lender is largely insulated from it. The receiver's duties are to act in good faith, to get a proper price on any sale, and to account for the money. They are not duties to look after your interests.
What you can still do:

Pay the debt, or refinance it. The receivership ends when the lender is paid. If there is equity, bridging finance [link to /finance-and-funding/bridging-finance] or a new commercial mortgage [link to /finance-and-funding/commercial-mortgages] can sometimes redeem the existing lender before a forced disposal crystallises the loss. Speed matters, because a receiver rarely achieves the price you would
Negotiate. Lenders appoint receivers to get repaid, not because they want to own buildings. A credible proposal to clear arrears or sell in an orderly way is sometimes accepted even after appointment

Check the appointment is valid. The power depends on the charge being by deed, the money being due, and the conditions for enforcement having been met. For a company, check whether the fixed charge was registered at Companies House. Non-registration will not by itself unwind the appointment, because an unregistered charge is void only against a liquidator, an administrator and creditors, but it changes everything if the company then goes into a formal procedure. Defective appointments happen, and solicitors can test one quickly

Look at the whole position. A receiver over one building is often the first visible step in a wider problem. If the company that owns it cannot pay its other creditors, the real question for the creditors as a whole is no longer the receiver; it is whether the company needs administration [link to /insolvency/administration], a company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] or liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation], and those decisions are better made now than after the disposal
What you cannot do is ignore it. The receiver does not need your cooperation.
When can a lender appoint an LPA receiver?

The power arises where the security is a mortgage or charge made by deed and the secured money has become due. The Act then restricts when it can be used: in outline, after a notice requiring payment has gone unanswered for three months, where interest is two months or more in arrears, or where some other term of the charge has been breached. In practice almost every commercial facility widens these rights so that a receiver can be appointed on any default, and it is the deed rather than the Act that governs the timing.

The appointment itself is simple. The bank signs a deed of appointment, the receiver accepts, and the receivership process has begun. No court approval is needed and, for an individual owner, nothing is filed anywhere. Where the owner is a company or an LLP, the lender must notify Companies House within seven days, and the appointment then appears on the public record.

The receiver can be anyone the lender chooses, provided they are not a body corporate. Where the borrower is a company there is a further bar, because it is an offence for an undischarged bankrupt, or someone subject to a bankruptcy or debt relief restrictions order, to act. Where the borrower is an individual, neither restriction applies. They do not need to hold an insolvency licence, and many are chartered surveyors working through specialist LPA receivership practices, which is why the property profession runs its own registration schemes for receivers. The bank picks; the owner has no say.
What an LPA receiver actually does

The statutory powers are narrow: to demand and recover the income from the property, to give receipts, to insure it if the lender directs that in writing, and to apply the money in a fixed order. Collecting rent and chasing rent debtors is the core of it. Almost everything else, including selling, comes from the deed, though the lender can also delegate its own statutory leasing powers to the receiver, which is why the first thing a competent receiver does is read it. In a typical receivership process the receiver will:
Notify tenants, collect the rental income, pursue debtors and arrears, and manage the asset day to day
Put insurance in place from day one, since a lapse in cover is the quickest way to lose value
Instruct professionals, usually solicitors and valuers, on title, value and marketing
Decide whether to hold and let or to sell
Market and sell the property, taking proper care over the price, which the courts measure against what the asset would fetch on the open market when it is sold
Apply the proceeds: the costs of the receivership, then the lender's debt, then any surplus to the owner or to the next secured creditor

The receiver's remuneration is a commission on the money recovered, capped by the Act at five per cent of the gross sum unless the deed or a court order allows more. Under the Act that five per cent also has to cover the receiver's own costs and expenses; it is the deed that puts the professionals' fees on top, and those professionals answer to the receiver, not to you. It all comes out of the asset before the owner sees anything.
LPA receiver, administrator, liquidator: the difference
LPA receiver
[IMAGE] "LPA receiver, administrator, liquidator": three cards.
Appointed by a lender over a specific charged property. Deals with that asset only. No court, no moratorium, not an insolvency procedure. The owner keeps running the rest of the business.
Administrator

Appointed over the whole company by the directors, the company, a floating charge holder or the court. A licensed insolvency practitioner. Brings a moratorium that stops creditors, including most fixed charge holders, enforcing without consent. Our administration [link to /insolvency/administration] page explains it.
Liquidator

Appointed to wind the company up and distribute what is left to creditors. A licensed insolvency practitioner. A secured creditor stands outside the winding up and can still enforce, which is why a receiver can be appointed before, during or after it.

The thing to take from the comparison is scope. A receiver is one lender's debt recovery tool over one asset. The other two are procedures for the company as a whole. If your problem is one building, receivership is what you are facing. If the building is one symptom of a company that cannot pay its creditors, you are facing something larger, and the receiver is a detail.
How receivership interacts with insolvency
The question directors ask most is whether putting the company into a formal procedure stops the receiver. It depends which.

Administration. A creditor needs the administrator's consent or court approval to enforce security once a company is in that procedure, and the administrator can require a receiver already in office to step aside. That can interrupt a receivership, but only where the procedure is genuine, and a bank holding a qualifying floating charge can appoint an administrator of its own choosing
Winding up. Does not stop a secured creditor. The receiver's agency for the company ends when a liquidator is appointed, but the receiver can carry on, and the lender keeps its security
A CVA. Cannot bind a secured creditor without consent, so it does not stop a receiver either
Personal insolvency. Bankruptcy or, in Scotland, sequestration [link to /debt-help-scotland/sequestration] leaves the secured lender's rights over the property intact
None of these makes a receivership go away. They are decisions about the company or the individual, to be taken on their own merits.
How a receivership ends

When the lender is repaid and the receiver is discharged, when the asset is sold and the proceeds distributed, or when the lender removes the receiver. A surplus after the secured debt and costs belongs to the owner or the next secured creditor. A shortfall is still owed, and for a company director that is the point at which a personal guarantee, if one was given, becomes the live issue. That crossover, from a property problem to a personal one, is where most of the real damage happens, and it is why the decisions in the weeks before a receiver is appointed matter more than the ones after.

We advise lenders and other fixed charge holders as well as owners. For a lender the questions are always the same: is the charge valid and registered, has the money fallen due, have the deed's conditions been met, and is this the right receiver for this asset. The appointment is fast and cheap compared with a court process, which is its attraction, but a defective one costs more to unwind than it would have cost to check, and where the borrower's real problem is a failing business, a receiver may recover the debt while leaving a relationship to manage.
Property in Scotland: there are no LPA receivers
[IMAGE] "Property in Scotland": a simple two-column vector panel (England and Wales vs Scotland) would help.

The Law of Property Act 1925 applies in England and Wales only. A lender holding a standard security over property in Scotland enforces it under the Conveyancing and Feudal Reform (Scotland) Act 1970, and the steps are different. The lender serves a calling-up notice, which demands payment, or a notice of default, which calls on the borrower to put a breach right. Once that notice period has run without the demand being met, the standard conditions give the lender its remedies: selling, entering into possession and drawing the rents, letting, and carrying out repairs. Where the property is used to any extent for residential purposes, and a flat above a shop counts, the lender cannot sell or take possession without either a warrant from the sheriff, which it can only apply for once it has met the pre-action requirements and shown it made real efforts to agree something else, or, where the property is empty, the written consent of everyone with an interest in it.

Company borrowers in Scotland are different again. Receivership in Scotland means a receiver appointed under a floating charge, a route the Enterprise Act largely closed for floating charges created on or after 15 September 2003, so for most Scottish companies the lender's real options are enforcing its standard security or appointing an administrator. If your property is in Scotland and a lender is threatening action, the LPA guidance you find online is describing another country's law. Scottish security enforcement is what we deal with from our Glasgow office.
Where we fit

Lancefield does not act as receiver and does not lend. What we do is work out, quickly, where you actually stand: whether the appointment is valid, whether the secured loan can be redeemed or restructured, whether the rest of the company is sound or whether the receivership is the first visible sign of something larger, and what your personal exposure is if there is a shortfall. Where debt restructuring [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring] or refinancing can solve it, we say so. Where it cannot, we tell you what the realistic outcomes are and bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] if the company, rather than the building, is the problem. If the shortfall is going to land on you personally, our Debt Help Scotland [link to /debt-help-scotland] section covers the options for an individual, and we deal with both sides of that problem together.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between an LPA receiver and a fixed charge receiver?

None in practice. Both describe a receiver appointed by a lender over a specific charged property. "LPA receiver" refers to the statutory power in the Law of Property Act 1925; "fixed charge receiver" describes the security the appointment is made under. Same person, same job.
Is an LPA receiver the same as a lasting power of attorney?

No. The initials collide but the subjects are unrelated. A lasting power of attorney lets someone make decisions for you if you lose capacity. An LPA receiver is appointed by a lender to deal with a charged property.
Can I stop an LPA receiver being appointed?

Before appointment, by curing the default, agreeing terms with the lender, or refinancing. After appointment, by redeeming the debt, by challenging a defective appointment, or in some cases by putting a company owner into the hands of an administrator, which restricts enforcement of security without the administrator's consent. What does not work is waiting.
Can the receiver sell without going to court?

Usually yes. The statutory powers alone stop short of a sale, but almost every modern deed extends them that far, and no court approval is needed. What the receiver cannot do is sell carelessly: the price has to stand comparison with the asset's open-market value at the date of sale.
Who pays the receiver?

You do, in effect. The commission, capped by statute at five per cent of gross receipts, a figure meant to cover the receiver's costs as well as the fee, and, because almost every deed extends that, the fees of the solicitors and agents instructed, are all taken out of what the asset produces, ahead of the lender and well ahead of anything coming back to you.
Are LPA receivers regulated?

There is no statutory licence, unlike an insolvency practitioner or a liquidator. Many receivers are surveyors or insolvency practitioners regulated by their own professional bodies, and the property profession runs registration schemes for receivers. The owner cannot choose the receiver; the lender can and should choose a competent one.
Does LPA receivership apply in Scotland?

No. The Law of Property Act 1925 applies in England and Wales. A lender with a standard security over Scottish property enforces it under the Conveyancing and Feudal Reform (Scotland) Act 1970, by calling-up notice or notice of default followed by sale or possession, and where the property is used to any extent for residential purposes it needs either a warrant from the sheriff or, if the property is empty, the written consent of everyone with an interest in it.

A receiver has been appointed, or a lender is threatening one?

The decisions that protect you are the ones taken early. One conversation will tell you whether the appointment holds up, whether the debt can be redeemed or restructured, and what the realistic outcomes are for the property, the company and you.

Dissolving a partnership

A traditional partnership has no separate legal shell to hide behind in England and Wales, and even in Scotland, where it does have its own legal personality, the partners stand behind its debts. That single fact shapes everything on this page. Dissolving a partnership is not just an administrative exercise in closing a business: it decides who pays what, and if the firm cannot pay, the answer is its members, personally, from their own assets.

This page covers general partnerships governed by the Partnership Act 1890. Limited liability partnerships are different: an LLP is a body corporate and is wound up much like a company, so if that is your structure, our liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] and administration [link to /insolvency/administration] pages are the right ones.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
The question to settle first: can the partnership pay its debts?
[IMAGE] "The question to settle first": two cards, solvent and insolvent.
Everything else follows from this, and partners routinely reach the end of a dissolution before facing it.
If the partnership is solvent

This is a winding up of the business affairs: realise the assets, pay the creditors in full, settle the accounts between the partners, and distribute what is left. It can still be difficult, particularly where partners disagree about value, but nobody's house is at risk and the process is essentially one of accounting and agreement.
If it is not

Then the partnership debts are the partners' debts. Creditors can pursue any one of them for the whole of what is owed, not merely a share, and go after personal assets to get it, in Scotland once the firm's own estate has been exhausted, because a Scottish partner stands behind the firm rather than alongside it. At that point the question stops being how to dissolve the partnership and becomes how each partner deals with a personal debt problem, which is where sequestration [link to /debt-help-scotland/sequestration], trust deeds [link to /debt-help-scotland/trust-deeds] and the rest of our Debt Help Scotland [link to /debt-help-scotland] section come in.

We are advisers on the second of these, and we work alongside your solicitor on the first. Partners in a struggling firm often spend months negotiating the split while the debt grows, when the useful conversation is about the debt.
What dissolution actually means
Legal advice on partnership dissolution distinguishes two things, and the distinction matters in practice.

A technical dissolution happens when the partnership as a legal arrangement comes to an end but the business carries on, usually with the remaining partners under a new partnership. A partner taking their exit from a firm that continues without them is the common example.

A general dissolution is the end of the business partnership itself: the firm is dissolved, the assets are sold, the creditors are paid and the affairs are wound up. That is what most people mean by dissolving a partnership, and it is what this page is mainly about.

In either case the partnership continues to exist for the limited purpose of winding up, and, in Scotland, for one other purpose: a dissolved firm can still be prosecuted for an offence committed before dissolution, for up to five years afterwards, with the partners exposed to the fine. The partners keep the authority they need to wind up the affairs of the partnership, to complete unfinished business and to realise the assets, and they remain bound by their duties to each other while they do it. What they cannot do is take on new obligations that have nothing to do with the wind-up.
How a partnership is dissolved

If there is a partnership agreement, it governs. A well-drafted agreement will say how a partner can retire, what notice is required, how the assets are valued, what happens on death or bankruptcy, and how disputes are resolved. Follow it: the courts will, and departing from it is how partnership disputes start.
Without an agreement, the Partnership Act 1890 supplies the default rules, and they surprise people. Under the Act, and subject to anything the partners have agreed:

Any partner can dissolve a partnership at will by serving notice to dissolve on the others. No reason is needed, no notice period applies unless the agreement provides one, and it takes effect from the date the notice to dissolve states

The death or bankruptcy of any partner dissolves the whole firm, unless the partners have agreed otherwise. This is the rule that catches families and long-standing firms, and it is the single strongest argument for having an agreement
A fixed-term partnership dissolves when the term expires or the venture it was formed for is completed

The court can make an order to dissolve the firm, on the application of a partner, where another partner is permanently incapable of playing their part, has behaved in a way that damages the business, has wilfully or persistently breached the agreement or made it unreasonably impracticable to carry on in partnership with them, where trading on can only lose money, or where winding the firm up is simply the fair thing to do
The partnership ends automatically if the business becomes unlawful

To cut off future liability, partners need to give actual notice of the dissolution to everyone who had dealings with the firm, and to advertise it in the Edinburgh Gazette, or in the London Gazette if the firm trades mainly from England or Wales. The two do different jobs. The advertisement is notice to people who had never dealt with the firm; anyone who had is entitled to go on treating a former partner as a partner until actual notice reaches them. Any partner can insist on the dissolution being publicly notified, and until third parties know, a former partner can still be held liable for obligations the continuing partners take on. The exception is a partner nobody knew was a partner: someone who dealt with the firm without knowing of them cannot rely on their apparent membership afterwards.
Winding up the business: the steps
[IMAGE] "Winding up the business": numbered flow.
Read the partnership agreement, or establish that there is not one. Everything that follows depends on it, and this is the point at which legal advice is cheapest
Agree the date of dissolution and record it in writing, along with who is doing what during the wind-up

Notify. Customers, suppliers, the landlord, the bank, insurers, HMRC: every business relationship the firm has. Publish in the Gazette, and cancel or reassign contracts, licences and direct debits. Tell the bank early, because a continuing guarantee or cautionary obligation is revoked as to future transactions by any change in the firm's constitution unless it says otherwise

Deal with employees. Where the business closes, the employees are dismissed and the usual notice, consultation and redundancy obligations follow. Where it is sold, or carries on under a new line-up of partners, continuity of employment is preserved by statute and TUPE may apply, so the staff transfer with their service intact

Realise the assets. Sell the stock, plant and property, collect the debtors, and decide what happens to the goodwill, the intellectual property and the business name, which is often the most contested item and rarely the most valuable

Pay in the statutory order. Unless the agreement says otherwise, the assets go first to outside creditors, then to repay partners' advances beyond their capital, then to repay capital, and only then is any surplus divided between the partners in the profit-sharing ratio

Settle the accounts between partners. Final accounts are drawn up and the balances between partners are worked out. Where the assets do not cover the liabilities and capital, the deficiency is borne by the partners in the same proportion as they shared profits

Deal with tax. The partnership makes a final return, each partner reports their share, and there may be capital gains or balancing charges on the assets. Your accountant should be in this from the start
The step partners skip is the notification. It is dull, it is cheap, and leaving it undone is how a departed partner discovers they are still liable for something a year later.
Who is liable for the debts
[IMAGE] "Who is liable for the debts": the scales vector panel fits here.
This is the part that changes lives, so it is worth being exact about it.

Every partner is liable, along with the others, for the liabilities the firm takes on while they are a partner. In England and Wales that liability is joint; in Scotland the Act makes each partner severally liable as well, so the partners are jointly and severally liable for the firm's debts. In both, a partner's estate stays severally liable after death for whatever is still unpaid. In plain terms: a creditor can pursue whichever partner is most able to pay for the whole amount, and it is then for that partner to seek a contribution from the others, which is only worth anything if the others have assets.
A few consequences follow that partners often get wrong:
Retiring does not end liability for what already exists. A partner who exits stays liable for the liabilities the firm took on during their time in it, unless the creditor agrees to release them

Nor does an indemnity from the continuing partners. An agreement between partners binds the partners, not the creditor. The creditor can still come to you; the indemnity is only as good as the person who gave it
Joining a firm does not import its history. Liabilities the firm ran up before someone became a partner are not theirs, unless they expressly agree to shoulder them
Failing to notify third parties leaves you exposed. Without notice of your retirement or the dissolution, someone who dealt with the firm can still treat you as a partner
The debts are personal. There is no limited liability to fall back on, which is why a partnership that cannot pay is a personal insolvency problem for each partner

If you are approaching that point, the advice is the same as for a director facing personal exposure: get the whole picture in front of one adviser, early, before options start closing. Our Debt Help Scotland [link to /debt-help-scotland] section covers the personal routes, and where a viable business is buried under historic debt, debt restructuring [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring] or a turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] review may reach a better answer than dissolution.
When the partners cannot agree

Most partnership disputes are about three things: whether the firm should end at all, what the assets are worth, and who has taken more than their share. The dissolution itself is often the easy part.

Where negotiation fails, any partner can ask the court to wind up the firm's business and affairs. In Scotland the court can dissolve the firm and appoint a judicial factor to take in the partnership estate, run or realise the business and distribute the assets, all under the supervision of the Accountant of Court. In England and Wales the equivalent is a court-appointed receiver or manager. Either way, seeking court orders is expensive, slow and public, and it consumes the value everyone is arguing about. Mediation, or an agreed independent valuation, resolves most of these disputes for a fraction of the cost, and it is worth exhausting those before anyone issues proceedings.

The other route worth naming: rather than dissolving, the partners can agree that one buys the others out and the business partnership carries on with a different line-up. Where there is a viable business and the argument is about people, that is frequently the better outcome for everyone, and it is a conversation an adviser without a stake in the fight can often start.
Partnerships in Scotland are different

In Scotland a partnership is a legal person distinct from its partners. It can own property and intellectual property, contract, sue and be sued in the firm's own name, and it can be sequestrated as an entity separately from the partners' own estates. The partners remain jointly and severally liable for the firm's debts, so separate personality is not limited liability. What it changes is the order of events. The firm's own estate is realised first and the partners answer for the shortfall, standing behind the firm's obligations rather than as the principal debtors. It also means assets belonging to the firm do not fall into an individual partner's own sequestration, and a trustee appointed over one partner's estate has no title to deal with them.

In practice that means an insolvent Scottish partnership has options that read differently from the guidance written for England and Wales. The firm can be sequestrated; the partners can be sequestrated; a trust deed may be the better route for an individual partner; and the interaction between the firm's estate and each partner's estate needs to be thought about deliberately rather than assumed. Most of the material online about dissolving a partnership does not address any of this, because it is written about English law. Scottish firms and Scottish partners are what we deal with from Glasgow.
Where we fit

Lancefield does not act for one partner against another and we are not your solicitor. What we do is establish the financial position: whether the firm is solvent, what the realistic value of the assets is, what each partner's exposure looks like, and whether the business is worth saving in some form.

Where it is solvent, we work with your accountant and solicitor to see it wound up cleanly. Where it is not, we set out each partner's personal options honestly, including the ones that earn nobody a fee, and introduce a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] where a formal procedure is genuinely needed. Partnership problems come to us from accountants and solicitors precisely because we have no stake in the answer.
Frequently asked questions
What does dissolving a partnership mean?

That the partnership relationship comes to an end. Partnership dissolution can be technical, where the business carries on under a new firm, or general, where the business itself is wound up: assets sold, creditors paid, accounts settled between the partners. The firm continues to exist for the purposes of winding up until that is complete.
Can one partner dissolve the partnership?

In a partnership at will with no agreement to the contrary, yes: any partner can serve a notice to dissolve on the others. Where there is a partnership agreement, it will usually set out a different and more orderly process for the exit, and that process governs.
What happens if there is no partnership agreement?

The Partnership Act 1890 fills the gaps, and its default rules are blunt. Equal profit shares regardless of contribution, dissolution on notice by any partner, and automatic dissolution of the whole business partnership on the death or bankruptcy of any partner. Few firms would choose these terms, which is the argument for putting an agreement in place.
Am I liable for the partnership's debts after I leave?

For any liability the firm took on while you were a partner, yes, unless the creditor releases you. An indemnity from the remaining partners protects you only as far as they can pay. And unless notice of your retirement reaches the people who dealt with the firm, you can also be held liable for what they take on afterwards.
What happens if the partnership cannot pay its debts?

The partners pay, from their own assets, and a creditor can pursue one partner for the whole amount. That makes it a personal insolvency question for each partner. In Scotland the firm itself can also be sequestrated as a separate legal person, and the right combination depends on the individual positions.
Does a partner's bankruptcy end the partnership?
Under the Partnership Act, yes, unless the partners have agreed otherwise. It is one of the strongest reasons to have a written agreement dealing with what happens on bankruptcy, death or incapacity.
How are the assets divided?

In the order the Partnership Act 1890 sets out, unless the partnership agreement says otherwise: outside creditors and other liabilities first, then partners' advances, then partners' capital, then any surplus in the profit-sharing ratio. Where there is a shortfall, the partners bear it in the same proportion as they shared profits.
Is an LLP dissolved the same way?

No. A limited liability partnership is a body corporate and is wound up under company insolvency procedures, and its members are not personally on the hook for its debts the way partners are. That protection is not absolute: in an insolvent liquidation a court can order a member to repay withdrawals made in the two years beforehand, where the member knew or had reasonable grounds to believe the LLP was, or would be made, unable to pay its debts, and the wrongful trading rules apply to them. An LLP cannot be sequestrated in Scotland at all. This page is about general partnerships under the Partnership Act 1890.
Closing call to action
Working out what dissolution actually costs you?

Whether the firm is solvent decides everything else. One conversation will tell you where the partnership stands, what each partner is exposed to, and whether there is a better answer than dissolution.

Debt help in Scotland

Scotland has its own debt solutions, its own legislation and its own government agency running them. If you have been reading about IVAs, bankruptcy petitions or Debt Relief Orders, that is English law and most of it does not apply to you.

This page sets out what actually exists here, what each option does to your home, your credit file and your job, and how to work out which one fits. It also says plainly where free help is available, because for a good number of people that is the right answer and we would rather tell you than sell you something.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
Start here: free advice exists, and it is good

Citizens Advice Scotland, StepChange and National Debtline are debt charities offering free, impartial money advice across Scotland. An approved money adviser, which includes advisers at Citizens Advice Bureaux and at organisations approved for the Debt Arrangement Scheme, can issue a certificate for sequestration, which is one of the routes into a debtor application. Seeing an approved money adviser is a statutory requirement for that application in any case. If your situation is straightforward, free money advice may be all you need, and we will say so rather than take a fee for repeating it.
These charities are not a lesser option. Their money advisers deal with more debt cases in a month than most commercial firms see in a year, and the support they offer costs you nothing. Use them.

Where a paid adviser earns their place is in the more tangled cases: a director whose company debt and personal debt are entangled, someone with a property and equity to protect, a person with assets or income that make the standard route the wrong one, or anyone who has been given advice that does not sound right and wants a second view.
The four routes, and what each one does to you
[IMAGE] "The four routes": four cards, teal icons consistent with the rest of the site.
Every option below is a formal Scottish process. Each has real consequences, and the differences between them matter enormously depending on whether you own a home and what your income looks like.
Debt Arrangement Scheme

You enter a debt payment programme, a statutory arrangement that lets you repay your debts in full over a longer period. Interest and charges are frozen from the day you apply, and creditors of the debts in the programme cannot take enforcement action while it runs. Complete the programme and those frozen interest and charges are written off; if it fails they can be added back. Your home is protected, though a programme can be approved on condition that you sell some other asset. Where you can realistically clear the debt given time, this is usually the best of the debt options available. It has no English equivalent at all.
[LINK] Debt Arrangement Scheme
Protected trust deed

You pay a monthly contribution, assessed against what you can actually afford, normally for 48 months, and the remaining unsecured debt is written off at the end if you keep to the terms. A protected trust deed treats your home differently from the way sequestration does, which is why it is often the more protective route for a homeowner. "Protected" means not enough creditors objected to stop it, since it takes a majority in number or a third by value to block one, so the rest are bound too. Until a trust deed becomes protected it does not stop them acting.
[LINK] Trust deeds
Sequestration

The Scottish term for bankruptcy. Your assets pass to a trustee who realises what can be realised, and the debts included are written off. There are two routes in, and the simpler Minimal Asset Process is built for people on a low income with no property. It is the most serious option and not the first one we reach for, but for some people it is genuinely the right one.
[LINK] Sequestration
An informal arrangement

Not everything needs a statutory solution. Sometimes the answer is a repayment plan, some breathing space, and a conversation with creditors who would rather be paid slowly than not at all. This is where free advice services do excellent work.

The Accountant in Bankruptcy is the Scottish Government agency that administers sequestration and the Debt Arrangement Scheme and maintains the public Register of Insolvencies. Its website sets out the current thresholds, which do change.
[LINK] Accountant in Bankruptcy

One term to be careful with: a debt management plan is not a Scottish statutory solution. It is an informal arrangement, usually run by a commercial debt management firm regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority, and it does not freeze interest or stop creditors the way a debt payment programme does. Some are perfectly reasonable. They are simply not the same thing, and the names are close enough to confuse.
Which debts these cover
Most of what people owe can go into a Scottish debt solution: credit cards, overdrafts, personal loans, catalogue and store accounts, payday lending, council tax arrears, and money owed to HMRC.

Council tax arrears deserve a particular mention, because in Scotland councils can enforce them quickly and aggressively, and they are a very common reason people reach this page. They are included in these processes like any other unsecured debt, which is often a relief to hear.

Secured lending itself does not go in: the mortgage survives every one of these processes. Mortgage arrears are a different question. You can choose to include them in a Debt Arrangement Scheme programme; in a trust deed or sequestration they stay with the lender, secured against the house. Court fines and, generally, student loans are also excluded. If you are receiving Universal Credit or another income-related benefit, that affects which route you qualify for rather than whether you qualify at all, and under the Minimal Asset Process it can be part of what gets you in.
How to tell which one fits
The honest short answer is that it depends on three things: whether you own property, whether you have surplus income after essential expenditure, and how much you owe relative to both.

You own a home with equity, and you have some surplus income. A protected trust deed [link to /debt-help-scotland/trust-deeds] is usually the first thing to look at, because your home is handled differently than it would be in sequestration

You can clear the debt in full given more time, and enforcement is the pressure. The Debt Arrangement Scheme [link to /debt-help-scotland/debt-arrangement-scheme] freezes interest and stops creditors acting, without writing anything off or risking assets

You have little income, few assets and no property. The Minimal Asset Process route into being sequestrated [link to /debt-help-scotland/sequestration] exists precisely for this, and it is quicker and cheaper than the alternatives

Your debts are mostly the company's, and you signed personal guarantees. Deal with the company first, or at least at the same time, because a guarantee will keep generating personal liability until the company position is resolved. Start with liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] or, if a creditor has already gone to court, with winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition]
The pressure is immediate and you need time to think. A moratorium gives you six months of protection from diligence while you take advice, whichever route you end up choosing
Anyone who tells you the answer before asking about your home, your income and your guarantees is selling rather than advising.

A money adviser will work through this with you properly, using a standard affordability assessment that every Scottish debt option is built around. That assessment is what determines whether a debt payment programme is realistic, what a protected trust deed contribution would be, and whether you fall inside the Minimal Asset Process. It is the same arithmetic whoever does it, which is another reason free debt advice is worth taking before you pay anyone.
If you are a company director

This is the situation we see most, and the one that free debt advice services are least equipped for. The company is struggling, you have signed personal guarantees on the bank facility or the lease, and the two problems have become one problem.

Solving them separately rarely works. Put the company through a liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] without addressing the guarantees and the lender simply turns to you. Sort out your personal debts while the company keeps trading at a loss and the exposure grows again behind you.

What is needed is a view of both at once: what the company procedure does to the guarantee, what the guarantee then does to you, and which order to take them in. That is the crossover the insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] section of this site deals with on the business side, and this section deals with on the personal side.

One point worth stating: you cannot act as a company director while sequestrated without the court's permission. If continuing to run a business matters to you, that alone may decide which route is right.
What debt help does not do
Three honest limits, because the promises made in this market are sometimes extraordinary.
It does not remove secured debt. A mortgage or any other secured lending survives every one of these processes. The security holds

A personal guarantee is a separate contract from the company's debt. Putting the company through a liquidation does not touch it. Your own liability under the guarantee can go into your personal solution and be written off with everything else, but the two have to be dealt with as two things

It does not repair your credit file quickly. The Accountant in Bankruptcy's guidance is that a sequestration stays on your credit file for six years. For most people at this point the damage has already been done by missed payments long before
What it does do is stop the position getting worse, put a defined end date on it, and hand the creditor pressure to someone whose job it is to absorb it.

That last part is what people underestimate. The formal options here stop creditor action on the debts they cover: no more letters, no more calls, no more enforcement. Whatever else is true, you get control of your own week back, and for a lot of people that is the change that matters most.
Where we fit
Lancefield is an adviser, not a trustee. Nobody here becomes your trustee in sequestration or supervises your trust deed, so we do not earn anything from you choosing one over another.

What we do is look at the whole position, including the business side if there is one, and tell you which route actually fits. Where that is a free service, we will say so. Where a formal solution is needed, we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] and stay alongside you through it.
[LINK] Sequestration · Trust deeds · Debt Arrangement Scheme · Accountant in Bankruptcy · Insolvency practitioner
Frequently asked questions
Is Scottish debt help really different from England?

Substantially. Sequestration [link to /debt-help-scotland/sequestration] is not the same thing as English bankruptcy, a protected trust deed [link to /debt-help-scotland/trust-deeds] is the closest Scottish relative of an IVA without being one, and nothing south of the border corresponds to the Debt Arrangement Scheme [link to /debt-help-scotland/debt-arrangement-scheme] at all. Different statutes, different timescales, and the body running it is the Accountant in Bankruptcy [link to /debt-help-scotland/accountant-in-bankruptcy] rather than the Insolvency Service. Guidance written for England will mislead you on the detail, which is the reason this section exists.
Will I lose my home?

Not automatically, and the answer depends heavily on which route you take, how much equity there is, who else owns the property and whether the mortgage is being paid. A homeowner should take advice specifically on this before applying for anything, because the routes treat property very differently.
Does it cost anything to talk to you?
No. The first conversation is free, confidential and commits you to nothing. If free advice elsewhere is the right answer for you, we will tell you that in it.
Will my employer find out?

Most people keep their jobs and most employers never know. Some professions and roles have restrictions, so check your contract and any professional body rules. Sequestration is recorded on the public Register of Insolvencies, though few employers go looking.
How long does it take to be free of the debt?

It depends on the route. The Minimal Asset Process discharges automatically after six months. A full sequestration can discharge from twelve months. A trust deed normally runs 48 months. The Debt Arrangement Scheme runs until the debt is repaid in full, which can be considerably longer, but the frozen interest and charges come off at the end and your home is protected.
Can I choose which debts to include?

Largely no. These are collective processes, and creditors are treated according to statutory rules rather than your preferences. Paying one creditor ahead of others before a formal process starts can itself cause difficulties later.
