Sequestration in Scotland, explained without judgment
[IMAGE - Hero] no photograph. This page should feel calm and private, not staged. Use the on-brand Mackintosh vector panel in navy and stone, or open straight on text.

Sequestration is the Scottish term for bankruptcy. It is a formal process that writes off debts you have no realistic prospect of repaying, and it exists because sometimes a situation cannot be fixed by paying more slowly.

If you are reading this, you are probably frightened about your house, your car and your job. Those questions are answered further down, plainly, before anything else. And it is worth saying early that sequestration is not the only option in Scotland, and it is not the first one we would reach for.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
Your home, your car, your job

[IMAGE - Home / car / job cards] three restrained teal line icons (house, car, briefcase). Vector only. Avoid anything that looks like a stock photo of a worried person, which would read as manipulative on this subject.
These are the three questions almost everyone asks first, so here they are first.
Your home

Your share of any property you own becomes an asset in the estate the trustee deals with, so a home you own is at risk. That does not automatically mean it is sold. Much depends on how much equity there is, who else owns it, and whether the mortgage payments are being maintained. Keeping up mortgage payments matters, because the lender's security survives the sequestration. If you rent, sequestration does not usually affect your tenancy directly, though your landlord may treat rent arrears as a debt included in the process. Two things are worth knowing. Your trustee cannot sell a family home without the consent of your spouse, civil partner or former spouse, or the sheriff's authority, and the sheriff can refuse a sale or postpone it for up to three years. And if the trustee has taken no step against your interest in the home within three years of the sequestration, it comes back to you, but that clock only starts on time if you tell the trustee about the property within three months of the award, so tell them. This is the single most important thing to take proper advice on before applying.
Your car

A car of modest value that you need for work or caring responsibilities can often be kept. A high value vehicle is more likely to be sold, or you may be asked to pay its value into the estate. Cars on finance are treated differently again, because the vehicle may not legally be yours yet.
Your job

Most people keep their jobs. Some professions and roles have restrictions, so it is worth checking your employment contract and any professional body rules. You cannot act as a company director, or be involved in forming or managing a company, while sequestrated without the court's permission.
What sequestration actually is

Sequestration transfers your assets to a trustee, who sells what can be sold and distributes the proceeds among your creditors. In return, the debts included are written off at the end of the process, whether or not they were paid in full.

It is administered by the Accountant in Bankruptcy [link to /debt-help-scotland/accountant-in-bankruptcy], the Scottish Government agency responsible for personal insolvency in Scotland. The trustee is either the Accountant in Bankruptcy or a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] appointed to act. Where an insolvency practitioner is appointed as trustee, they take on statutory duties to your creditors as well as responsibility for administering your estate, which is why the role has to be held by someone licensed and regulated.

Sequestration is recorded on the Register of Insolvencies, which is public. It also affects your credit rating: the sequestration appears on your credit file and will make borrowing harder and more expensive for several years. For many people the credit rating damage has already been done by missed payments and defaults long before they reach this point, which is worth weighing honestly rather than treating a good credit rating as something still to protect.

This is a Scottish process under Scottish law. It is not the same as bankruptcy in England and Wales, or as bankruptcy in Northern Ireland, which has separate insolvency legislation of its own, and the alternatives are different too. A protected trust deed [link to /debt-help-scotland/trust-deeds] is the Scottish equivalent of an IVA, and the Debt Arrangement Scheme [link to /debt-help-scotland/debt-arrangement-scheme] has no English counterpart at all. If you have been reading English guidance and applying it to your own position, some of it will not hold here.
The two routes into sequestration
Minimal Asset Process (MAP)

Sometimes called MAP bankruptcy, this is the simpler, cheaper route for people on a low income with few assets and no property. The application fee is £50, and it is waived if you are on a qualifying benefit or assessed as having no surplus income, which covers almost everyone eligible for MAP in the first place. The process is shorter, and there is less trustee involvement. To qualify you must owe no more than £25,000 in total, own assets worth no more than £2,000 with no single asset worth more than £1,000, and own no land. A vehicle you reasonably need is left out of that total if it is worth £3,000 or less, and student loans do not count towards the £25,000. There is no minimum debt: the old £1,500 floor was removed in February 2023. You also need either an assessment showing you can pay nothing towards your debts, or six months of qualifying benefits with no other income. You cannot use MAP if you have been sequestrated in the last five years, or used MAP in the last ten. Discharge comes automatically six months after your bankruptcy is awarded, unless the Accountant in Bankruptcy takes you out of MAP first, which it can do if your assets turn out to be worth more than the limit, if you are assessed as able to contribute, or if you do not co-operate.
Full administration sequestration

The standard route, used where MAP does not apply, typically because you own property, have assets of some value, or have surplus income. A trustee is appointed to realise assets and administer the estate, and discharge is a decision taken on the trustee's report rather than something that happens by itself.
Figures correct as at July 2026. Thresholds are set by the Accountant in Bankruptcy and do change, so ask us to confirm them rather than relying on a page you found online.

You can apply for your own sequestration, and most people do. Whichever route you use, the law requires you to see an approved money adviser first. That is a statutory precondition rather than a formality, and in practice the adviser is the one who submits your application. For MAP you also need a Certificate for Sequestration from that adviser. For full administration you need the certificate, or to meet the test for apparent insolvency, or to have granted a trust deed that creditors would not let become protected. You also need to owe at least £3,000. A creditor owed above a set amount can also petition for your sequestration, but only if you are apparently insolvent as well. Owing the money is not enough on its own.
What happens during the process
You apply through the Accountant in Bankruptcy, or a creditor petitions the court
A trustee is appointed to take control of your estate
Assets that can be realised are identified and sold, with certain essentials protected
If you have surplus income, you will normally be asked to make payments under a Debtor Contribution Order, assessed from what is left after reasonable living costs
Creditors submit claims and are paid from whatever the trustee realises
You are discharged, and the included debts are written off
Any contribution order can continue after discharge, so the payments and the discharge are two separate things

Under MAP, discharge is automatic at six months. In a full administration sequestration it can come from twelve months onwards, on the trustee's report rather than automatically. Either way the trustee's work on the estate can carry on beyond your discharge, and contributions may continue past it.
What your creditors can and cannot do
This is usually the part that brings the most immediate relief, because the pressure people are living under comes from creditors rather than from the debt itself.

Once you are sequestrated, most creditors must stop contacting you directly and must deal with your trustee instead. They cannot continue diligence, which is the Scottish term for enforcement action such as earnings arrestment or bank arrestment, in respect of the debts included. Ongoing interest and charges on those debts stop. Creditors who want a share of whatever the trustee realises have to submit a formal claim rather than chase you for payment.

Creditors keep some rights. A secured creditor such as your mortgage lender retains its security over the property, so it can still repossess if the mortgage payments are not maintained. A creditor can object to your discharge if it believes you have not cooperated. And any creditor owed a debt that is not covered by sequestration, such as a court fine, can still pursue you for it.

Unsecured creditors, meaning credit cards, personal loans, overdrafts and most trade creditors, generally rank equally and share whatever is left after the costs of the process and any preferential claims. In many cases unsecured creditors receive very little, which is precisely why sequestration writes off the balance.

There is also a step you can take before deciding anything. A moratorium gives you six months of protection from diligence while you take advice and choose a route. It is entered on the Register of Insolvencies, and a money adviser can apply for it.
Which debts are included, and which are not

Most unsecured debt is included and written off: credit cards, personal loans, overdrafts, catalogue debt, most utility arrears, council tax arrears and, in many cases, business debts you are personally liable for. If a debt is unsecured and it existed at the date of sequestration, the working assumption is that it is included.

Some are not. Student loans, court fines, compensation orders and debts arising from fraud or breach of trust are not written off. Child maintenance is a special case: arrears that built up before the date of sequestration are written off, but maintenance falling due from that date onwards is not, and the Child Maintenance Service can still act on it. Secured debts such as your mortgage are treated differently, because the lender's security over the property survives.

If you have signed a personal guarantee for a business, the guaranteed debt is a personal debt, and it can be included. For directors and sole traders whose business and household finances have become tangled together, this is the point where the two sides of the problem have to be looked at as one. That crossover is a large part of what we do.
The alternatives, which usually deserve a look first
[IMAGE - Alternatives section] two teal line icons for trust deed and DAS.
Sequestration is the most serious option, not the default. In Scotland there are two formal alternatives and several informal ones.
Protected trust deed

You pay a monthly contribution worked out by a statutory assessment of what you can afford, normally for 48 months from the date the deed is granted. It can run longer if you miss payments, or if you agree to keep paying beyond that, which is common where there is equity in your home. At the end your trustee applies for you to be discharged and the remaining unsecured debt is written off, though that depends on the deed having become protected and on you keeping to the terms. Your home is treated differently than in sequestration, and for homeowners this is often the more protective route.
[LINK] Trust deeds
Debt Arrangement Scheme (DAS)

A statutory payment programme that lets you repay the debt itself in full over a longer period, with interest and charges frozen from the day you apply and creditors of the debts in the programme barred from taking enforcement action. Complete it and the frozen interest and charges are written off; if it fails they can be added back. Your home is protected, though a programme can be approved on condition that you sell some other asset. If you can realistically clear the debt given time, this is usually the better answer.
[LINK] Debt Arrangement Scheme
If the debt is your company's, not yours

Directors often arrive here because a business has failed and a personal guarantee has been called in. If that is your position, the company side needs its own answer, whether that is liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation], a CVA [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva], or dealing with a winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition] that has already been served. Sorting the personal position while leaving the company unresolved rarely works, because the guarantee keeps generating new liability.
[LINK] Insolvency practitioner · Liquidation

There are also informal arrangements, and sometimes the right answer is simply a repayment plan and some breathing space. Free debt advice is available in Scotland from Citizens Advice Scotland, StepChange and National Debtline, and a money adviser or debt adviser at any of them can issue the certificate you need to apply. We will tell you when free advice is all you need.
Where we fit
Lancefield does not act as your trustee. Only the Accountant in Bankruptcy or a licensed insolvency practitioner can do that, and we do not take those appointments.

What we do is give you a clear read on your position before anything is decided, including whether a formal process is needed at all. Because nobody here is appointed as your trustee, we have no stake in which route you take and no reason to steer you toward one. If a trust deed protects you better than sequestration, we will say so. If the Debt Arrangement Scheme is the right answer, we will say that. And if the honest answer is that you need free advice rather than us, we will tell you that too.
Where a formal appointment is needed, we bring in a licensed practitioner we know and trust, and we stay alongside you through it.
Frequently asked questions
How long does sequestration last?

It depends which route you are in. Under the Minimal Asset Process you are discharged automatically six months after your bankruptcy is awarded. In a full administration sequestration the Accountant in Bankruptcy can discharge you from twelve months onwards, but that is a decision based on your trustee's report rather than an automatic date, and it can be refused or delayed if you have not co-operated. Contributions from surplus income can continue beyond discharge, and the Accountant in Bankruptcy's guidance is that it stays on your credit file for six years.
Will everyone find out?

Sequestration is entered on the Register of Insolvencies, which is a public register. In practice, most people's friends, neighbours and colleagues never look at it. Your employer is not notified as a matter of course unless your role or profession requires it.
What if I have almost nothing?

That is what the Minimal Asset Process exists for. The £50 application fee is waived for anyone on a qualifying benefit or assessed as having no surplus income, so in practice it costs nothing; there is less trustee involvement, and discharge comes automatically at six months. The same waiver applies to the £150 fee on the full route, so do not rule that out on cost alone. It is built for people on a low income without property, and since the minimum debt requirement was removed in 2023 there is no longer any floor to fall below. We can check whether you fall inside the asset and debt limits.
What happens to my benefits?

Sequestration does not stop you claiming welfare benefits. Your benefit income is taken into account when the trustee assesses whether you have surplus income to contribute, and in many cases people whose income is mainly from benefits are assessed as having nothing to pay. Benefit overpayments are treated as debts, and whether a particular overpayment is written off depends on how it arose, so it is worth listing them when you take advice.
Can I apply myself?

Most sequestrations are applied for by the debtor rather than forced by a creditor, so yes in that sense. But you cannot lodge the application yourself. Seeing an approved money adviser comes first and is required by law rather than merely advisable, and it is that adviser who submits it for you. For MAP you need a Certificate for Sequestration from them; for full administration you need the certificate or must meet the test for apparent insolvency. You do not need a solicitor.
What restrictions apply while I am sequestrated?

You cannot act as a company director or manage a company without the court's permission. You must tell a lender you are sequestrated if you are seeking credit of £2,000 or more, and for credit of any amount at all while your debts total £1,000 or more. You must cooperate fully with your trustee, including disclosing assets and any change in your circumstances. Failing to cooperate can extend the restrictions.
Does sequestration affect my partner?

Your partner's own debts and their sole assets are not included. Jointly owned assets and joint debts are affected, and if you own a home together their position needs looking at carefully. A joint bank account is likely to be frozen at the outset.
I am a director. Does this close my company?

Not automatically, but you will almost certainly stop being a director of it. Acting as a director while sequestrated is a criminal offence without the court's permission, and most companies' articles remove a director from office the moment they are prohibited from acting. Permission from the court does not put you back on the board; the company has to appoint you again. Where the company is also insolvent, the two problems are best dealt with together rather than one at a time.
Is this the same as bankruptcy in England?

It is the Scottish equivalent, but the process, the terminology and the alternatives differ. Sequestration is administered by the Accountant in Bankruptcy rather than the Insolvency Service, and the Scottish alternatives are protected trust deeds and the Debt Arrangement Scheme rather than IVAs.

Protected trust deeds
[IMAGE] "How a trust deed becomes protected": a simple flow from signing to protection would help.

In Scotland, and nowhere else in the UK, you can deal with unmanageable debt by granting a trust deed. You transfer your estate to a trustee, who realises what can be realised, takes contributions from your disposable income for an agreed period, and distributes the proceeds among your creditors. At the end of it the balance of the debts covered by the deed is written off. Where it becomes protected, and most do, the creditors bound by it can no longer pursue you or take diligence against you.

Protected trust deeds are a real and useful remedy, and also the debt solution most heavily marketed to people in Scotland, because arranging one earns a fee. Both things are true at once. The purpose of this page is to explain what it actually does, and to be honest about the two situations in which something else would serve you better.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
Is a trust deed actually the right answer for you?
[IMAGE] "Is a trust deed actually the right answer for you?": two cards.

We arrange nothing, protected trust deeds included. Nobody here becomes your trustee, we take no fee from a trust deed, and we are not paid by anyone who does. That is why this section comes first rather than last.
It may suit you if

You have unsecured debts of at least £5,000, which is the statutory minimum, typically credit cards, loans and overdrafts, and you genuinely cannot repay them in a reasonable time. You have disposable income you could make contributions from each month, and your circumstances are stable enough to keep those payments up for the full term. You want the creditor pressure to stop, and you accept that some of what you own may have to be realised to pay them.
Something else may suit you better

If you could repay the debt in full given time and protection from interest, the Debt Arrangement Scheme [link to /debt-help-scotland/debt-arrangement-scheme] offers a Debt Payment Programme that does exactly that and writes nothing off, which means it does not touch your assets in the same way. If you have almost no disposable income and few assets, sequestration [link to /debt-help-scotland/sequestration], the Scottish form of bankruptcy, may be quicker and cleaner, and you would be discharged sooner. And if the debt is a company debt rather than yours, the answer may be on the insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] side entirely.

If you have been recommended a protected trust deed by someone who would be paid to arrange it, and nobody mentioned a Debt Payment Programme, ask why. It is a fair question and any reasonable source of debt advice will have a reasonable answer. If a creditor is already taking action against you, ask about a moratorium too. A moratorium buys time to get proper debt advice before you commit to anything.
How a trust deed becomes protected
This is the part that matters, and it is the part the marketing tends to skip.

Signing a trust deed does not by itself stop creditors taking action. What it creates initially is an ordinary trust deed, and that binds nobody except the creditors who sign up to it. The trustee registers it in the Register of Insolvencies and must send the paperwork to every known creditor within seven days. Creditors then have five weeks from registration to object. The deed becomes protected unless objections come in from a majority of them in number, or from creditors holding at least a third of the debt by value. Once protected, it binds every creditor covered by it, including those who never replied, and they can no longer take diligence against you for those debts. One narrow exception is worth knowing: a creditor who was never notified, or who objected in time, keeps a limited right to ask the court for your sequestration instead, and the court will only grant it if that is genuinely in the creditors' best interests.

If too many object, the deed does not become protected. It can still run as an ordinary trust deed with whoever signed up, but everyone else is free to continue their action against you, including going to court, and in practice a failed protection means reconsidering the whole approach.

The trustee must be a licensed insolvency practitioner, and the arrangement is supervised by the Accountant in Bankruptcy [link to /debt-help-scotland/accountant-in-bankruptcy], Scotland's insolvency regulator, which also maintains the public Register of Insolvencies where the deed is recorded. Note one consequence of signing: while the trust deed subsists you cannot apply for your own sequestration, so it is a decision that closes a door as well as opening one.
What happens to your home
This is the first question almost everyone asks, and the honest answer is that it depends on your equity, not on the trust deed itself.

Your interest in your home forms part of the estate conveyed to the trustee. Your mortgage itself sits outside the trust deed and you keep paying it as normal, but the equity above the mortgage is what the trustee looks at. Where there is little or none, it is common for arrangements to be made that let you keep the property, sometimes by a third party paying the value of your interest, and sometimes because the equity is not worth realising. Where there is significant equity, the trustee has a duty to creditors to realise it, and that can mean the property has to be sold or the equity bought out. Where an agreement is reached to keep it, the payments for the equity typically run on after the four-year period rather than being found at the start. There is also a formal route, agreed before the deed is granted, that keeps the house outside the estate altogether where the lender agrees not to claim, and it requires a proper valuation by a chartered surveyor first.

What you should not do is sign anything before this has been worked through with a valuation and a redemption figure in front of you. An arrangement that looks affordable monthly can still end with the sale of a house, and finding that out in year three is not the same as knowing it in month one. If keeping the property is your priority, say so at the outset, because it may change which option is right.
The rest of what it affects

Your credit rating. The trust deed is recorded in the Register of Insolvencies, which is public and searchable, and credit reference agencies pick it up, so it appears on your credit file. The effect on your credit rating lasts years beyond the end of the arrangement, and it is one of the reasons a Debt Payment Programme suits some people better

Your vehicle. A car of modest value that you need for work is often retained; a valuable one is an asset like any other. Where the vehicle is on hire purchase it does not belong to you in the first place, and the agreement has to be dealt with separately

Your job. For most people, nothing changes. A minority of professions and roles have restrictions or notification requirements, and certain positions become difficult. Check your contract and any professional body rules before you sign, not after

Being a company director. A trust deed does not itself disqualify you, which surprises people. Sequestration is different: it is a criminal offence for an undischarged bankrupt to act as a director or take part in running a company without the court's permission. What a trust deed may do is trigger a term in the company's own articles of association, which under the standard Model Articles remove a director automatically where a composition is made with their creditors generally, or breach a shareholders' agreement, a lending covenant or an employment contract. Read the articles first
Windfalls during the term. An inheritance, a redundancy payment, a lottery win or a compensation award received while the deed runs is generally claimed for the creditors
New credit. The trust deed will restrict you from taking on credit during the arrangement, including credit cards, and any change in your income has to be reported
The trustee, the term and the money

The trustee is not your adviser. As insolvency practitioners, trustees owe their duty to the creditors as a body, and their job is to realise what can be realised and distribute it. That is not a criticism, it is the design of the thing, and it is precisely why having someone independent explain the options to you beforehand matters.

You make contributions from your disposable income for the agreed term, which for most protected trust deeds is four years. The payments are set from a proper assessment of what you actually have left after reasonable living costs, including your mortgage or rent, using the Common Financial Statement, which is the statutory assessment tool, rather than a figure someone thinks you can manage. Social security benefits cannot be counted towards a contribution. If your circumstances change materially, the contributions can be reviewed in either direction, and you are discharged at the end.

A few debts survive the discharge whatever happens: student loans, court fines and penalties, compensation orders, aliment, and anything you incurred through fraud or breach of trust. A secured lender also keeps its rights over the security. Everything else covered by the deed, which for most people means credit cards, loans, overdrafts and similar unsecured debt, is written off at the end.

The trustee's fees and outlays come out of the money collected, before the creditors are paid. That is normal and it is disclosed, but it is worth understanding: a proportion of what you pay in each month funds the administration rather than reducing your debt. Ask for the fee basis in writing before you sign.
What happens if you cannot keep it up
This is the risk the marketing of protected trust deeds does not lead with, and it is the reason the affordability assessment at the start matters so much.

If you stop paying, the trustee will first look at whether the contributions can be varied. Where the payments genuinely cannot be sustained, the trust deed can fail, though since 2024 there is a middle path: where circumstances have changed and there is no realistic prospect of resuming, the trustee can apply for an early discharge instead of letting the deed collapse. A failed trust deed is the worst of both worlds: the money you have paid in is gone, a good deal of it into fees, the debts revive to the extent they have not been paid, and your creditors are free to pursue you again. The trustee may also petition for your sequestration, in other words to have you made bankrupt.

So the affordability figure at the outset should be conservative and should assume that some months will be worse than the one you are in now. An arrangement that only works if nothing goes wrong for four years is not an arrangement, it is a hope.
Trust deed, sequestration or DAS
[IMAGE] "Trust deed, sequestration or DAS": three cards. The most useful element on the page.
Trust deed

Voluntary, four years for most protected trust deeds, and you are discharged from the remaining debt at the end. Your assets, including any equity in your home above the mortgage, are available to the trustee. Suits someone with real disposable income and credit cards, loans or other debt they cannot clear in a sensible time.
[link: Sequestration]

Scotland's bankruptcy. Usually shorter, often cheaper to enter, and administered by a trustee who may be the Accountant in Bankruptcy. Being made bankrupt carries a wider public record and more restrictions while it lasts, and you are discharged sooner. For someone with minimal income and few assets it is frequently the more honest answer.
[link: Debt Arrangement Scheme]

A Debt Payment Programme that freezes interest and charges and stops creditor action while you repay in full over a longer period. Nothing is written off, which is why providers promote it least, and nothing is realised, which is why it is often the right answer for someone with equity in a home and a mortgage they want to keep.

The choice between them turns on three things: how much disposable income you really have, how much equity sits in your assets after the mortgage, and whether repaying the debt in full over a longer period is realistic. Anyone recommending one without having established all three is guessing.
If the debt came from a business
This is where most debt advice stops and where a large share of our work begins.

If you are a company director who signed a personal guarantee, or a sole trader, or a partner in a firm, you have two problems that have to be solved together. The company or the firm has its own position, and you have yours, and the order in which they are dealt with changes the outcome. Settling the personal side before the business position is resolved can leave you having paid for a liability that would have reduced. Dealing with the business first without understanding your guarantee exposure can leave you facing a claim you had not planned for.

Our creditors' voluntary liquidation and partnership liquidation [link to /insolvency/partnership-liquidation] pages cover the business side. What matters here is that the two are looked at as one problem by one adviser, which is the thing a debt-advice firm and a firm of insolvency practitioners each do half of.
Where we fit

Lancefield takes no appointments and arranges no trust deeds. Nobody here becomes your trustee, we receive no fee or commission from the insolvency practitioners who do, or from anyone else, and there is no product at the end of this conversation.

What we do is establish the whole picture, including the business side if there is one, and tell you which of the routes actually fits your numbers, including the ones that pay nobody anything. Where a formal arrangement is the right answer we introduce you to an appropriately qualified person to advise on and administer it, and we stay alongside you.
That is the difference between advice and a sales process, and on this subject it is worth insisting on.
Frequently asked questions
What is a protected trust deed?

A voluntary arrangement, available only in Scotland, in which you convey your estate to a trustee and make payments from your disposable income for an agreed period, usually four years. Once protected it binds all the creditors it covers, they cannot pursue you or take diligence for those debts, and you are discharged from the remaining debt at the end. It is a trust deed for creditors, granted to deal with debt, and not the trust deed sometimes drawn up alongside a will for estate planning, which is a different document altogether.
Will I lose my house?

It depends on the equity above your mortgage rather than on the trust deed itself. Where there is little or none, arrangements are often made that let you keep the property. Where there is significant equity, the trustee has a duty to realise it for the creditors, and that may mean a sale or a buyout. Get a valuation and a redemption figure before you sign, not after.
Will my employer find out?

There is no general obligation to tell an employer, and for most people nothing changes. The Register of Insolvencies is public, so it is discoverable. Some professions and some roles have their own rules, and certain contracts and professional bodies require disclosure, so check yours before you sign. One thing worth knowing: if payments due from your wages are missed on two consecutive occasions, the trustee can instruct your employer directly to deduct them. Keeping the payments up is what keeps this private.
Can I be a company director during a trust deed?

A trust deed does not itself disqualify you from acting as a director. Sequestration is a different matter, because an undischarged bankrupt commits an offence by acting as a director or taking part in running a company without the court's permission. What a trust deed can do is trigger a clause in the company's own articles of association, which usually remove a director automatically on a composition with creditors generally, or breach a shareholders' agreement or a contract of employment. The answer is in your own documents rather than in insolvency law.
What happens if my circumstances change?

Tell the trustee early. Contributions can be reviewed up or down where circumstances change materially. What causes real damage is stopping payments without telling anyone, because a failed trust deed leaves the money paid in gone, the debts revived and the creditors free to act again.
Is a trust deed better than sequestration?

Not inherently. Protected trust deeds are better for some people and worse for others. Someone with real disposable income and assets worth protecting is often better off in a trust deed; someone with minimal income and few assets is frequently better off sequestrated and discharged sooner. The comparison has to be done on your numbers, ideally with independent debt advice rather than a provider's.
Does a trust deed cover my business debts?

It covers debts for which you are personally liable, which includes personal debt such as credit cards and loans, a personal guarantee you have given and the debts of a sole trade or a partnership. It does not deal with a limited company's own debts, which sit with the company. Where both exist, they need to be looked at together.
Who regulates trust deeds?

The trustee must be one of the licensed insolvency practitioners authorised to act, and the Accountant in Bankruptcy supervises protected trust deeds and maintains the Register of Insolvencies in which the trust deed is recorded.

The Debt Arrangement Scheme

The Debt Arrangement Scheme, always shortened to DAS, is the Scottish Government's statutory way for Scottish residents to repay debt over a longer period without any of it being written off. You agree a Debt Payment Programme, you make a single affordable monthly payment, that money goes to a payment distributor who divides it among your creditors, and while the payment plan runs the interest and charges are frozen and your creditors cannot take diligence against you.

It is the least promoted form of debt management in Scotland and, for a particular kind of person, the best one. Nothing is written off, so it earns a provider considerably less than a Scottish trust deed does. Nothing is realised either, which is exactly why it suits someone with equity in a home they want to keep.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
What a debt payment programme actually does

It freezes interest and charges. From the day the application goes in, not from approval, interest and charges stop being payable, and once the programme completes they cease to be owed at all. For someone whose balances have been rising despite paying every month, this alone changes the arithmetic completely
It stops diligence. Creditors covered by the programme cannot use earnings arrestment, bank arrestment or attachment against you, and cannot petition for your sequestration for those debts

It consolidates everything into one payment plan. A single monthly payment to a payment distributor, who divides it among your creditors, instead of managing a dozen separate arrangements with credit cards, loans and catalogues

It repays in full. The debt you owe on the day you apply is paid, over a longer period. The interest and charges that would otherwise have piled up are the only thing extinguished, and that is the trade for everything above. There is one long-stop: after twelve years, where seventy per cent of the original debt has been paid, the balance can be composed and discharged

It does not touch the home you live in. There is no trustee and nothing is conveyed to anybody. A programme can carry a condition that you realise an asset, but the regulations expressly except the house or mobile home you live in, and since 2018 it can only be brought in at all if you choose to include it
That last point is the one that decides it for a great many people, and it is the difference that gets least airtime.
Who it suits, and who it does not
[IMAGE] "Who it suits, and who it does not": two cards.
It suits you if

You have a reliable monthly surplus, you could clear the debt in full given enough time and no more interest, and you have something worth protecting: equity in a home, or simply a strong preference for keeping your credit rating from taking the harder hit a formal insolvency brings. It also suits people whose profession or employment makes an insolvency awkward.
It does not suit you if

The debt is so large relative to your income that repaying it in full would take an unreasonable period. There is a point past which a programme becomes a life sentence rather than a solution, and at that point a trust deed [link to /debt-help-scotland/trust-deeds] or sequestration [link to /debt-help-scotland/sequestration], which do write debt off, is the more honest answer. It also does not suit someone whose income is too irregular to commit to a monthly figure.

The honest test is arithmetic. Take the total debt, divide it by what you can genuinely afford each month, and look at the number of years that produces. If the answer is a period you can live with, DAS is very likely your answer. If it is not, it is not, and no amount of preferring it will change that.
Why you may not have been told about it
Worth saying directly, because it explains a pattern people notice.

A Scottish trust deed generates a fee for the firm that arranges and administers it. Sequestration generates a fee too. A Debt Payment Programme is administered by an approved money adviser, and where those advisors sit in the free advice sector, as many do, there is no commercial fee at all. The result is entirely predictable: the option that pays least is mentioned least.

That is not an accusation of dishonesty against anyone. It is a structural observation about how debt advice is paid for in the United Kingdom, and it is why the Financial Conduct Authority banned debt packagers from taking referral fees altogether in 2023, having found the fees paid for trust deeds and IVAs were far higher than for anything else. It is also why our position on this page is what it is: we arrange nothing, and we have nothing to gain from which route you take.
How you get one

Speak to an approved money adviser. Only an approved money adviser can submit a DAS application. Most of these debt advisers sit in local authorities, Citizens Advice Bureaux and other free-to-client services, and we can point you to one

Ask about the moratorium. Applying for a moratorium gives you six months' protection from diligence while you get advice and put the application together, and you can use it once in any twelve months. It is the thing to do first if a creditor is already moving against you

Build the financial statement. Income, reasonable living costs including your mortgage or rent, and what genuinely remains. This information is the whole application, and an over-optimistic figure here is what causes payment plans to fail later
The application goes to the DAS Administrator. That role sits with the Accountant in Bankruptcy [link to /debt-help-scotland/accountant-in-bankruptcy]

Creditors are notified and may object. A creditor who does not respond within twenty-one days is deemed to consent. Where creditors holding nine tenths by value consent, the programme is approved automatically. Where they do not, the DAS Administrator decides whether it is fair and reasonable, against prescribed criteria, and can approve it over an objection
The Debt Payment Plan starts. You make one monthly payment to a payment distributor, who distributes it to your creditors, and the interest and charges stop

The application itself is free to you, and a money adviser cannot charge an individual a fee for this work at all. There is a fee within the scheme, taken from what is distributed: twenty per cent to the payments distributor and two per cent to the Accountant in Bankruptcy. Creditors receive seventy-eight pence in the pound rather than you paying anything extra.
Your home, and why this is the section that matters

Under a Debt Payment Programme nothing is conveyed to a trustee, because there is no trustee. Your home is not part of any estate and nobody has a duty to creditors to realise it. The Administrator does look at any equity in land you own when deciding whether a programme is fair and reasonable, but the regulations expressly except the property you live in from being realised. You keep paying your mortgage as normal, outside the programme, and the DAS deals with the unsecured debt: credit cards, loans, overdrafts and the like. Mortgage arrears themselves are treated differently and should be raised with the adviser separately.

Compare that with a Scottish trust deed, where your interest in the property forms part of the estate conveyed to the trustee, and significant equity has to be realised for the creditors, potentially by a sale. For a homeowner with equity, that difference is frequently worth more than everything else on this page combined.

This is the single most common reason we tell someone to go and look at DAS. If you own a home with equity in it and you have been recommended a trust deed, get a second view before you sign anything.
What can go wrong

Missing payments. A programme can be revoked where arrears reach the equivalent of two months' payments. If it is revoked, the protection ends, the interest and charges that had been suspended become payable again back to the date you applied, the revocation itself counts as apparent insolvency, and you are back where you began with time lost
An over-optimistic budget. The commonest cause of the above. The figure should assume that some months will be worse than this one
A change in income. Payment plans can be varied where circumstances change, and a variation is far better than silence. Tell your debt adviser early
A creditor who will not engage. The fair and reasonable test exists precisely for this, and an objection does not automatically defeat an application
The debt was never going to be repayable. Where the arithmetic at the outset was wrong, a programme delays a decision rather than solving anything

Taking on new credit. Unlike a trust deed, the credit restriction here is in the regulations rather than in an agreement, with narrow exceptions for things like emergency repairs and trade credit in the ordinary course of business
DAS, trust deed or sequestration
[IMAGE] "DAS, trust deed or sequestration": three cards, the decision element of the page.
Debt Arrangement Scheme

Repay in full over longer. Interest and charges frozen, diligence stopped, no trustee, no assets realised, no insolvency, and a softer effect on your credit rating. Suits a reliable monthly payment and assets worth protecting.
[link: Trust deed]

A formal insolvency. Contribute for a set term, usually four years, then the balance is written off. Your estate including any equity in your home is conveyed to a trustee. Suits someone who cannot repay in full in a sensible period.
[link: Sequestration]

Scotland's bankruptcy. Usually the shortest route and often the cheapest to enter, with the widest public record and the most restrictions during it. Frequently the right answer for someone with minimal income and few assets.

All three stop creditor action. The differences that decide between them are whether debt is written off, whether your assets are realised, and how long you are committed for. Any recommendation made without weighing all three is not a recommendation, it is a default.
If the debt came from a business

DAS is for individuals habitually resident in Scotland, and it covers debts for which you are personally liable. A director who has given a personal guarantee, a sole trader and a partner in a firm can all use it for their own liabilities, and business debts such as HMRC arrears in a sole trade can be included where the liability is personal.

There is also a separate route for the firm itself, known as Business DAS. A partnership, a trust or an unincorporated body can have its own programme, provided a money adviser certifies that it can pay within five years and is still trading. A sole trader is an individual and uses ordinary DAS. Where you are a partner, a debt can go into your programme or the firm's, but not both.

What DAS does not do is deal with a limited company's own debts, which stay with the company and need the routes on our insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] side. Where both exist, the sequence matters: settling your personal position before the company's is resolved can mean paying for a liability that would have reduced. That joined-up view is the thing neither a money adviser nor an insolvency firm usually provides on its own, and it is the reason this section of the site exists.
Where we fit
Lancefield does not administer debt payment programmes and takes no fee from any debt remedy. We are not the approved money adviser who submits your application, and we will tell you who is.

What we do is establish the whole position, including the business side where there is one, work through the arithmetic honestly, and tell you which of the three routes your numbers actually support. Where that is DAS, we point you at an approved money adviser and you pay us nothing further. Where it is a trust deed [link to /debt-help-scotland/trust-deeds] or sequestration [link to /debt-help-scotland/sequestration], we say so just as plainly.
Having no product to sell is the whole of what we offer on this page.
Frequently asked questions
What is the Debt Arrangement Scheme?

Scotland's statutory debt management scheme, run by the Scottish Government through the Accountant in Bankruptcy. Student loans are excluded from it by the regulations. You agree a Debt Payment Plan, make one affordable monthly payment that a payment distributor divides among your creditors, and while it runs the interest and charges are frozen and creditors cannot take diligence against you. You repay the debt in full over a longer period; nothing is written off.
Is DAS a form of insolvency?
No, and that is one of its main attractions. There is no trustee, nothing is conveyed to anybody, and it is not a sequestration or a trust deed. It is a statutory payment arrangement.
Will I lose my house?

No. There is no trustee and nothing is conveyed to anybody, and the regulations expressly except a house or mobile home you occupy as your main residence from being realised. Since 2018 it can only be included at all if you choose to include it. You continue paying your mortgage as normal outside the programme. This is the main reason DAS suits homeowners with equity better than a trust deed does.
Does it stop interest and charges?

Yes, that is the core of it. The freeze runs from the date of application rather than approval, and once the programme completes the suspended interest and charges cease to be owed altogether. For many people that is the difference between an arrangement that works and one that never finishes.
Can my creditors refuse?

A creditor can object, but an objection does not automatically defeat the application. Where creditors holding nine tenths of the debt by value agree, it is approved automatically. Otherwise the DAS Administrator decides whether the programme is fair and reasonable against prescribed criteria, and can approve it over an objection. A creditor who simply does not reply within twenty-one days is treated as consenting.
How long does a programme last?

As long as it takes to repay the debt at the agreed rate, so it depends on the balance and what you can afford. There is no statutory maximum for an individual, though the Administrator has to be satisfied the period is fair and reasonable, and after twelve years a composition can close out the remainder. The trade is that nothing is written off, so the period runs longer than a trust deed's fixed term.
Does it appear on my credit file?

Yes. The programme is recorded on the DAS Register, which is public, and credit reference agencies pick it up, so your credit rating is affected. The effect is generally regarded as less severe than a trust deed or sequestration, but it is real and it lasts.
Who can apply for me?

Only an approved money adviser can submit a DAS application. Most such advisors are in local authorities, Citizens Advice Bureaux and other free services. We are not one, and we will point you to one.
Closing call to action
Been told a trust deed is your only option?

We administer nothing and take no fee from any of these routes. One conversation will tell you whether repaying in full under DAS is realistic, or whether something that writes debt off is the honest answer.

The Accountant in Bankruptcy, explained

[IMAGE - Hero] no photograph, and no imagery of an official building, which would read as intimidating on a page people reach while frightened. Use the Mackintosh vector panel in navy and stone, or open on type.

The Accountant in Bankruptcy is the public body that runs personal insolvency in Scotland. It awards bankruptcy, acts as trustee in a large share of cases and supervises the trustee in the rest, keeps the public register of Scottish insolvencies, and runs the statutory repayment scheme. Most people meet the name on an envelope, and the letter inside rarely explains what the organisation is.

This page covers what the AiB is, what it does, when it becomes your trustee, what it publishes about you, and how to deal with it. It is written for the person told to send an application there, and for the director whose company trouble has turned personal too.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
What the Accountant in Bankruptcy is

The AiB, as it is shortened in its own letters and almost everywhere else, is a Scottish Government executive agency: inside government, but at arm's length from ministers, with its own chief executive and its own statutory duties. Most of those duties come from the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 2016. The Accountant in Bankruptcy is also a person, a statutory office holder appointed by Scottish Ministers, whose staff work out of Kilwinning in Ayrshire.

It holds two roles that pull against each other. It regulates, overseeing every trustee other than itself and taking complaints about how that trustee has behaved. It also administers cases itself, and in a great many of them it is the trustee. One body can therefore be your case handler, your trustee and the referee at once.
What the AiB actually does
[IMAGE - "What the AiB actually does"] one restrained teal line icon per list item, or none at all. Do not illustrate a courtroom: the AiB is not a court, and the page says so.
Awards bankruptcy. Apply for your own bankruptcy and the AiB decides, not a court. Creditors wanting you made bankrupt against your will petition the sheriff court
Acts as trustee. In a debtor application the AiB becomes trustee over your estate unless a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] is named and agrees to act
Supervises every other trustee. An insolvency practitioner acting as trustee in a Scottish bankruptcy, or under a protected trust deed, accounts to the AiB for the case
Runs the Debt Arrangement Scheme. As DAS Administrator it approves each debt payment programme and oversees the money moving through it
Keeps the Register of Insolvencies. The public record of Scottish personal insolvency cases, and of Scottish liquidations and receiverships
Grants moratoriums. A short application buys a period during which most enforcement against you must stop while you take advice
Publishes the numbers. The quarterly Scottish Statutory Debt Solutions Statistics, and the Notes for Guidance that trustees and money advisers work from
Two of those matter far more than the rest: whether the AiB is your trustee, and what reaches the register.
When the AiB is your trustee

A trustee takes control of your estate, sells what can be sold, deals with creditors' claims and pays out what there is. Somebody does that job in every bankruptcy, and here it falls to the AiB by default.

The AiB acts as trustee wherever nobody else is appointed. In a debtor application you may name an insolvency practitioner willing to act, and that person becomes your trustee instead. It is also trustee in every Minimal Asset Process bankruptcy, and it picks up any case where a trustee resigns, dies or is removed without replacement.

Your trustee is not your adviser and is not acting for you. The duties are owed to creditors, and they take in how the debt arose, what assets you have not mentioned and whether you have income to spare. Being straight from the first form is the most useful thing you can do.

Creditors then claim through the appointment rather than chasing you. They deal with the trustee rather than with you, and they cannot continue diligence, the Scottish word for enforcement such as an earnings arrestment or a bank arrestment. Creditors keep some rights: a secured lender still holds its security over your home, and creditors can object to your discharge.

Where you have surplus income, it is assessed and you are asked for a monthly payment, set by statutory calculation rather than by negotiation. That payment runs for a fixed period. No contribution can be taken from social security benefits, and where your income comes solely from benefits the contribution is fixed at zero.
The Register of Insolvencies

[IMAGE - Register of Insolvencies section] a simple navy diagram of the three routes, bankruptcy, trust deed and Debt Arrangement Scheme, showing which of them the AiB administers and which it supervises. This is the one visual that earns its place, because the supervise-versus-administer distinction is the hardest idea on the page.

The AiB keeps that register, and it is genuinely public: anyone with an internet connection can search it, free, without saying who they are or why. This is the part most people find hardest, and it is better faced now than discovered later.

An entry names you, gives an address, and records the date of the award, the trustee's name and contact details, and the date you are discharged. It does not name your creditors. A trust deed appears once the trustee registers notice of it, and Scottish liquidations and receiverships appear too, which is how creditors check a customer.

Very few people are ever looked up. Credit reference agencies do check, and so do some lenders and some employers in regulated roles. The larger effect is on your credit rating: a bankruptcy sits on your credit file for years counted from the award rather than from your discharge. For most people the credit rating damage arrived long before, with the defaults that led here.

Your bank account is a separate question. Bankruptcy does not close a bank account by itself, but banks often freeze or close one on learning of it, particularly where the same bank is owed money. Opening a basic bank account elsewhere first, with wages and benefits paid into it, saves trouble later.
How the AiB differs from the Insolvency Service

The Insolvency Service is a UK government agency, an executive agency of the Department for Business and Trade, whose personal insolvency work covers England and Wales, and its official receivers act there. It has no role in Scottish personal insolvency, and the AiB has none south of the border. The nearest thing to an IVA in England is a protected trust deed here, and the statutory repayment scheme has no English counterpart.

Some differences are structural. In England and Wales a debtor's bankruptcy application goes to an adjudicator; here it goes to the AiB, and there is no official receiver because the AiB does that work itself. Nor does the AiB license insolvency practitioners: professional bodies authorise them across Great Britain, and the AiB supervises how they run Scottish cases.

Corporate insolvency runs the other way round. Liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] and administration are largely GB-wide law, so a Scottish company closing follows broadly the same statute as an English one, and the AiB appoints nobody to a company. A director facing a failed business and a personal shortfall deals with two systems in the same month.
Dealing with the AiB
Everything runs on your case reference. Quote it on every letter, form and call
Most dealings are with the trustee, not a switchboard. Where an insolvency practitioner holds the appointment, the AiB supervises rather than handles the case
Answer the forms fully and on time. A half complete statement of assets and liabilities invites more questions
Report changes as they happen. A new job, a drop in income, a move or an inheritance all have to be disclosed, and any payment can be reassessed either way
Ask for a review if a decision looks wrong. Many AiB decisions can be reviewed on request, with an appeal to the sheriff from the review, and the time limits are short
Complaints have their own route. The AiB runs a complaints procedure, and what it does not resolve can go to the Scottish Public Services Ombudsman

One thing causes most of the frustration we hear about: the AiB administers the process, it does not advise you on whether the process suits you. Its staff cannot say whether a trust deed would protect your home better than bankruptcy would. The law requires an approved money adviser before any debtor application in any event, and free advice is available from Citizens Advice Scotland, StepChange and National Debtline.
Where the AiB fits among your options
Most people who reach this page are working out which of three formal routes applies. The AiB touches all three.
Bankruptcy, or sequestration

The formal name is sequestration [link to /debt-help-scotland/sequestration], though bankruptcy is the ordinary Scottish word and the AiB uses both. Assets are realised, creditors receive what there is, and the balance is written off. The AiB is either your trustee or the supervisor of the practitioner who is, and under the Minimal Asset Process it is always the trustee.
Protected trust deed

A voluntary arrangement with your creditors, run by an insolvency practitioner and supervised by the AiB rather than administered by it. You pay a contribution for a set period and the remaining unsecured balance is written off at the end, provided the deed became protected and you kept to its terms. Our page on trust deeds [link to /debt-help-scotland/trust-deeds] explains how protection is obtained.
Debt Arrangement Scheme

A statutory repayment programme: you repay the debt in full over a longer period, interest and charges frozen, creditors unable to enforce, and nothing written off because nothing needs to be. The AiB approves it as DAS Administrator. See Debt Arrangement Scheme [link to /debt-help-scotland/debt-arrangement-scheme].

If the debt is your company's rather than yours, the AiB is not the body you need. A winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition] already served, a director-led CVL [link to /insolvency/creditors-voluntary-liquidation-cvl], or a partnership insolvency [link to /insolvency/partnership-liquidation] where partners carry personal liability are corporate questions first. The rest of Debt Help Scotland [link to /debt-help-scotland] covers the personal side, and the two are best dealt with together.
Where we fit
Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes your trustee, and we have nothing to gain from you entering any particular process, which is the reason the advice can be straight.

We read your position before anything is filed and tell you which route fits, or that none of them does yet. Where a formal appointment is genuinely needed we bring in a licensed practitioner we know and trust. If free advice is all you need, we will say so. Get in touch [link to /contact] when you are ready.
Frequently asked questions
Is the Accountant in Bankruptcy the same as the Insolvency Service?

No. The AiB handles personal insolvency here. The Insolvency Service is a UK government agency whose personal insolvency work covers England and Wales, and its official receivers have no function north of the border. The process, the terms and the alternatives all differ, so English guidance will mislead you.
How do I apply for bankruptcy?

You see an approved money adviser first, which the law requires rather than recommends, and that adviser lodges the application for you. A Minimal Asset Process bankruptcy is the shorter route for people on a low income with almost nothing to realise; full administration bankruptcy covers everyone else. The Minimal Asset Process carries limits on what you can owe and own, and those limits change, so check them rather than assuming. The AiB decides the application either way.
What happens to my home?

Your share of a property you own forms part of the estate the trustee deals with, so a home you own is at risk, though a sale is not automatic. Equity, joint ownership and whether the mortgage is kept up all bear on it, and a secured lender keeps its security either way. A trust deed treats a home differently, which is why homeowners should take advice first.
What happens to my creditors?

They deal with the trustee instead of with you. Creditors submit claims, interest and charges on the included debts stop, and enforcement for those debts stops. Creditors share whatever is realised after the costs of the process and any preferential claims, which in many cases is very little. That is the point of the process rather than a flaw in it, and creditors know it going in.
Will my bankruptcy appear on a public register?

Yes, on the Register of Insolvencies, which anybody can search free of charge. The entry shows your name, an address, the date of the award, the trustee's details and the date of your discharge, but not the names of your creditors. Your employer is not told as a matter of routine unless your role or profession requires it.
Can the AiB stop creditors chasing me before I apply?

It can, for a while. A moratorium application to the AiB gives protection from most diligence while you decide what to do, and it can be used once in a rolling period. It does not reduce the debt, but it buys room to take proper advice rather than signing up to the first thing offered.
Closing call to action
Not sure whether the AiB should be hearing from you at all?
We will read your position, tell you which route actually fits, and say so plainly if the answer is free advice rather than us. It costs nothing and commits you to nothing.
