Business restructuring

Restructuring is what a business does while it still has choices. It covers the changes that fix the underlying position: reshaping debt, improving cash flow, selling or closing the part that is losing money, and getting an honest read on whether the business works once those things are done.

It sits before insolvency, not after. That distinction is the whole point of this section, because by the time most companies speak to a restructuring specialist the useful options have already narrowed.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
The question underneath everything

Broadly there are two kinds of work here. Financial restructuring changes the company's liabilities: what it owes and how it is funded. Operational restructuring changes how the business runs: what it sells, at what margin, and at what cost. Cost reduction and efficiency improvements belong on the operational side. Most companies that come to us need some of both, and treating a financial restructuring as sufficient when the operational problem is untouched is the most common way this work fails.
Every restructuring decision turns on one thing: is there a viable business under the current problem?

If there is, then the debt, the structure and the cost base are all solvable, and the work is worth doing. If there is not, then restructuring delays an outcome rather than changing it, and the honest answer is to say so early rather than spend eighteen months and a lot of money arriving at the same place.

Answering that question properly is why an independent review [link to /restructuring/independent-business-review] exists. It gives you, and any lender who is asking, an objective read on whether the business model works once the immediate pressure is removed. It is often the first piece of work we do, because everything else depends on the answer.
What restructuring covers
[IMAGE] "What restructuring covers": six cards with the teal service icons used sitewide.
Turnaround

Addressing the cause rather than the symptom. Operational and financial change in companies that are underperforming but fundamentally sound: pricing, cost base, working capital, management information, and the discipline to act on it.
[LINK] Turnaround
Debt restructuring

Reshaping what the company owes so that repayment matches what the business can actually generate. Renegotiating terms, consolidating facilities, dealing with a lender's concerns before they become a default.
[LINK] Debt restructuring
Independent business review
An objective assessment of viability, usually commissioned by a lender but valuable to a director in its own right. It establishes the facts everyone then negotiates around.
[LINK] Independent business review
Contingency planning

Preparing a fallback before circumstances force the decision. It is the least urgent-sounding service here and frequently the most valuable, because a plan made calmly beats one made under a deadline.
[LINK] Contingency planning
Exit planning
Getting a business ready to be sold or wound down on your terms, over a horizon long enough to influence the outcome. Sale, succession, or an orderly solvent closure.
[LINK] Exit planning
Corporate simplification

Removing dormant and redundant companies from a group structure, reducing filing obligations, cost and risk. Usually executed through solvent liquidations, which is where it touches the insolvency side of the practice.
[LINK] Corporate simplification
How a restructuring process actually runs
Companies arrive at this expecting something abstract. In practice the restructuring process follows a fairly consistent sequence, and knowing it makes the whole thing less daunting.

Establish the facts. What the company actually owes, to whom, secured or unsecured, and what the cash position looks like week by week rather than month by month. A surprising number of companies cannot answer this on day one, and nothing useful happens until they can
Test viability. Strip out the financing problem and ask whether the trading business generates cash. This is the independent business review question, and it determines everything that follows

Map the stakeholders. Lenders, HMRC, landlords, key suppliers, shareholders and employees all have different interests and different degrees of power over the outcome. A restructuring that ignores one of them tends to fail at exactly the point that stakeholder notices
Build the plan. What changes, in what order, funded how, over what period. The plan has to be credible to the people being asked to support it, not merely to you
Negotiate. Lenders and creditors are asked to agree new terms. Companies that come with evidence get better outcomes than companies that come with optimism
Implement and monitor. The plan runs, and performance is measured against the forecast every month. Corporate restructuring fails more often through poor follow-through than poor design
Most of the value sits in the first two steps. Companies that get an honest answer on viability early either save a great deal of money or stop spending it on something that was never going to work.

The output of all this is a restructuring plan: a written document setting out the financial position, the changes proposed, the funding required and the forecast that results. Lenders and other companies in the chain will judge you on that plan, so it needs to survive scrutiny rather than merely sound encouraging. A restructuring plan built on assets nobody has valued, or on financial projections that assume the last three years were unrepresentative, will not.
Getting the stakeholders onside
Business restructuring is, in the end, a negotiation with stakeholders who have money at risk. Each of them behaves differently and each needs handling.
Lenders

A secured lender's first instinct is to protect its position, which usually means it would rather support a credible plan than enforce and recover less. What it will not tolerate is surprises, or forecasts that turn out to be optimistic. Lenders often commission an independent business review before agreeing anything, and it is better to expect that than to resist it.
HMRC

Frequently the largest unsecured creditor in an owner-managed company. HMRC will discuss Time to Pay, and is considerably more receptive before enforcement has started than after. Where tax debt is the core problem, engaging early is the single highest-value action available.
Key suppliers

A supplier that cannot be replaced has more sway than the size of its debt suggests. Identify those companies early. Some will support a restructuring for the sake of the ongoing relationship if they are told what is happening.
Shareholders
Restructuring often changes the shareholding, particularly where new money comes in. Owner-managers should understand what dilution they are accepting before agreeing to funding, not after.
Employees
Rarely consulted, frequently the people who know where the money is going. They also notice long before any announcement, and silence is generally read as worse news than the truth.
Where restructuring meets the formal procedures
There is no hard border between restructuring and insolvency. Several formal procedures are restructuring tools, and choosing one does not mean the business is finished.

A company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] is a restructuring of the ordinary unsecured debt, binding those creditors to a repayment plan while the company keeps trading and the directors stay in control. Secured creditors keep their security and preferential creditors keep their priority unless they agree otherwise. Administration [link to /insolvency/administration] provides a statutory moratorium, holding creditors off while a rescue or a sale is arranged, and a pre-pack administration does that with a buyer already lined up. Each requires a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] to take an appointment, so each is a formal insolvency procedure, but the purpose of all three is preserving something rather than ending it.

On the solvent side, corporate simplification [link to /restructuring/corporate-simplification] and exit planning [link to /restructuring/exit-planning] use a members' voluntary liquidation to close down companies that have served their purpose, which is restructuring of a very different kind: tidying a group rather than rescuing one.

What decides between an informal restructuring and a formal procedure is usually whether anyone can block it. If creditors will agree to new terms voluntarily, no formal process is needed. If one creditor can block a sensible outcome that everyone else supports, a procedure that binds the minority becomes the only route. Where the dissenting creditors are ordinary unsecured ones, that is the practical case for a CVA. Where the creditor holding things up is secured or preferential, a CVA cannot bind them without their agreement, and a restructuring plan under Part 26A of the Companies Act 2006 is the procedure that can. Either option is worth understanding before it is needed rather than after.

Directors sometimes resist involving an insolvency practitioner at all, on the reasonable-sounding basis that doing so makes the situation official. In practice an insolvency practitioner advising on options has taken no appointment and nothing is formal, and their view on whether administration or a CVA would work is worth having early. The point at which you cannot avoid an insolvency practitioner is the point at which you have lost the ability to choose which one.
When restructuring is the right call
Some patterns come up repeatedly, and they are worth recognising early.

Profitable but out of cash. A business can be trading well and still be unable to pay its debts as they fall due. That is a working capital and funding problem, not an insolvency one, and it is very fixable
One loss-making part dragging the rest down. Where a group or a division is the problem, restructuring can isolate it without losing what works
A lender getting nervous. Covenant pressure or a facility coming up for renewal is a reason to act now, with a plan, rather than wait to be asked
The numbers have stopped being trustworthy. If management information is poor, nobody, including you, actually knows whether the business works. That is fixable and it is usually first
A change of ownership coming. Retirement, a departing shareholder, or a sale in mind, all of which go better with two years' preparation than two months'
When it is not
We would rather say this here than after taking a fee.

Restructuring will not save a business whose product or market has gone. It will not fix companies that cannot generate cash at any plausible cost base. And it will not help where the position has already deteriorated so far that creditors have taken control of the timetable, which is what a winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition] effectively does.

Where that is the case, the options move to the insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] side of the practice: a company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] if the business is viable but the debt is not, administration [link to /insolvency/administration] if protection and a sale are needed, or liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] if the answer is closure. Knowing which side of that line you are on is exactly what the first conversation establishes.
Refinancing, and when new money is the answer

Refinancing is often the cleanest form of debt restructuring available. Where a business is fundamentally sound but the debt is the wrong shape, replacing expensive short-term borrowing with facilities that match the trading cycle can solve the problem without changing anything else.

The usual candidates are invoice finance where cash is tied up in the sales ledger, asset finance to release value from equipment, and refinancing property to spread repayment over a sensible horizon. Companies in the same industry frequently use quite different funding structures, and the mix that suits a contractor is not the one that suits a manufacturer.

Two cautions. Refinancing that simply buys time without changing the underlying economics postpones the problem and adds cost to it. And most new facilities will require personal guarantees, so a director should understand exactly what they are signing before improved cash flow makes it feel routine.
We are advisers rather than brokers. Where funding is the answer we will say so and introduce you to people who arrange it, and we will tell you plainly if we think more debt is the wrong medicine.
Selling, buying, and reshaping the group

Not all corporate restructuring is defensive. Mergers and acquisitions are restructuring tools, and for companies in a difficult position a sale of part of the business is frequently the fastest route to stability.

Selling a profitable division to fund the rest is a legitimate and often overlooked option. So are acquisitions of the assets of companies that fail, which is how a good deal of consolidation in any industry actually happens. Both need the same groundwork: clean numbers, a defensible valuation, and enough time to run a proper process rather than a distressed one. Mergers need that groundwork twice, once for each side.

For groups, the work is frequently about efficiency rather than survival. Dormant companies still carry filing obligations, director duties and annual cost, even where they qualify for audit exemption. Removing them reduces cost and risk, and that is what corporate simplification does.

Where a sale cannot be arranged in the ordinary way because time has run out, a pre-pack administration can achieve one immediately. It is a legitimate route, and a sale to a connected party within the first eight weeks needs either creditor approval or an independent evaluator's report, precisely because it moves fast.
Why the timing is a legal question, not only a commercial one

Directors owe their duties to the company, and normally that means to the shareholders. Once a company is insolvent or bordering on insolvency, or an insolvent liquidation or administration becomes probable, those duties shift and creditors' interests have to be taken into account. The Supreme Court settled the point in 2022 and was clear that a distant risk of trouble is not enough to engage it: the company has to be at or near the line.

That matters here because it is the same line this whole section is about. Carrying on and hoping, once you knew or should have concluded there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding an insolvent liquidation or administration, is what wrongful trading means, and it can be met with an order to contribute personally to the company's assets. Taking advice, documenting what you decided and why, and acting on it is the practical answer, and it is another reason the date on which you pick up the phone matters more than the sophistication of the plan.
Why the timing matters more than the technique

The single biggest determinant of outcome in business restructuring is when someone picks up the phone. Not the sophistication of the plan, not the size of the adviser, not the finance available. The date.

A company with six months of runway has access to funding, can negotiate with creditors from a position of choice, can sell an asset properly rather than quickly, and can plan a restructuring over a sensible horizon. The same company with six weeks of runway has almost none of that, and the same advisers will be recommending very different things.

Directors delay for understandable reasons: it feels like admitting failure, they expect a big invoice, or they think asking for advice starts something formal. None of those is true of an initial conversation, and the cost of waiting is usually far higher than the cost of asking.
Where we fit

Lancefield advises. We do not take insolvency appointments, which matters more in this section than anywhere else on the site, because it means we have no interest in whether your restructuring succeeds or fails. A firm whose income comes from formal appointments has a quiet incentive that we do not have.
We work alongside your existing accountants rather than replacing them, and we bring in licensed insolvency practitioners, lenders or solicitors where a specific piece of work needs them.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between restructuring and insolvency?

Restructuring is a set of voluntary changes made while the company still controls its own decisions. Insolvency is a formal statutory procedure, usually involving a licensed insolvency practitioner taking an appointment. The practical difference is control: in restructuring you still have it. Many companies end up in a formal procedure precisely because restructuring was left too late.
Does restructuring mean redundancies?

Sometimes, but not always, and less often than people assume. A restructuring might be entirely financial: renegotiating debt, changing facilities, or improving how working capital is managed. Where headcount is involved it is usually because a specific activity is loss-making rather than because of a general cut.
Will our lender have to know?

In most cases yes, and generally that is to your advantage. Lenders respond considerably better to a director who arrives with a plan than to one who stops communicating. A lender that discovers a problem itself will react more conservatively than one brought into the conversation early.
How long does a restructuring take?

A review to establish the position takes weeks. The rest of the restructuring process takes months, sometimes longer where funding or a sale is involved. What it should never be is instant, and anyone promising a fast structural fix is describing something else.
Can you help if we are already in difficulty?

Yes, and the earlier the better. Even where formal insolvency turns out to be the right answer, going into it with the position properly understood produces a better outcome than arriving at it by default.
Do you work with our existing accountant?

Routinely. Your accountant knows the business and handles the compliance work; we handle the specific restructuring question. Replacing them is rarely in anyone's interest and it is not what we are there for.

/restructuring/turnaround
Business turnaround
[IMAGE] "Is your business a turnaround, or something else?": three cards, and the most important element on the page.

A turnaround is the work of fixing an underperforming company while it is still a going concern: finding what is actually causing the problem, stabilising the cash position, and changing the things that made the business lose money in the first place. It is the service that sits furthest from insolvency on this site, and the one that most often makes the rest of it unnecessary.

Most turnaround work starts late. By the time an owner accepts that the pattern is not going to correct itself, they have usually spent a year telling themselves it is a temporary dip. The businesses that recover are rarely the strongest ones. They are the ones that got help while there was still enough liquidity to act.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
Is your business a turnaround, or something else?
We take no insolvency appointments, so we have nothing to gain from calling your situation worse than it is, or better. Three honest categories:
Too early

The business is profitable but under strain: growing faster than its working capital allows, or carrying a cost base that has drifted. This is ordinary management improvement and often does not need a turnaround specialist at all. What it may need is a hard look at the numbers, which is what an independent review [link to /restructuring/independent-business-review] gives you.
A turnaround

The business is losing money or barely covering its costs, cash is tight, and the causes are structural rather than one-off. There is still a viable business underneath, there are still stakeholders willing to be talked to, and there is enough liquidity to make changes before they run out. This is the page you want.
Past turnaround

The debt is beyond what the business could service even if it performed perfectly, or the market it serves has gone. Change alone will not fix that. What is needed is a company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] to deal with the historic debt, administration [link to /insolvency/administration] to protect and sell what is worth saving, or an orderly winding the company up [link to /insolvency/liquidation]. Spending six months on a turnaround here consumes the value that would have paid creditors.
Most people arrive convinced they are in the second category. A fair number are in the first or third. Establishing which is the first thing worth paying for, and it takes days rather than months.
What actually causes it
[IMAGE] "What actually causes it": the growth or waterfall vector panel would fit.
After enough of these, the causes repeat. It is almost never the reason the owner gives first.

Margin erosion nobody tracked. Prices held while costs rose. The business is as busy as ever and makes less on every job. This is the single most common cause we see in owner-managed businesses, and the most fixable
Working capital swallowed by growth. More sales, more stock, more debtors, and the cash gap widens. A profitable company can run out of money this way and frequently does
A cost base built for a bigger business than the one that now exists, or for a market that has moved
One customer, one contract or one supplier carrying too much of the risk. When it goes, there is no cushion
Management information that arrives too late to act on. Accounts three months in arrears mean every decision is made about a business that no longer exists
Debt taken on for the wrong reason, or on terms the business could only service in a good year
A problem the owner already knows about and has not addressed, usually because it involves a person

The diagnosis matters because the wrong one is expensive. Cutting costs in a business whose real problem is pricing makes it smaller and no more profitable, and it is the most common wasted year in this work.
The first ninety days
[IMAGE] "The first ninety days": numbered flow.
Turnaround work front-loads. What happens in the first three months decides whether there is a business to improve.

Stabilise the cash. A weekly short-term cash forecast, built properly and updated every week, replacing the monthly management accounts as the instrument you steer by. Almost every business we work with does not have one when we arrive, and every one of them keeps it afterwards

Establish the true position. What the business actually owes, to whom, and when. What it is actually owed and how much of that will really arrive. Where the liquidity is trapped: stock, debtors, work in progress, an overdrawn account nobody has looked at

Find the profit by product, customer and job. Not the overall margin. The distribution. There is nearly always a segment losing money that the average conceals, and finding it is often the whole answer
Buy time with the people who can grant it. HMRC, the bank, the landlord, key suppliers. Approached early with a credible plan, most will work with you. Approached after a default, most will not
Decide what stops. The loss-making line, the customer who never pays, the site that does not work. These decisions get harder the longer they wait and they are the ones owners most want to defer
Fix the reporting. Whatever the plan, it needs numbers that arrive within days rather than months. Without that, nobody can tell whether the turnaround is working
Stabilisation is not the same as recovery. It buys the room in which the actual changes can be made, and a plan that stops at stabilisation simply postpones the problem.
Getting the stakeholders to hold
A turnaround is as much a negotiation as an operational exercise, because everyone with a claim on the business can end it while you are still fixing it.

The bank or lender. Wants to know that someone competent has their hands on it and that the information is reliable. Lenders support turnarounds far more often than directors expect; what they will not tolerate is being surprised. If yours has commissioned an independent review [link to /restructuring/independent-business-review], that is a signal to engage, not to retreat

HMRC. Usually the largest creditor in a struggling small company. Time to Pay is available and is granted on a realistic proposal, but arrears that keep building while other creditors are paid become a conduct issue later

Suppliers. Continuity of supply is often the thing the business cannot survive losing. Key suppliers generally prefer a customer that recovers to one that fails owing them money, and will say so if asked honestly

Employees. The people who will deliver the changes and the ones who see the wobble first. Uncertainty costs you the staff you can least afford to lose. What you can say may be limited, but silence is read as the worst case
Shareholders and family. In an owner-managed business these are often the same people, and the emotional weight of the decisions sits with them
The common thread is that early, honest contact preserves support, and late contact destroys it. That is not a moral observation. It is what we watch happen.
The plan, and making it survive

A turnaround plan is a small number of specific changes with owners, dates and a number attached to each. Anything longer than a page or two is a report rather than a plan, and reports do not change businesses.

What separates the plans that work is that someone is held to them weekly, that the financial performance is measured against the forecast rather than against last year, and that the difficult item is still on the agenda in week three. That is where an outside adviser earns their fee: not for knowing what needs doing, which the owner usually does, but for making sure it happens and for saying the thing everyone in the business is avoiding.

Where the numbers show the plan is not working, the plan changes or the route changes. A turnaround that misses its targets month after month is consuming the value that other options would have preserved, and knowing when to stop is part of the discipline.
Trading on while insolvent: the line to watch
This is the part that generic turnaround advice leaves out, and it matters more than any of the commercial work.

If the company is or becomes unable to pay its debts, a director's duties shift towards the interests of creditors. Continuing to trade past the point where insolvent liquidation or administration could no longer realistically be avoided, with the creditors worse off as a result, is wrongful trading, and it can carry personal liability.

That does not mean a turnaround is dangerous. It means a turnaround needs a documented basis: a plan that a reasonable director could believe in, contemporaneous evidence of the advice taken and the reasoning applied, and a review point at which you will stop if it is not working. Directors who do that are in a materially stronger position than those who simply pressed on, and our contingency planning [link to /restructuring/contingency-planning] page covers how to build the fallback alongside the plan.
The practical rule: take advice at the point when you first wonder whether you should, not at the point when someone tells you that you must.
When a turnaround needs something formal alongside it
Operational change fixes the future. It does not remove what the company already owes, and where the historic debt is the binding constraint, the commercial work needs a formal instrument beside it.
Debt restructuring [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring] where the borrowing is serviceable on different terms: reprofiled repayments, consolidated facilities, or new money on a realistic basis
A [link: CVA] where the debt is beyond renegotiation but the trading business is sound. It binds the whole unsecured creditor body to a repayment plan and leaves the directors in control
Administration [link to /insolvency/administration], where the business needs protection from creditors while the change is made or a sale arranged
A [link: pre-pack administration], where the trade is viable but the company is not, and the value would be lost in a public process

Running the commercial turnaround and the formal route in parallel is normal and often the best outcome. What does not work is doing the operational work for a year first and reaching the formal conversation with the value already spent.
Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes your administrator or liquidator, so we have no interest in a turnaround failing and no reason to recommend a formal procedure that would generate a fee for us.

What we do is establish quickly whether there is a viable business under the problem, tell you honestly which of the three categories at the top of this page you are in, and then either do the work with you or tell you it is not needed. Where a licensed appointment is genuinely required, we bring in an insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] we know and trust and stay alongside you through it.

We work with owner-managed businesses across Scotland, in the sectors where this comes up most: hospitality and leisure, construction and the supply chain around it. Big Four restructuring experience, applied at a scale where the owner is in the room.
Frequently asked questions
How long does a turnaround take?

Stabilisation is usually the first ninety days. Genuine recovery, meaning a business that is reliably profitable again rather than merely surviving, is more often twelve to eighteen months. Anyone promising a faster structural change is describing cost-cutting, which is not the same thing.
What does turnaround support cost?

It depends entirely on scope: a diagnostic review is a fixed fee and modest, while hands-on implementation over months is not. We scope and price it before starting, and we will tell you if the likely benefit does not justify the cost.
Will the bank find out we have taken advice?

Not from us. Advice is confidential and nothing is filed or published. In practice, though, telling a lender you have brought in specialist support usually helps rather than harms: it is evidence that the problem is being managed, which is what they want to see.
Can a turnaround work if we already owe HMRC?

Frequently, yes. HMRC arrears are the norm in this work rather than the exception, and Time to Pay is available on a realistic proposal. What causes the damage is arrears that keep growing while other creditors are paid, because that becomes a conduct question in any later insolvency.
What if it does not work?

Then you find that out with more options open than you would have had otherwise, and with a documented record of having acted responsibly. That is why the review points and the fallback plan matter. A turnaround that fails having been properly run leaves a director in a very different position from one that simply drifted.
Is this the same as an insolvency process?

No. A turnaround is a commercial exercise in an ongoing business, with no court, no appointment, no publicity and no register entry. It can run alongside a formal procedure where the historic debt needs dealing with, but by itself it is simply management change with outside help.

/restructuring/debt-restructuring
Debt restructuring

Corporate debt restructuring means changing what a company owes, or when and how it repays, so that the financial obligations match what the business can actually generate. It covers everything from reprofiling a single loan to a full renegotiation across several lenders, and it is the right answer where the trading business works but the borrowing on top of it does not. Some of it is balance sheet restructuring; most of it, in an owner-managed company, is simpler than that.

The question that decides whether debt restructuring will succeed is simple, and it is worth asking before anything else. Is this a company that can service its borrowing on different terms, or one that cannot service it at all? Restructuring solves the first. It only postpones the second, and postponing costs money that would otherwise have gone to creditors.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
When debt restructuring is the right answer
We take no insolvency appointments and we are not brokers, so we are not paid by the outcome. The honest test has three parts.

The business is viable on its own terms. Strip out the debt service and the company makes money, or would within a reasonable period. If it does not, the problem is the trade and a turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] comes first

The borrowing is serviceable on some realistic profile. A longer loan term, a lower interest rate, a payment holiday, interest-only for a period, or a smaller principal after a partial repayment. If no realistic profile works, the answer is a CVA [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva], administration [link to /insolvency/administration] or a liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation], and the question becomes an insolvency one rather than a refinancing one

The lenders have a reason to say yes. A lender agrees to a restructuring plan when it expects to recover more that way than by enforcing. Your job, and ours, is to show that arithmetic honestly, with a cash flow that supports it

Where all three hold, debt restructuring is usually achievable and often undramatic. Where the third fails because the security covers the debt comfortably, expect a harder conversation: a lender that is fully covered has less to lose from enforcing.
The options, and what each is actually for
[IMAGE] "The options, and what each is actually for": six cards, 3+3.
Reprofiling the repayments

Extending the loan term, moving to interest-only for a period, or agreeing a payment holiday, the measures a lender groups under the heading of forbearance. The cheapest and most common form of debt management, and the one most often agreed, because the lender keeps its principal, its interest rate and its security and simply waits longer. It suits a company with a temporary cash flow squeeze and a credible recovery, and it is where most debt restructuring in owner-managed businesses begins and ends.
Debt consolidation and refinancing

Replacing several facilities with one, or moving to a different lender on a better interest rate. Debt consolidation simplifies the covenants and often reduces the monthly cost, but consolidation does not reduce what is owed. Where refinancing is the route, we introduce you to a finance and funding [link to /finance-and-funding] specialist rather than acting as broker ourselves.
Releasing trapped working capital

Often the fastest improvement available and frequently missed. Invoice finance against the debtor book, asset finance against plant already owned, or a sale and leaseback of property. It changes the shape of the balance sheet rather than the size of the debt, and it can create the room a restructuring needs.
Debt for equity

Debt-for-equity swaps exchange some of what a lender is owed for a shareholding. A debt-for-equity swap removes borrowing permanently and is standard practice in larger corporate debt restructurings, where bondholders and lending syndicates sit around the table, but it dilutes the owner and is rare in owner-managed businesses because the creditor rarely wants the shares. Worth knowing about; worth being realistic about.
A negotiated write-down

A creditor accepts less than the full amount to settle. It happens, usually where the alternative is demonstrably worse for them, and it needs evidence rather than argument. Informally agreed write-downs bind only the creditors who sign, which is their limitation.
A formal arrangement

Where the unsecured creditor body is too large or too fragmented to negotiate with individually, a CVA [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] binds all of them to a repayment plan once 75% by value approve it and a majority of the unconnected creditors do not vote it down. It is the instrument for exactly the situation informal restructuring cannot reach.
HMRC, and why it is different
In most owner-managed companies HMRC is the largest creditor, and it does not behave like a bank.

Time to Pay is a genuine and widely granted arrangement, but it is a payment plan rather than a restructuring of the debt: HMRC expects the full amount, and expects you to keep filing and paying current taxes, or to come back and ask for a new bill to be added to the plan. A proposal that assumes a write-down of taxes is not a proposal HMRC will engage with, and a second Time to Pay arrangement after a first one failed is a much harder conversation than the first.

What causes lasting damage is letting arrears of taxes build while other creditors are paid. Beyond the immediate risk of enforcement, it is exactly the kind of conduct an insolvency practitioner has to report on if the company later fails, and it is treated as a conduct issue rather than a commercial one.
What lenders actually agree to
[IMAGE] "What lenders actually agree to": the scales vector panel fits.
We sit on both sides of these conversations, and the pattern is consistent.
They will extend time far more readily than they will reduce principal. Time costs them margin. A write-down costs them capital and has to be justified internally

They want reliable information, presented once. A short-term cash flow forecast, a realistic set of assumptions, and an explanation of what went wrong that does not blame the weather. Borrowers routinely underestimate how much credibility a well-built cash flow buys

They will commission their own view. An independent business review [link to /restructuring/independent-business-review] is the normal step for anything material, and it is a signal to engage rather than to panic. The review establishes the facts everyone then negotiates around

They want to see the equity contribute. Where owners are asking a lender to wait, lenders ask what the shareholders are putting in. Sometimes that is money; more often it is deferred remuneration, a director's loan left in place, or a personal guarantee

They will not restructure into a loss. If enforcing recovers more than waiting, they enforce, and the conversation turns into an insolvency one. Where a lender holds a fixed charge over property, that may mean an LPA receivership [link to /insolvency/lpa-receivership] in England and Wales or enforcement of a standard security in Scotland
They move faster on a live default than on a warning. Approach before the covenant breaks, not after
None of that is unreasonable, and understanding it changes how the proposal is written. Most failed restructurings we see failed on presentation rather than on substance.
The restructuring process
[IMAGE] "The restructuring process": numbered flow.
The debt restructuring process is the same whether one lender is involved or five, and it runs in a set order.

Establish the real position. The financial obligations in full: total borrowing, interest rate and loan term on each facility, security, covenants, personal guarantees. What is secured on what, and in what order. Directors frequently do not have this in one place, and it is where the work starts

Build the forecast. Weekly short-term cash flow, and a longer projection showing what the business can service. It has to survive a lender's scrutiny, so the assumptions matter more than the presentation
Identify what is achievable. Which of the restructuring options above fit the facts, what each would deliver, and which lenders and other stakeholders need to agree to what

Prepare the proposal. One document, consistent across every lender, showing the position, the plan and what each creditor is being asked for. Different stories to different lenders is the fastest way to lose the room
Negotiate. Usually several rounds with the stakeholders in turn. Secured lenders first, since their consent frequently conditions everyone else's
Document it. Amended facility agreements, new security, waivers, standstill agreements. This is solicitors' work and it is not the place to economise
Monitor and report. Restructured facilities come with tighter reporting and covenants. Meeting them is what keeps the arrangement alive and the stakeholders committed

Timescales for the debt restructuring process run from a few weeks for a single-lender reprofiling to several months where there are multiple secured creditors, pension obligations or a formal arrangement involved.
What it means for you as a director
Two things to be clear-eyed about.

First, personal guarantees normally survive a restructuring unless the lender expressly releases them, and lenders rarely do. That matters most on unsecured business loans [link to /finance-and-funding/unsecured-business-loans], where the guarantee is often the only security the lender has. If anything, a restructuring is the moment a lender asks for more security rather than less. Establish what you have already guaranteed before you negotiate, because it changes what you should be willing to agree to. Where a guarantee is called, that becomes a personal debt matter, with bankruptcy (sequestration in Scotland) at the far end of it, and our Debt Help Scotland [link to /debt-help-scotland] section covers the options.

Second, restructuring while insolvent carries the same duties as trading while insolvent. If the company is or becomes unable to pay its debts, your duties shift towards creditors as a whole, and a restructuring that a reasonable director could not have believed in is not a defence. Take advice, document the basis of the plan, and set a review point at which you stop. Our contingency planning [link to /restructuring/contingency-planning] page covers building the fallback in parallel, which is what turns a restructuring attempt into a reasoned decision rather than a gamble.
When debt restructuring is the wrong answer
It is worth saying plainly, because nobody else on this subject does.

Where the borrowing could never be repaid on any realistic profile. Debt restructuring here buys months and spends the value that would have gone to creditors, and the honest answer is insolvency advice
Where the trade itself has stopped working. New terms on the borrowing do not fix a business that loses money before debt service
Where the only new money available is expensive short-term borrowing taken to service existing debt. This is the most common route from a difficult position to an impossible one

Where a single creditor can and will enforce regardless. If a winding up petition is coming, the timetable is no longer yours and the winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition] page is the more urgent read
In each of those, the better outcomes come from the formal insolvency routes: a CVA, administration, or an orderly liquidation while there is still something to distribute.
Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments and does not lend or broker. Nobody here earns a commission on a facility or a fee from an appointment, which means we have no interest in your debt restructuring being bigger, faster or more formal than it needs to be.

What we do is establish what the company can genuinely service, build the case, and put it to your lenders in a form they can say yes to. Where the honest answer is that the debt cannot be restructured into something serviceable, we say so early, while the alternatives are still worth having. Where new money is the answer, we introduce a specialist rather than arranging it ourselves.
We advise lenders and other creditors too, which is the reason we can tell you in advance what yours is likely to accept.
Frequently asked questions
What is corporate debt restructuring?

It means changing the terms of what a company owes so that repayment fits what the business generates. That can mean a longer loan term, a lower interest rate, a payment holiday, debt consolidation, debt-for-equity swaps, or a negotiated reduction. It is agreed with creditors rather than imposed, which is the difference between it and a formal insolvency procedure.
Is this the same as debt settlement, or bankruptcy?

No. This page covers corporate debt restructuring: a company renegotiating its financial obligations with its own lenders. It is not the consumer debt settlement plans advertised for personal loan and credit card balances, and it is not sovereign debt restructuring, where a government renegotiates with its bondholders. Nor is it bankruptcy, which in the UK is a personal insolvency procedure (sequestration in Scotland) rather than something that happens to a company. The nearest formal company procedures are a CVA and administration.
Will my lender agree?

A lender agrees when it expects to recover more by agreeing than by enforcing. That makes it an evidence question rather than a persuasion one. Reliable forecasts, an honest account of what went wrong, and a plan the numbers support are what move it. A lender that is fully covered by its security has less reason to wait, and that is worth knowing before you start.
Does restructuring damage the company's credit rating?

Renegotiated terms, missed payments and any formal arrangement are visible to credit reference agencies, and a supplier who checks the company's credit score will see it. That is the company's record rather than your personal credit score; the two are separate files. It is a real cost and worth weighing. It is a smaller cost than a default or an insolvency procedure, which is the comparison that matters.
Can I restructure a bounce back loan or a CBILS facility?

Sometimes. Those facilities carry a government guarantee to the lender, which changes the lender's incentives and limits what it can agree to unilaterally. Pay As You Grow options exist on bounce back loans. Ask the lender what flexibility the scheme rules leave it, because the answer differs by product and by bank.
How long does it take?

A single-lender reprofiling of the loan term can be agreed in weeks. A multi-creditor debt restructuring with security to redocument runs to several months. The timetable is usually set by whichever lender is slowest to commit, and by how long it takes to produce information they trust.
What is the difference between this and a CVA?

Corporate debt restructuring is consensual and binds only the creditors who agree to it. A CVA is a formal procedure under the insolvency legislation, and it binds every unsecured creditor once 75% by value approve it, provided more than half the unconnected creditors do not vote against. Where a handful of creditors can be negotiated with, restructure. Where there are too many, or one refuses to move, the formal route reaches further.

We take no appointments, and we neither broker nor arrange facilities, so the answer you get is the one the numbers support. One conversation will tell you whether a restructuring is achievable and what your lenders are likely to accept.

Optimised exit planning

Business exit planning is the work of getting a business ready to leave: settling on an exit strategy, which means deciding which route out fits, then spending the time before the exit making the company worth more to whoever takes it on, or making a closure orderly rather than forced. All business owners exit eventually. The difference between a planned exit and an unplanned one is usually measured in years of preparation and a substantial share of the value.

The uncomfortable part is that most owner-managed businesses are not saleable in the form their owner imagines. Not because they are bad businesses, but because they depend on the owner, or the numbers do not evidence what the owner knows to be true, or there is no obvious buyer for that size of company in that sector. All three are fixable with enough notice. None is fixable in the last six months.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
The routes out
[IMAGE] "The routes out": five cards, 3+2 per the count-aware grid.

There are five, and a business exit strategy is simply one of them with a date attached. The honest work is establishing which of them your business actually supports rather than which one you had in mind.
Trade sale

Selling to a competitor, a supplier, a customer or a consolidator. Usually the highest price, because a trade buyer can strip out duplicated cost and buys market share as well as profit. It is also the most intrusive process: full due diligence, warranties, and a buyer who will know everything about the business before completion.
Sale to a financial buyer

Private equity or an investment company: an investor buying for a return rather than an operator buying for strategic fit. Realistic for businesses above a certain scale and profitability, with growth opportunities an investor is prepared to fund, and usually structured so that some of the price depends on financial performance targets being met after completion. Owners frequently stay on for a period, which is either the attraction or the problem depending on the owner.
Management buyout

Selling to the management team, often funded partly by the business itself over time. The price is normally lower than a trade sale but the process is faster, more private, and business operations continue in familiar hands. It works where there is a management team capable of running it without you, which is the same thing that makes a trade sale easier.
Family succession

Passing the business to family members, usually the next generation. The financial questions are the easy part; governance, fairness between family members who are in the business and those who are not, and whether the successor actually wants it, and has their own vision for it, are the hard ones. Started early, succession planning works well. Assumed rather than planned, it is how family businesses fail.
Solvent closure

Where there is no buyer, or where the business is genuinely the owner and does not survive without them, the right answer is to stop while the company is solvent, pay everyone in full, and take the reserves out as capital through an MVL [link to /insolvency/members-voluntary-liquidation-mvl]. This is a legitimate and frequently optimal exit, not a failure, and it is the route the rest of the internet does not discuss.
A sixth route exists and is worth naming so nobody drifts into it: running the business until it stops. That is not an exit strategy, and it converts a solvent closure into an insolvent one.
Why the work starts years ahead
[IMAGE] "Why the work starts years ahead": the growth or clock vector panel.
The value of a business at exit is set long before the exit, by things that take time to change.

Owner dependence. If the customer relationships, the technical knowledge and the decisions all sit with you, a buyer is not buying a business, they are buying a job with your name on it. Building a management layer takes two to three years and is the single largest lever on price

The quality of the numbers. Buyers pay for evidenced profit, not explained profit. Clean management accounts, a defensible normalisation of the owner's remuneration and personal costs, and a couple of years of consistency are worth more than a good story
Customer concentration. One customer at forty per cent of revenue takes a visible chunk off the multiple, and diversifying takes years

Contracts and recurring revenue. Repeatable income is valued far above the same profit earned project by project. Where the business can be moved towards contracts, that shift in business strategy is worth making before the sale rather than describing during it

The awkward items. A property in the company that a buyer does not want, a related-party arrangement, dormant subsidiaries, a pension advisory [link to /financial-advisory/pension-advisory] issue, unresolved litigation. Each is a discount or a delay at due diligence, and each takes months to tidy. Corporate simplification [link to /restructuring/corporate-simplification] deals with the group-structure half of that

Your own position. What you need from the exit, your vision for what comes afterwards, how long you are prepared to stay, and the same questions for any other shareholders. Business owners who have not answered these negotiate badly
Two to three years is the usual horizon for material improvement. A year is enough to tidy and prepare. Under six months, you are selling what you have, in whatever market conditions you find.
What the business is actually worth
[IMAGE] "What the business is actually worth": a simple bridge from reported profit to adjusted earnings would help comprehension.

Most owner-managed businesses are valued on a multiple of sustainable earnings, adjusted for what a new owner would really face: your remuneration replaced with a market-rate manager, one-off items stripped out, and any personal costs removed. That adjusted figure is usually lower than the profit most business owners have in mind and higher than the one their accounts show, which is why the first honest valuation conversation is often uncomfortable.

The multiple applied depends on things a buyer can see rather than things you can assert: sector, scale, growth, recurring revenue, customer spread, market conditions at the time, and how much of the business walks out with you. Two companies with the same profit can be worth very different amounts, and the gap between them is exactly what business exit planning is for.

The structure matters as much as the headline. Cash at completion, deferred consideration, an earn-out tied to future performance targets, shares in the buyer, a period of consultancy. A high price mostly payable later, conditional on targets being met by a business you no longer control, is not the same as the number in the press release. Our corporate finance [link to /financial-advisory/corporate-finance] and transaction support [link to /financial-advisory/due-diligence] pages cover the deal side, including mergers and acquisitions.
Preparing the business
Build the management layer. Delegate genuinely, including the customer relationships. The test is whether business operations run for a month without you
Fix the reporting. Monthly management accounts that arrive within a fortnight and reconcile to the year end. Buyers discount uncertainty and this is where uncertainty shows
Normalise the accounts. Take the personal costs out, document the adjustments, and let a couple of clean years accumulate before you go to market
Sort the balance sheet. Deal with the director's loan account, the property, the dormant subsidiaries and the old assets. Anything a buyer has to ask about is a negotiating point for them

Secure what you are selling. Written customer contracts, employment contracts for key staff, registered intellectual property, any regulatory requirements met and documented, a lease with enough term left

Prepare for due diligence early. Assemble the financial records and other information a buyer's advisers will want before you need it. Deals fall over on delay and surprises far more often than on price
Almost all of this improves the business whether you sell or not, which is why the investment is worth making even where the exit is uncertain.
Tax, and the point of getting it right early

How an exit is structured determines how it is taxed, and the decisions that matter are made before a deal is agreed rather than after. Selling shares and selling the trade and assets produce very different outcomes for the seller. Business Asset Disposal Relief has qualifying conditions that must be met for a period before the disposal, so eligibility is something to check years ahead rather than assume at completion. Where the exit is a solvent closure, the distribution comes out as capital through a liquidation and there is a separate set of rules, covered on our MVL [link to /insolvency/members-voluntary-liquidation-mvl] page.

We are not tax advisers and this page is not tax advice. What we do is make sure the tax question is asked at the point when the answer can still change, and work alongside your accountant so that the structure and the tax position are decided together rather than sequentially.
When the honest answer is that there is no buyer

A meaningful share of owner-managed businesses cannot be sold at any price the owner would accept. The business is the owner, or the sector has no acquirers at that scale, or the profit does not survive replacing the owner's labour at market rate.

That is not a failure and it is not the end of the planning. It changes the objective: instead of maximising a sale price, you are maximising what the business generates between now and closure, and then closing it while it is solvent so the accumulated reserves come out to the shareholders efficiently. Done deliberately, that is frequently worth more than a distressed sale would have been, and it is entirely within your control.

What makes it go wrong is deciding too late. A business run past the point where it can pay its own way turns a solvent closure into an insolvent one, and the difference between an MVL [link to /insolvency/members-voluntary-liquidation-mvl] and a creditors' voluntary liquidation is the whole of the owner's remaining value plus an investigation into their conduct.
Where we fit
Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments and sells no investment or wealth management products. Nobody here earns a commission on what you do with the proceeds, and nobody becomes your liquidator.

That matters on this subject more than most, because the exit-planning field is largely populated by advisers whose interest begins after the money arrives. Ours does not. We are paid for the advice about the business, which means we can tell you the company is not saleable in its present form, or that the right exit is an orderly closure rather than the sale you were hoping for.

We work alongside your accountant and, where a sale is the route, corporate finance advisers who run the process. Where the exit is a solvent liquidation we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] to take the appointment. And where an independent review [link to /restructuring/independent-business-review] shows the business needs work before it is ready for either, we say so.
Frequently asked questions
How long before an exit should I start planning?

Two to three years for material improvement in what the business is worth, because the biggest levers all take that long: reducing owner dependence, evidencing profit, and spreading customer risk. A year is enough to tidy up and prepare properly. Below six months you are selling the business as it stands. Family succession usually runs on the same clock, because succession planning has to prepare the successor as well as the business.
What is my business worth?

Usually a multiple of sustainable earnings, adjusted for a market-rate replacement for you and stripped of one-off and personal items. The multiple depends on sector, scale, recurring revenue, customer concentration and how much of the business depends on the owner. Any figure quoted without those adjustments is a guess.
Should I tell my staff?

Not at the beginning, and not all at once. Key management usually need to know before a business sale process starts, particularly if a buyout is a possibility, if family members are taking over, or if they will be asked to meet a buyer. The rest of the team normally hears at or near completion. Confidentiality agreements and a controlled sequence are part of the planning.
What if I want to stay involved?

That is a legitimate objective and it shapes which business exit strategy fits. Financial buyers often want the owner to stay; trade buyers frequently do not want them for long; a management buyout or a family succession can be structured with a phased handover. Deciding what you actually want before you go to market is what stops it being decided for you.
Is closing the business a failure?

No. Where there is no buyer, closing a solvent company through a members' voluntary liquidation and taking the reserves out as capital is often the best available outcome and entirely respectable. What is a failure is running past the point of solvency and losing the choice.
Do I need a corporate finance adviser as well?

For a trade sale or a private equity deal, yes, and we work with them. Business exit planning is the years of preparation before the exit process; corporate finance is running the process itself. For a management buyout or a solvent closure the requirement is lighter, and often the accountant and ourselves are enough.
Closing call to action
Is the business ready for the exit you have in mind?

We take no appointments and sell no products, so we have no stake in which exit strategy you choose. One conversation will tell you what the business would realistically fetch, what would move that, what targets to set, and how long it needs.

/restructuring/independent-business-review
Independent business review

An independent business review, universally shortened to IBR, is an objective assessment of whether a business is viable and what its realistic prospects are. It is usually commissioned by a lender, normally paid for by the borrower, and produced by a firm that reports to the lender. If yours has just asked for one, that combination is the first thing to get straight, because it explains everything about how the process feels.

The second thing to get straight is what it means. Being asked for an IBR is not the bank calling in the debt. It is the bank saying it no longer has enough information to be comfortable and wants an independent view before it decides anything. That is a moment of risk, but it is also the point at which a well-handled business gets more time rather than less.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
Why your lender has asked for one
Something has changed in how the bank sees the account. Common triggers, in rough order of frequency:
A covenant breach, or a forecast that shows one coming
A facility approaching renewal where the numbers no longer support automatic rollover
Late or unreliable information. Management accounts that arrive months in arrears, or that do not reconcile to the statutory accounts, generate more anxiety than bad numbers delivered on time
A material change in performance: a loss, a big customer gone, margins visibly compressing
A request for more money, particularly if the last projection was missed
A move to the bank's business support or restructuring team, which almost always precedes a request for a review

Sector risk, where the lender is reviewing a whole book rather than singling you out. That is the moment a contingency planning [link to /restructuring/contingency-planning] exercise earns its keep, because you can see it coming

The trigger matters, because it tells you what the reviewer will be asked to focus on. A lender worried about a covenant wants to know about headroom and forecast reliability. One worried about a sector wants to know how exposed you are relative to peers.
What an IBR actually looks at
[IMAGE] "What an IBR actually looks at": eight-item list; the grid or layers vector panel fits.
Scope varies with the lender's concern, but the core is consistent.
The current financial position, verified rather than accepted. Real cash, real debtors, real creditors, real stock, and what the balance sheet does not show
Short-term cash flows. A thirteen-week cash flow forecast is the standard instrument, and the reviewer will test its assumptions rather than take them
The integrity of the forecasts. Not whether they are optimistic, which they usually are, but whether the assumptions behind them are defensible and whether previous forecasts were met
The business model and market. Where the profit comes from by product, customer and contract, and whether that is durable
Management. Whether the team has the information, the capability and the willingness to act. Reviewers form a view on this and it carries real weight
The funding structure. What is owed to whom, on what security, and whether the facilities fit the business

Options. What could be done: turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] measures, debt restructuring [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring], refinancing with another lender, asset sales, new equity from existing or outside investors, or a formal insolvency procedure
Downside. What the lender would recover in an insolvency, usually with an estimated outcome statement comparing scenarios
That last item is the one directors find hardest to see in a document about their own business. It is standard, it is in every IBR, and its presence does not mean anyone has decided anything.
Who sees it, and who pays

The lender commissions it and is the reviewer's client. The borrower almost always pays, under the facility terms that oblige the company to meet the lender's professional costs. The report goes to the lender, not to the company's wider creditors or other stakeholders. You will usually see it, and you should always ask to, but you are not entitled to it as of right unless the engagement says so.

That arrangement feels wrong the first time. It is standard across the industry and it is not a trap: the reviewer's value to the lender depends entirely on being independent, which means they are not simply writing what the bank wants to hear. A reviewer who produces an unbalanced report is worth nothing to the bank the next time.

What you can influence is the scope. Before it starts, ask what the terms of reference are, whether you will receive the report, and whether you will have the chance to comment on factual accuracy before it is issued. Reasonable lenders agree to all three.
How to come out of one well
[IMAGE] "How to come out of one well": the most valuable section on the page and worth visual emphasis.
This is the part no other page on the subject covers, and it makes a material difference.
Cooperate fully and quickly. Delay and reluctance are read as concealment, and the reviewer will say so in the report. Nothing costs a director more credibility

Get your own numbers straight first. If you can, produce the thirteen-week cash flow forecast before the reviewer asks. Arriving with it says more about management quality than anything you can assert

Do not present the optimistic case. Reviewers test forecasts for a living and an unrealistic one destroys trust in everything else you say. A conservative forecast that is then beaten is worth far more than an ambitious one that is missed
Have your own plan. A director who can set out a business plan with numbers attached changes the report. A director waiting to be told what to do also changes it
Bring your own adviser. You are entitled to advice on your side of this. Somebody who has written IBRs knows what the reviewer is testing and what a good answer looks like
Do not hide the bad item. It will be found, and being found is much worse than being told

The consistent pattern: reviewers are not looking for a perfect business. They are looking for management that understands its own position and is acting on it. That is what they report on, and it is largely within your control even when the numbers are not.
What happens afterwards
[IMAGE] "What happens afterwards": five outcomes, could work as an ordered scale from continued support to withdrawal.
The lender takes a decision, and the realistic range is narrower than most directors fear.
Continued support, unchanged. Common where the review shows a viable business with a temporary problem
Support with conditions. Tighter covenants, more frequent reporting, a monitoring role for the reviewer, or specific actions with deadlines. This is the most common outcome

A restructuring of the facilities. Reprofiled repayments, a new term, sometimes additional security. Our debt restructuring [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring] page covers what lenders typically agree to in these negotiations
A requirement to raise money or sell something. New equity, an asset disposal, or a sale of the business, usually with a timetable attached

Withdrawal of support. The rarest outcome, and one lenders reach reluctantly because enforcing usually recovers less than waiting. Where it happens, our administration [link to /insolvency/administration] and liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] pages set out what follows

A properly conducted IBR frequently helps the borrower, because it replaces the lender's anxiety with information and gives the negotiations that follow a shared set of facts. Businesses with a real problem and credible management come out of reviews with more time more often than not.
Pre-lend reviews, and commissioning one yourself
The same discipline is used at two other moments.

A pre-lend review is commissioned before a lender advances money rather than after it worries about it: the same testing of forecasts, model and management, applied to a proposal. Borrowers who go through one and are approved get better terms than they would have had, because the lender is pricing less uncertainty.

And a director can commission a review for their own purposes, which is the version we most often recommend. Where you suspect a problem but are not sure of its size, an independent assessment of your financial position gives you the facts before your lender asks for them, on your terms and with the report addressed to you. It is also the natural first step if you are considering an exit, since it establishes what a buyer's adviser will find. Our exit planning [link to /restructuring/exit-planning] page picks that up.
Where we fit
We do this work from both sides, and we are explicit about which side we are on in any engagement.

For lenders and other creditors, we conduct reviews: independent, evidenced and delivered on a timetable, with a clear view on viability and options rather than a description of the position. The wider restructuring [link to /restructuring] section sets out what happens next in each direction.

For directors, we advise on the other side of the table. What the reviewer will test, how to prepare, what to have ready, how to respond to a draft, what to do with the outcome, and how to handle the negotiations over the facilities that often follow. Because we take no insolvency appointments, we have no interest in the review concluding that a formal procedure is needed.
We do not act for both parties on the same engagement, and we say at the outset which role we are in.
Frequently asked questions
Does an IBR mean the bank is calling in our facility?

No. It means the bank wants an independent view before deciding anything. Withdrawal of support is the least common outcome, because enforcing typically recovers less than continuing to lend to a business that recovers. The review is the step before a decision, not the decision.
Do we have to pay for it?

Almost always, under the facility terms that require the borrower to meet the lender's professional costs. It is worth asking for a fee estimate and a defined scope before it starts, and reasonable lenders will provide both.
Do we get to see the report?

Usually, but ask at the outset rather than at the end. The reviewer's client is the lender, so disclosure to you, and to any other stakeholders, is a matter for the engagement terms. You should also ask for the chance to comment on factual accuracy before it is issued, which is normal and which most lenders agree to.
Can we choose who does it?
Typically the lender selects from firms it knows, though it will often accept a suggestion. What you can influence more usefully is the scope and the timetable.
How long does it take?

For an owner-managed business, usually two to four weeks from instruction to draft, depending on the state of the information. Poor management information is the single biggest cause of delay, and delay costs credibility as well as money.
Should we get our own advice?

Yes. The reviewer is not your adviser and cannot be. Having someone on your side who has written these reports changes how well you prepare and how the report reads, and it costs a fraction of the review itself. Contact [link to /contact] us before the reviewer arrives rather than after the draft lands.
Closing call to action
Has your lender asked for a review?

We conduct these for lenders and we advise directors going through them, and we tell you at the outset which side we are on. One conversation will tell you what the reviewer will test and how to be ready for it.
