/restructuring/corporate-simplification
Corporate simplification

Corporate simplification is the removal of dormant companies, redundant entities and duplicated ones from a group structure. Most organisations accumulate them without deciding to: an acquisition brings three subsidiaries with it, a trading name gets its own company, a joint venture ends but the entity does not, a property is held separately for reasons nobody can now recall. Each one carries filing obligations, professional fees, directors' duties and a small amount of risk, indefinitely, in return for nothing.

The work is straightforward and the benefit to the organisation is durable: lower costs, simpler corporate governance, and a group structure a lender or a buyer can follow. What makes it worth doing properly rather than quickly is the choice of how each company is closed, because the wrong route on a company holding reserves is expensive in a way that is difficult to reverse.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
What each dormant company actually costs you
Owners consistently underestimate this, because no single item is large.

Compliance costs. A confirmation statement for every entity, every year, whether or not it does anything, and accounts too unless the entity qualifies as an exempt dormant subsidiary. That exemption is bought by the parent guaranteeing the subsidiary's liabilities, which is rarely free. Then the finance team's time and the accountancy fee on top

Directors' duties. Every company needs directors, and those directors carry statutory duties to a company they have probably not thought about since 2019. That is a corporate governance exposure as much as an administrative one. Filing defaults attract a civil penalty against the company and a criminal offence against every director in default, and it is the conviction rather than the penalty that lands on the public record against a name

Risk that does not expire. Old trading liabilities, dilapidations on a lease nobody cancelled, warranties given on a disposal, a guarantee the group forgot it gave. A dormant company is not a closed one, claims can be brought against it, and if one of them cannot be met the entity is heading for a creditors' voluntary liquidation rather than a tidy closure
Audit and consolidation drag. More entities means more group reporting, more intercompany reconciliation, and more work for the finance team at every year end

Deal friction. In due diligence on a sale, a buyer's advisers examine every company in the group. Each dormant entity is a set of questions, a warranty and a potential retention. This is where the real cost lands, and it is why the tidy-up belongs in exit planning [link to /restructuring/exit-planning] rather than after it
Trapped value. Reserves sitting in a subsidiary that could be in the shareholders' hands
Individually, small. Across fifteen entities over ten years, a material and entirely avoidable running cost for the business.
The decision that matters: strike-off or solvent liquidation
[IMAGE] "The decision that matters": two cards side by side. This is the commercial heart of the page.
There are two ways to close a solvent company, and choosing between them is the whole of this exercise for any entity holding money.
Strike-off

An application to Companies House to dissolve the company. Cheap, simple, and the right answer for a genuinely empty entity. Its limit is tax: a distribution before strike-off is treated as capital only up to £25,000 in total, and only if the company is actually dissolved within two years and its debts and receivables have been settled. A pound over, or a dissolution that does not happen in time, and the whole amount is taxed as income, not just the excess, retrospectively if need be. A creditor can also object during the two-month Gazette period, and the registrar will not strike the company off while a valid objection stands.
Members' voluntary liquidation

A formal solvent liquidation conducted by a licensed insolvency practitioner. It costs more and takes longer, and in return the whole distribution is treated as capital however large it is, subject to the anti-phoenixing rule that recharacterises it as income where the shareholder carries on a similar trade within two years and tax avoidance was a main purpose, the company's affairs are formally closed off with a liquidator's final account, and creditors are dealt with properly rather than left to object. Our MVL [link to /insolvency/members-voluntary-liquidation-mvl] page covers it in full.

The practical rule across a group: strike off the genuinely empty entities, and put anything holding reserves above the threshold through an MVL. Our liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] page sets out how the solvent and insolvent routes differ. Getting that wrong on a single subsidiary can cost more than the whole simplification project. Note also that the twelve-month statutory test for solvency applies to each company separately, so each entity is assessed on its own position rather than the group's.
How the work runs
[IMAGE] "How the work runs": numbered flow.

Map the group structure. Every entity, its status, its accounts, what it owns and owes, who its directors are, and whether it is actually dormant or merely quiet. The management team is regularly surprised by what this turns up
Decide what each company is for. Anything with a business purpose stays. Every other entity is a candidate, and the burden is on keeping it rather than closing it

Do the diligence before closing. Intercompany balances, guarantees given, leases, contracts with change-of-control or dissolution clauses, pension participation, VAT group membership, registered intellectual property, and any bank account or asset still in that company's name. This diligence is the whole of the risk, and it is where a rushed project goes wrong

Deal with the assets. Transfer intellectual property, property and contracts to the entity that should hold them, settle intercompany balances, and distribute or transfer cash. Intra-group transfers have tax consequences and this is where your accountant earns their fee
Choose the route per entity. Strike-off or MVL, decided on the numbers rather than by default

Execute and close. Strike-off applications, or an MVL run by a licensed practitioner. A strike-off cannot be applied for if the company has traded, changed its name or disposed of trading property in the previous three months, or while any insolvency or scheme process is live, so that three-month clock starts when the entity actually goes quiet rather than when you decide to close it. Then final tax returns, deregistrations, and closing the bank accounts
Tidy what remains. Fewer entities, correct names, a structure chart someone can read

For a group of five to fifteen companies the whole exercise typically runs six to twelve months, governed less by the work than by tax clearances and the wait for dissolution, which follows three months after the liquidator's final account is registered. It is a project the finance function can run alongside its normal work rather than a service that takes the business over.
What to check before you close anything
Dissolution is difficult to undo and the assets of a dissolved company can pass to the Crown as ownerless property, so the diligence matters more than the closing.
Assets still in the company. A bank account, a small shareholding, a registered trade mark, a domain name, a property title never transferred. These are the ones that surface afterwards
Guarantees and cross-guarantees. Group borrowing frequently makes every company a guarantor. Closing one can breach the facility
Leases and dilapidations. A lease held by a dormant company is a live liability until it is assigned or surrendered
Employment history. Old employees, TUPE history, and any pension scheme the entity participated in
Litigation or claims, threatened or possible, including warranties given on an earlier sale

Whether it is really dormant. Dormant means no significant accounting transaction in the year, meaning one that has to go into the accounting records, and a single one is enough to break it. The confirmation statement fee and a handful of other registrar fees are specifically disregarded, which is why entities get wrongly assumed dormant in both directions. Where an entity turns out to be insolvent rather than dormant, the insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] page explains what changes

A company can be restored to the register after dissolution, but it is a court process. The cheaper administrative route exists only where the registrar struck the company off, not where you applied to strike it off yourself, so for a voluntary strike-off the court is the only way back. It costs considerably more than the check that would have avoided it.
Why it is worth doing before a sale

On any transaction, due diligence works through every company in the group. Dormant companies generate enquiries, and enquiries generate warranties, indemnities, retentions and delay. A group structure with four clean companies is a materially easier deal than the same business held through fourteen, and the difference shows up in the timetable, the legal fees and occasionally the price.

It is also work that cannot be done at the last minute. An MVL takes months, and a buyer will not wait for a tidy-up to complete. Two years before an intended exit is the right time, which is why this sits alongside exit planning [link to /restructuring/exit-planning] in the same restructuring [link to /restructuring] section. If you are not sure the group is ready, an independent review [link to /restructuring/independent-business-review] establishes the position first.
Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Where a solvent liquidation is the right route we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] to take the appointment, and we stay alongside you and your accountant through the project.

What we add is the decision-making rather than the filing: which entities can go, what diligence has to be done before each one does, and whether a strike-off or an MVL is right for each company on its own numbers. It is a service your accountant and your management team run with us rather than hand over. It is unglamorous work with a clear return, and it is the point where our restructuring and insolvency sides meet, since a solvent liquidation is an insolvency procedure used for an entirely positive purpose.
Frequently asked questions
What is corporate simplification?

Reducing the number of companies in a group by closing the dormant companies and redundant entities, having first moved any assets and dealt with any liabilities they hold. The aim is lower costs, less administration and less risk for the organisation, and a group structure that is easier to explain to a lender or a buyer.
Should we strike off or liquidate?

Strike off a genuinely empty company. Use an MVL where the company holds reserves above £25,000, because up to that figure a pre-strike-off distribution is treated as capital and above it the entire amount is taxed as income. Decide per entity, on its own numbers.
How long does it take?

Six to twelve months for a group of five to fifteen companies. Strike-offs complete in a few months; an MVL runs longer because of HMRC clearance and the period before dissolution. Preparation, moving assets and settling intercompany balances, is usually the longest part.
Can we reverse it if we close the wrong company?

A dissolved company can be restored to the register, but where you applied for the strike-off yourself the administrative route is not available and it has to be a court application, and in the general case within six years of dissolution. Assets left in the company at dissolution pass to the Crown as ownerless property, dealt with in Scotland by the King's and Lord Treasurer's Remembrancer. Which is why the checking stage matters far more than the closing stage.
Does this need an insolvency practitioner?

Only for the MVLs. A strike-off is an application the directors make. Where an entity holds reserves worth doing an MVL for, only a licensed insolvency practitioner can act as liquidator, and we introduce one.
Is this only for large groups?

No. The most common case we see is an owner-managed business with three to six companies accumulated over the years, one of them holding cash nobody has taken out. The arithmetic works at that scale as well as it does for a large organisation, and the corporate governance benefit is proportionally greater because the same small management team carries every directorship.
Closing call to action
How many companies are you filing for that do nothing?

We take no appointments, so we have no interest in which route each entity takes. One conversation will tell you which companies can go, what has to happen first, and whether a strike-off or a liquidation is right for each.

/restructuring/contingency-planning
Contingency planning

A contingency plan is the answer to a question most directors avoid asking: what do we do if this does not work? If the refinancing is declined, if the contract is not renewed, if the biggest customer goes elsewhere or goes under. Not a forecast, and not a prediction that any of it will happen. A worked-through answer, prepared while there is still time to choose between options rather than take the only one left.

It is the least urgent-sounding service we offer and, measured by what it saves, frequently the most valuable. Everything else on this site is something you do once a problem has arrived. This is the one you do before.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
Why the timing decides the outcome
[IMAGE] "Why the timing decides the outcome": the clock vector panel is the obvious fit, and this is the page it was drawn for.
The uncomfortable arithmetic of financial distress is that your options narrow as your position weakens, and they narrow faster than most directors expect.

A company with six months of runway can sell a division, refinance, negotiate with a landlord, restructure its debt, run a proper sale process, or decide to close in an orderly way and pay its creditors. The same company with six weeks can do almost none of that. The buyer knows you are forced. The lender has already made its decision. The sale that would have realised full value becomes a fire sale, and a solvent closure becomes an insolvent one.

Nothing about the business changed in between. Only the time did. That is the entire case for doing this work early, and it is why our restructuring [link to /restructuring] page argues that timing matters more than technique.
When to build one
The trigger is not distress. It is a foreseeable event with a real chance of going the wrong way, and a consequence you have not worked through.
A refinancing or facility renewal that is not certain. The single most common one. If the answer is no, what happens on the Monday after?
A major contract, tender or customer up for renewal, where losing it would take the business below the line
A lender that has started asking different questions, moved you to a different team, or commissioned an independent review [link to /restructuring/independent-business-review]
A large, uncertain liability: an HMRC enquiry, a dispute, a dilapidations claim, a warranty exposure from an earlier sale
A sector or supply chain under visible strain, where you can see what is coming towards you before it arrives
A shareholder or partner dispute that could force a sale or a split
A personal deadline, such as a guarantee falling due, retirement, or ill health
If any of those is on your horizon and you have not written down what you would do, the plan is worth an afternoon.
What a contingency plan actually contains
[IMAGE] "What a contingency plan actually contains": numbered flow, or a six-item grid.
It is a short, practical document, not a consultancy report. Ours generally cover six things.

The trigger points. What specific event or number means the fallback is now live. A cash balance, a date, a decision from a third party. Written down in advance, because the hardest part of any plan is admitting the moment has arrived

The real cash position, forward. A short-term cash forecast that survives contact with reality, showing the point at which the company runs out of room. Most plans fail here, on optimistic debtor collection

The options, priced and ranked. Sale, refinancing, a turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] programme, a company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva], administration [link to /insolvency/administration], a pre-pack administration, or an orderly winding the company up [link to /insolvency/liquidation]. What each would realistically achieve, what it costs, how long it takes, and what has to be true for it to work

The preparation each option needs. Some routes require weeks of groundwork: a buyer identified, a valuation done, funding lined up, information ready for a purchaser's adviser. Doing that work in advance is what makes the option real rather than theoretical

Your personal exposure, mapped. Every personal guarantee, the director's loan account, anything you have secured on your own property. This is the part directors most often discover too late, and it frequently changes which option they choose
Who does what, and who is told. Advisers, lenders, key staff, and the order in which they hear anything
The output is usually a handful of pages. Its value is not the document. It is that the thinking is done, so that the day it is needed you are executing a decision rather than making one.
What it is not
Two things this page is regularly confused with, and neither is what we do here.
It is not business continuity planning

Continuity and disaster-recovery planning deals with fires, floods, cyber incidents and IT failure: how the business keeps operating through a disruption. Useful, and someone else's speciality. This page is about financial contingency, where the risk is solvency rather than operations.
It is not a decision to do anything

Building a plan commits you to nothing. Most of the plans we write are never executed, because the refinancing lands or the contract renews. That is a good outcome and the work still earned its place: you spent the intervening months making decisions with the downside understood rather than guessed at.
Directors' duties, and why a plan protects you

Once a company is unable to pay its debts, or close to it, a director's duties shift towards the interests of creditors, and the decisions taken in that period are the ones examined later if things do not recover. Wrongful trading is not about a company failing. It is about what you knew, when you knew it, and what you did next.

A director who identified the risk early, took advice, documented the options and acted on a plan is in a materially stronger position than one who pressed on and hoped. That holds whether or not the plan was ever needed. The paper trail a contingency plan creates is one of the better protections a director can give themselves, and it costs a fraction of what defending the alternative costs.
How we run it

It is deliberately light. A first conversation to understand the business and what is coming. A short piece of work on the numbers and the options, usually one to three weeks depending on complexity and how good the information is. Then a document, a conversation about it, and a review point tied to whatever the trigger event is.

Where the review shows the business needs attention now rather than a plan for later, we say so, and the work becomes a turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] or a debt restructuring [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring] conversation instead. Where it shows the company is fine, we say that too, and you have spent very little to find out.
Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes your administrator or your liquidator, which means we have no financial interest in your contingency plan ever being executed, and no reason to steer you towards the formal option that would generate a fee for the firm.

That is the whole reason this service can be honest. An adviser who takes appointments and tells you to prepare for administration is describing work they might later be paid for. We are not, so when we tell you the fallback should be a solvent sale, or that you do not need a plan at all, you can take it at face value.
It is also why accountants and solicitors send us clients at this stage rather than later: they know the client will come back to them, not be absorbed into a process.
Frequently asked questions
Is it not premature to plan for something that may not happen?

That is the objection, and it is the wrong way round. The plan costs little and commits you to nothing. The alternative is discovering your options at the point when most of them have expired. Directors almost never regret having done this; they regret the months they spent deciding whether to.
Does taking advice make insolvency more likely?

No. It makes it less likely, because problems addressed early are more often solved without a formal procedure at all. What advice does is remove the excuse of not knowing, which is why some directors avoid it. The regime is not aimed at directors who acted on what they learned.
Who needs to know we are doing this?
Nobody, unless you decide otherwise. This is confidential advisory work. It is not filed, published or notified anywhere, and there is no register of companies that have taken advice.
How long does it take?

Usually one to three weeks from the first conversation, depending on the size of the business and the state of the management information. Where a trigger event is days away rather than months, we work to that instead and cut the scope to what is decision-useful.
What does it cost?
It is a fixed fee agreed before we start, scoped to the size of the question. It is by a wide margin the cheapest piece of work on this site, and the only one bought before it is needed.
What if the plan says the business cannot be saved?

Then you have found that out while you still have choices about how it ends, which is a materially better position than finding out when a creditor forces the timing. An orderly solvent closure and a compulsory winding up are very different outcomes for a director, and the difference between them is usually months of notice.
Closing call to action
Is something coming that you have not planned for?
We take no appointments, so we have no stake in whether your fallback is ever used. One conversation will tell you whether a plan is worth building and what it would need to cover.

Corporate finance

Corporate finance is the advice around the transactions that change who owns a business, what it is worth and how it is funded: mergers and acquisitions, selling a company, buying one, valuing shares, raising capital, or reshaping the capital structure so that the people running the business are the people who own it. For most owners it is the largest financial event of their working life, and it happens once.

That asymmetry is the whole reason advisers exist in this market, and it is why this sits inside our restructuring [link to /restructuring] and advisory practice rather than alongside a lender. The buyer across the table has done twenty deals. Their advisers do nothing else. The seller has done none, and is negotiating on terms they are seeing for the first time, in a document written by someone else's solicitor.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
What we advise on
[IMAGE] "What we advise on": six cards, 3+3.
Selling a business

Preparing the company for sale, identifying and approaching buyers, running a competitive process where the market supports one, and negotiating the deal through to completion. The preparation is where most of the value is won, which is why it belongs alongside exit planning [link to /restructuring/exit-planning] rather than starting when the business goes to market.
Mergers and acquisitions

Buying a company or a trade, or merging two: assessing whether the target is worth what is being asked, structuring the transaction and its funding, and managing the process through to completion. Most acquisitions by owner-managed businesses are trade purchases rather than mergers, but the discipline is the same. The financial due diligence itself sits on our transaction support [link to /financial-advisory/due-diligence] page.
Management buyouts and buy-ins

Structuring a purchase by the management team, including how much of the price the business itself can fund out of future profits, what the funders will require, and how the equity is split between the team. Frequently the best outcome where a trade sale would break up something worth keeping.
Valuations

What a business or a shareholding is actually worth, and on what basis. For a transaction, a share transfer, a shareholder agreement, tax purposes, or simply so an owner knows. Where the value is disputed rather than negotiated, that is forensic work and our forensic services [link to /financial-advisory/forensic-accounting] page covers it.
Capital raising

Working out what capital structure the business needs and what it can support: debt, equity, or a mix, and on what terms. Capital investment from a private equity house comes with governance conditions as well as money, and those terms deserve as much attention as the valuation. We advise on the structure and introduce funders. We are not brokers and we do not arrange the facility, which our finance and funding [link to /finance-and-funding] page explains.
Shareholder reorganisations

Buying out a departing shareholder, bringing in a new one, resolving a deadlock, or reshaping a group so the ownership matches the intention. These transactions rarely make headlines and frequently do more for shareholder value than a sale would. Often the quiet transaction that prevents a dispute later.
What a business is worth, and why the number moves

Most private companies are valued on a multiple of sustainable earnings, adjusted to show what a new owner would actually inherit: the owner's remuneration replaced at market rate, personal costs removed, and one-off items stripped out. The multiple then depends on things a buyer can verify rather than things a seller asserts.
Scale. Larger companies attract higher multiples for the same profit, because they carry less risk and reach more buyers, including private equity firms that will not look below a certain size
Recurring revenue. Contracted or repeat income is worth substantially more than the same profit earned job by job
Customer concentration. One customer at a large share of revenue is the most common single reason a multiple is marked down
Owner dependence. If the business needs you, the buyer is acquiring a problem alongside the profit
Growth and market position. Demonstrated, not projected. Buyers discount forecasts heavily and pay for track record
Quality of information. Reliable monthly accounts and a clean audit trail reduce perceived risk, and perceived risk is what the multiple prices

Two companies with identical profits routinely sell for very different amounts. The gap is not luck. It is the preparation, which is why the conversation is worth having years before the transaction rather than at the point of sale.
Structure: the difference between the price and the money
[IMAGE] "Structure: the difference between the price and the money": the strongest section on the page. A simple bridge from headline price to cash actually received would carry it better than prose.
This is the part owners understand least and regret most, and it is more important than the headline number.
Cash at completion. The only part that is certain. Every other element depends on something happening afterwards
Deferred consideration. A fixed amount paid later. Its value depends entirely on the buyer still being able to pay it, so who the buyer is matters as much as what they promise

Earn-out. A payment contingent on the business hitting targets after the sale, when you may no longer control the decisions that determine whether it does. Earn-outs are where sellers most often lose money they had counted as theirs. If you accept one, the mechanics of how performance is measured and what the buyer may not do to the business matter more than the headline figure
Shares in the buyer. Value that depends on somebody else's company, usually with restrictions on when you can sell
Warranties and indemnities. Promises about the business that, if wrong, let the buyer claim money back. The cap, the time limits and the disclosure exercise decide your real exposure after the deal
Retentions and escrow. Money held back against warranty claims, sometimes for years

A headline price with half of it deferred, conditional and warranty-exposed is not the same offer as a lower price paid in cash. Comparing offers properly means valuing the certainty, not just the total, and it is the single most useful thing an adviser does.
How a deal actually runs
[IMAGE] "How a deal actually runs": numbered flow.
Preparation. Financial information assembled and normalised, a financial forecast a buyer will believe, the equity story written, and the obvious problems fixed before a buyer finds them
Approach. A targeted list of credible buyers rather than the widest possible net. Confidentiality agreements before anything meaningful is shared

Initial offers. Indicative and non-binding, usually subject to due diligence. This is the point at which a seller has the most negotiating power, and it is where structure should be agreed rather than left

Heads of terms. The commercial deal in outline, including exclusivity. Once exclusivity is granted, the balance of power shifts decisively to the buyer, so what is agreed here matters more than its non-binding status suggests
Due diligence. The buyer's advisers examine everything. Surprises here cost price or kill deals, which is why preparation earns its keep
Documentation. Share purchase agreement, disclosure letter, ancillary documents. Solicitors' work, with the adviser keeping the commercial deal intact through the drafting
Completion, and afterwards. Funds flow, and any post-completion accounts, earn-out periods and warranty periods begin
Three to nine months from decision to completion is typical for an owner-managed business, and the timetable is usually set by due diligence and by how ready the information was.
When not to do a deal

We are paid for advice rather than by completion, so this section can exist. Some deals should not happen, and telling clients so is part of the job. Some deals should not happen, and telling clients so is part of the job.
When the business is not ready and a year of preparation would change the price by more than the delay costs
When the market is wrong for that business and waiting is genuinely better than accepting a discount
When the structure transfers the risk to you. A high headline price mostly in earn-out, from a buyer whose ability to pay depends on the business continuing to perform without you

When the buyer cannot fund it. Private equity buyers and trade acquirers alike need their capital confirmed, and establishing this early avoids months of due diligence on a transaction that was never going to complete

When there is no buyer at any acceptable price. For some owner-managed businesses the honest answer is an orderly solvent closure through an MVL [link to /insolvency/members-voluntary-liquidation-mvl], and that is a legitimate outcome rather than a failure

When the business needs fixing rather than selling. A struggling company sold in distress realises a fraction of its value, and a turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] or an independent review [link to /restructuring/independent-business-review] is the right route first
Where we fit

Lancefield advises. We are not a broker, we do not arrange finance or deal in investments, and we take no insolvency appointments. We do not advise on listed-company transactions such as an initial public offering: our services are for private, owner-managed companies. Where a transaction needs funding we introduce experts; where it needs a licensed appointment, we bring one in. We are not an accountancy firm either: on the accountancy and tax side we work with your own accountant rather than replacing them.

What we bring that a pure corporate finance house does not is the other end of the story. We spend the rest of our time on organisations in difficulty, including businesses that got into difficulty because of how a deal was structured: an earn-out that failed, an acquisition funded with debt the business could not service, warranties that turned into claims. That experience shapes how we advise on structure, and it is why our advice tends to be more conservative about deferred consideration than a fee-on-completion adviser's would be.

We work alongside your accountant and your solicitor rather than replacing either, and we hand the client back. Where the funding structure itself is the question rather than the transaction, our capital management [link to /financial-advisory/capital-management] page covers it, and the wider financial advisory [link to /financial-advisory] section sets out how the pieces fit together.
Frequently asked questions
What does a corporate finance adviser actually do?

Corporate finance services cover preparing the business and its information, identifying and approaching the right counterparties, negotiating price and structure, and managing the transaction through due diligence to completion. The value is concentrated in preparation and in structure, which is where the difference between the headline price and the money received is decided.
What is my company worth?

Usually a multiple of adjusted sustainable earnings, where the adjustment replaces the owner with a market-rate manager and strips out personal and one-off items. The multiple depends on scale, recurring revenue, customer concentration, owner dependence and the quality of the numbers. Any valuation quoted without those adjustments is a guess.
How long does selling a business take?

Three to nine months from decision to completion for a typical owner-managed business, plus whatever preparation is needed beforehand. Due diligence is the usual bottleneck, and the better prepared the information, the shorter it is.
Should I accept an earn-out?

Sometimes, but treat it as the risky part of the price rather than part of the price. Look at who controls the decisions that determine whether the targets are met, how performance is measured, what the buyer is prevented from doing to the business, and what happens if you leave. Value the certain money and the contingent money separately.
Do I need a corporate finance adviser as well as my accountant?

For a sale or an acquisition of any size, yes, and the two do different jobs. Your accountancy adviser knows the business and handles the tax and the numbers. The corporate finance experts run the process and negotiate the commercial deal. On a small management buyout the requirement is lighter and your accountancy firm plus ourselves is often enough.
Can you help raise the money?

We advise on what structure the business needs and can support, whether that is debt, a capital investment from a private equity house, or a mix, and we introduce funders we know. We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities and we take no commission from lenders, which is the reason we can tell you when more debt is the wrong answer.

Thinking about a transaction?

We are paid for advice, not on completion, so we have no stake in a deal happening. Contact us and one conversation will tell you what the business would realistically fetch, what structure to expect, and whether now is the moment.

/financial-advisory/forensic-accounting
Forensic accounting and forensic services

Forensic accounting is the application of accountancy and investigation to questions that will be decided by a court, a tribunal, an arbitrator or a negotiated settlement. It covers three things: finding out what happened to the money, quantifying what someone has lost, and presenting both in a form that survives challenge from the other side.

The distinguishing feature is not technique. It is audience. Ordinary accountancy work has to be right; forensic accounting has to be right and also demonstrable, by someone who did not want it to be true, months later, under cross-examination. That constraint shapes everything about how the work is done.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
What we are instructed to do
[IMAGE] "What we are instructed to do": six cards, 3+3.
Fraud and financial crime investigation

A fraud investigation establishes whether money has been taken, how, by whom and how much. Employee theft, false invoicing, procurement fraud, bribery and corruption, misappropriation by a director or partner, and the concealment that usually accompanies financial crime. The output is evidence for a disciplinary, a civil claim, an insurance claim, a police report or a government investigation, and it has to be gathered in a way that keeps all of those options open.
Expert witness and quantum

Quantifying loss in a dispute and giving evidence on it. Loss of profits from a breach of contract, business interruption, the value of what was destroyed or withheld. Reports prepared in compliance with the standards courts require, with the reasoning exposed so it can be tested rather than asserted.
Valuation in dispute

Where the value of a company or a shareholding is contested: a shareholder dispute, a divorce, an unfair prejudice petition, or a buyout where the parties cannot agree the number. Different from the valuation work on our corporate finance [link to /financial-advisory/corporate-finance] page, because the audience is a judge rather than a buyer.
Professional negligence

Assessing whether financial advice or accountancy work fell below the standard required, and what that professional negligence cost the client. Instructed by claimants and defendants alike, and the work has to be equally rigorous either way.
Insurance claims

Preparing or reviewing insurance claims where the loss is financial: business interruption, fidelity and crime cover, and disputes about the measure of indemnity. Insurers commission work on insurance claims as often as policyholders do.
Asset tracing and recovery

Following funds and identifying where value has gone. Frequently instructed alongside an administration [link to /insolvency/administration] or a liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation], where money has left a company before it failed, and often the point at which our forensic and insolvency work meet.
The expert's duty, and why it decides whether the report is useful
This is the part that separates evidence from advocacy, and the sales-led pages on this subject leave it out.

The duty an expert witness owes runs to the court, and it outranks any duty to whoever is paying. In practice that means independence, a report kept within the limits of the expert's own expertise, the facts and assumptions set out where they can be seen, and, critically, an acknowledgement of anything that qualifies the opinion or points the other way. An expert who omits the inconvenient point is not helping the client; they are creating an opening for the other side and putting their whole report at risk.

So the honest version of what a good forensic accountant offers a solicitor is this: an opinion that is genuinely defensible, reached without being told what it should be, and delivered with the weaknesses identified early enough to be dealt with. That is what an instructing solicitor is buying, and it is not the same as agreement. Where our analysis does not support the client's case, we say so at the outset, when it is still useful, rather than discovering it in the witness box.

In Scotland that duty comes from the case law rather than a rule of court. The Supreme Court in Kennedy v Cordia (Services) LLP adopted the Ikarian Reefer duties for Scottish civil cases, and went further than the English rules do: it treated independence and impartiality as a question of admissibility rather than of weight. A Scottish court can refuse to hear a report that does not meet them.

For that reason we distinguish clearly between advisory work, where we assist a party, and expert work, where we owe the duty to the court. Both are legitimate. Confusing them is what gets reports excluded.
How a forensic investigation runs
[IMAGE] "How a forensic investigation runs": numbered flow.

Scope it properly. The single biggest cause of wasted forensic cost is an open-ended instruction. What question is being answered, for what forum, by when, and what is the proportionate depth given what is at stake

Secure the evidence. Accountancy records, bank statements, the accounting system's audit trail, emails, contracts. Preservation matters from day one, particularly where an employee is still in post and has access
Establish the baseline. What the records show, and how reliable they are. In fraud work, the pattern of what is missing frequently carries more information than what is present

Analyse. Reconstructing transactions, tracing funds through accounts, testing the numbers against the documents and the documents against each other. Where the matter involves bribery or corruption, the payment trail and the approval trail are examined separately
Quantify. Building the loss calculation on stated assumptions, with sensitivities, so that a change in one assumption does not collapse the whole figure
Report. In the form the forum requires, with the reasoning visible
Support through to conclusion. Meetings of experts, responding to the other side's report, and giving evidence if it goes that far

Matters frequently settle. A well-constructed report is often what causes them to, because it converts an argument into a number both sides can see the basis of, which is why forensic accounting is as much a dispute resolution tool as a litigation one.
In the Scottish courts
Most of the forensic accounting content online describes English procedure, and the practical differences matter if your case is in Scotland.

Proceedings run in the Court of Session or the sheriff court, with a Commercial Court in the Court of Session and a commercial procedure in some sheriff courts for disputes of a commercial or business nature. The vocabulary is different: pursuer and defender rather than claimant and defendant, a proof rather than a trial, and documents lodged as productions. The evidence is that of a skilled witness, which the Rules of Court call a report of a skilled person, though everyone says expert in practice. Recovery of documents runs through commission and diligence rather than the English disclosure regime, and the statutory power is available before proceedings are even raised, which is worth knowing early. The timetable in a commercial action is actively managed by the judge.
None of that changes the accountancy. It changes how the work is packaged, when it has to be ready, and who it is addressed to. We are Glasgow-based and this is the system we work in.
Where forensic work meets insolvency
This is our unusual angle, and it comes from the practice rather than the marketing.

A large share of financial wrongdoing, including outright financial crime, surfaces when a company fails, because that is when someone independent looks properly at the records for the first time. Our insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] page explains who does that looking and why they are obliged to. Money paid to connected parties, assets transferred before the collapse, a director's loan account that grew without explanation, or trading that continued long after it should have stopped. Where a government body such as the Insolvency Service is already investigating, an independent analysis is worth having early. In Scotland the relevant challenges are gratuitous alienations and unfair preferences, and the equivalent claims elsewhere are transactions at an undervalue and preferences.

We work on both sides of that: instructed by an insolvency practitioner to run the forensic investigation and quantify what was lost, and instructed by directors who need an independent analysis of transactions being questioned. Because we take no insolvency appointments ourselves, we can act in either direction without a conflict, which a firm that also takes appointments frequently cannot. Our insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] and liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] pages cover the procedures that generate this work.
What it costs, and keeping it proportionate

A forensic investigation is charged on time, because its scope is genuinely unknowable at the outset. What is controllable is the shape of it: a defined first phase with a decision point at the end, rather than an open instruction.

We will tell you early where the cost of proving something is likely to exceed what proving it is worth. That happens more often than the industry admits, particularly in smaller frauds where the money has already been spent and the perpetrator has nothing to recover from. A short scoping exercise that concludes the claim is not worth pursuing has saved the client a great deal, and we would rather deliver that answer than bill for the alternative.
Where we fit

Lancefield is an independent advisory firm. We perform no audits, sell no financial products, and take no insolvency appointments, so there is no other engagement waiting behind the forensic instruction and nothing our conclusion could be shaped by. Nor do we sell compliance or anti-fraud systems, which is a common second engagement behind a fraud investigation elsewhere.

Solicitors are the usual route in, and we work the way instructing solicitors need: scoped, on time, with the difficulties raised early rather than late. The wider financial advisory [link to /financial-advisory] section sets out the rest of what we do. Where the matter is heading for arbitration or an expert determination, dispute resolution routes that run outside the court, our commercial arbitration [link to /financial-advisory/commercial-arbitration] page covers that route. Where the question is about a transaction rather than a dispute, transaction support [link to /financial-advisory/due-diligence] is the right page.
Frequently asked questions
What is forensic accounting?

Accountancy and investigation applied to a question that will be tested by a court, tribunal, arbitrator or negotiation. It covers investigating what happened to money, quantifying financial loss, and presenting the analysis so that it stands up to challenge. The distinguishing feature is that a forensic accountant's work has to be demonstrable, not merely correct.
What does a forensic accountant do that an auditor does not?

An audit gives reasonable assurance that the accounts as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether caused by fraud or by error, working from samples and to materiality thresholds. The auditing standard itself recognises that fraud concealed by forgery, unrecorded transactions, misrepresentation to the auditor or collusion carries a higher and unavoidable risk of going undetected. A forensic accountant investigates a specific question without a materiality threshold, follows individual transactions wherever they lead, and produces evidence rather than an opinion on the accounts as a whole. That is a difference in design, not a criticism of the accountancy profession.
Can you act as an expert witness?
[IMAGE] "The expert's duty": the scales vector panel is the obvious fit and this is the page it belongs on most.

Yes. For a forensic accountant, acting as an expert witness is a distinct role from advising a party. As an expert the overriding duty is to the court rather than to whoever is paying, which means the report has to set out its assumptions, acknowledge what qualifies the opinion, and stay within our expertise. We are explicit at the outset about which role we are being instructed in.
We suspect an employee is stealing. What should we do first?

Preserve the evidence and contact [link to /contact] someone before confronting anyone. Secure the accounting records and system logs, restrict access carefully, and do not alert the individual before you have what you need. Employment law, financial crime reporting and any insurance claim all have their own compliance requirements, and the order in which you act affects all three.
How much does a forensic investigation cost?

It is charged on the forensic accountant's time, because the scope cannot honestly be fixed before anyone looks. What we do is agree a defined first phase with a cost and a decision point, so you learn what you are dealing with before committing to the full investigation.
Will you tell us if our case is weak?

Yes, at the point when it is still useful. An expert who only tells a client what they want to hear produces a report the other side takes apart, which is worse than no report. Where the analysis does not support the case, saying so early is the most valuable thing we can do.
Closing call to action
Need an independent view of the numbers?

We perform no audits and take no appointments, so there is nothing behind the instruction shaping the answer. One conversation will tell you whether the question can be answered, what it would take, and whether it is worth answering.

/financial-advisory/due-diligence
Transaction support and due diligence

Due diligence is the investigation a buyer runs before committing money, and the preparation a seller does before letting anyone look. It answers one question in detail: is this company what it appears to be? The price adjustments, the warranties and the money held back at completion all follow from what that investigation finds. Larger firms sell the same work as transaction services.

We do the financial workstream, for the buyer and for the seller, on owner-managed deals across Scotland. It sits inside our financial advisory [link to /financial-advisory] practice. We charge for the work rather than the deal, so when the numbers do not support the offer we say so. Much of our other work is with a company in difficulty because of an acquisition nobody examined.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
What due diligence actually is

An audit tests whether a set of accounts is fairly stated. Due diligence asks something else: what would a new owner of this company inherit? It is an investigation rather than a compliance exercise, and it produces findings rather than an opinion. Whether the transaction is a merger, a trade purchase or a management buyout, the question is the same.

Scope is agreed at the start and deliberately narrow. Nobody examines everything, and the best reviews do not try to. A proportionate financial due diligence review concentrates on the few places where the value of the business could be materially wrong, and says what was left alone.
Buy-side: is the company what it appears to be?

You are making an investment decision on evidence that is entirely historic. A buy-side review takes the numbers a seller has presented and establishes which of them survive into the first Monday after completion. Most of the financial risk sits in the first four items.

Quality of earnings. Reported profit restated as sustainable trading profit: one-off gains out, the owner's pay at a market rate, personal costs removed, policy changes unwound. The normalised EBITDA this review produces is what the multiple applies to
Revenue quality. Where income comes from, how much is contracted or repeating, customer concentration, and whether any was recognised early
Working capital. How much cash the company needs at its normal level of trade. Understate it and the buyer funds the gap weeks after completion
Debt-like items. Unpaid tax and time to pay arrangements, overdue creditors used as finance, deferred consideration from an earlier deal, dilapidations, pension deficits, accrued holiday
Tax exposures. Historic PAYE and VAT treatment, the employment status of contractors, open HMRC enquiries, and anything a later inspection could unpick
Forecast credibility. Whether the assumptions trace back to something that has already happened, and whether the synergies behind the offer belong to the target company or to the buyer
Operational reality. Technology and systems, capacity, and the few people the trading depends on, which is where the operational investment of year one hides

Two findings recur above all others on owner-managed deals: working capital understated, and profit that depends on an owner working for less than the job is worth. Neither is dishonest. Both move the number.
Vendor due diligence: examined before the buyer arrives

Vendor due diligence is the same investigation run on your own company, commissioned by the seller before the market sees anything. The point is that the buyer's adviser finds nothing that stalls the deal.

What kills owner-managed deals is rarely the price. It is delay, surprise and unpriced financial risks. A buyer who finds in week six what the seller could have explained in week one does not simply adjust the offer. Every unexplained item is then treated as a financial risk.

Awkward things get fixed while there is time. Related-party balances, a property nobody wants, dormant subsidiaries, an unresolved employment matter. corporate simplification [link to /restructuring/corporate-simplification] handles the group-structure half
The numbers get told once. A normalised earnings position the vendor can defend, with the adjustments already made and evidenced
Competitive tension survives. With more than one bidder, late information is what lets a buyer reopen terms after the others have gone home
The owner keeps running the business. Deals fail because trading dips while the seller answers data requests
Vendor work belongs with exit planning [link to /restructuring/exit-planning]. Treat it as an investment in the sale rather than a cost, and start it well before the memorandum goes out.
Financial, legal, commercial and tax: who does which
[IMAGE] "Financial, legal, commercial and tax": four-column split showing who owns each workstream.
Due diligence is spoken about as one job. It is at least four, run by different people at once, and knowing which is which stops you paying twice.
Financial due diligence. Earnings, working capital, debt-like items, cash and tax exposure. Done by accountants, and it is our part

Legal. Title to the shares, contracts, property, employment, litigation, and the change of control clauses a new owner triggers by buying the company. Done by solicitors, and in Scotland by a Scottish firm: the title system and the rules for ending a commercial lease are not the English ones

Commercial due diligence. The market, the customers, the competition, and whether the growth in the forecast is available to anybody at all. Usually a specialist firm, and the workstream most often skipped
Tax. Historic exposure, plus the structure of the deal. Run alongside the financial work, because each keeps finding the other's problems

Operational and IT. The technology and systems the business runs on, capacity, key people, and the operational investment a buyer faces in year one. On smaller deals it folds into the commercial and financial scope

ESG due diligence. Environmental, social and governance exposure. Standard where private equity or institutional investors sit behind the deal. On a small acquisition, ESG due diligence is a section rather than a workstream

Somebody must own the whole list, because the gaps between workstreams are where things get missed. On a merger that is the corporate finance lead, and our corporate finance [link to /financial-advisory/corporate-finance] page covers the role.
How a financial due diligence review runs
[IMAGE] "How a due diligence review runs": numbered flow, six steps.
Scoping. What the review is for, what it will test, what it will not, what it costs and on what terms. In writing, before anything starts
Information request. One specific list covering the finances, the technology and the people, sent early. The pace of the whole review is set here
Analysis. The numbers rebuilt from the underlying records rather than lifted from the accounts, and management answering questions in a session rather than by email
Interim findings. Anything that could change the price, the terms or the deal itself is raised the day it is found. A review that saves bad news for the final report has failed
Report. Findings quantified where they can be, each with a recommendation attached: adjust, warrant, indemnify, hold back, or reconsider
Support to completion. Findings have to survive the drafting, so we stay involved while the deal is active
What the findings do to the deal

[IMAGE] "What the findings do to the deal": the strongest section. A flow from one finding to its possible outcomes (adjust, warrant, indemnify, retain, walk) would carry it better than the list alone.

Findings are worth only what is done with them. A report that sits in a folder while the transaction completes on the terms originally offered has cost money for nothing. Six things a finding can become, and choosing between them is where the negotiation happens.

A price adjustment. A finding that changes sustainable earnings is multiplied by whatever multiple the deal was struck on, so a modest error in profit becomes a large one in the consideration. In a merger it moves the share exchange ratio instead

A completion mechanism. How the consideration is trued up afterwards: completion accounts measuring cash, debt and working capital on the day, or a locked box fixing the balance sheet at an earlier date

A warranty. A statement by the seller that something is true, with a claim if it is not. Warranties cover the unknown, and taking one instead of an adjustment for a problem already found is a poor trade for a buyer
An indemnity. A pound for pound promise covering one identified exposure, usually a tax one. For the problems the investigation found but could not size
A retention. Part of the consideration held back against claims, sometimes for years. The only protection that does not depend on finding the seller afterwards
A condition, or no deal. Some findings cannot be priced. A key contract with a change of control clause and a customer who will not confirm they are staying is a reason to pause

Disclosure runs alongside it. The seller discloses against the warranties, and anything properly disclosed generally cannot then be claimed for. Good transaction services work stays with the commercial terms through the drafting rather than stopping at the report.
When due diligence is not worth doing
We are paid for the work rather than for the deal, which is what lets this section exist.

When the cost is out of proportion to the investment at risk. On a small asset purchase with no history, no employees and no liabilities coming across, the financial risk is small and a full review buys comfort rather than information
When value sits in assets rather than earnings. If it is property or plant, a valuation and a solicitor matter more than an earnings review
When you already know. A management buyout team that has run the company for a decade does not need a stranger to explain its own working capital cycle
When nobody has written the scope. Open-ended instructions produce long reports and large fees. Our recommendation is usually to narrow the terms of the work to the value genuinely at risk

When the company needs fixing rather than buying. A distressed target is a different exercise, and an independent review [link to /restructuring/independent-business-review] answers the question better
On a smaller transaction the right scope is a short review of earnings, cash and tax, delivered in days rather than weeks. And if the seller will not release the information, that is the finding.
Where we fit

Lancefield advises. We take no insolvency appointments, we are not FCA authorised, we do not arrange finance, and no part of our fee depends on a deal completing. Where funding is needed we introduce a trusted specialist firm rather than broking it, which our capital management [link to /financial-advisory/capital-management] and finance and funding [link to /finance-and-funding] pages set out.

What we bring to transaction services that a pure deals team does not is the other end of the story. Much of our work is with a business under operational and financial pressure, sometimes because of an acquisition: debt the trading could not service, working capital that belonged to somebody else, an earn-out built on a forecast nobody tested. Where a target is genuinely distressed and the route is a purchase out of administration [link to /insolvency/administration], we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] we know and trust, because nobody here takes the appointment.

We work with your own accountant and your solicitor rather than replacing either. Where a finding turns into a dispute rather than a negotiation, that is forensic services [link to /financial-advisory/forensic-accounting]. Where the real question is whether to sell the business at all, restructuring [link to /restructuring] and, for a solvent closure, an MVL [link to /insolvency/members-voluntary-liquidation-mvl] are honest alternatives.
Frequently asked questions
What are due diligence services?

The investigations run before a deal completes: financial, legal, commercial and tax, with operational, technology and ESG work added on larger transactions. Financial due diligence, our part, tests earnings, working capital, debt-like items and the tax exposure a buyer inherits with the company. Larger firms sell due diligence services as transaction services.
How long does financial due diligence take?

Two to six weeks from a complete information pack is typical for financial due diligence on an owner-managed company, and the timetable is set by how ready the seller's records are. Private equity or bank funding behind the deal makes the review longer, because several workstreams report into one deadline.
What due diligence is needed for a merger or acquisition?

Financial, legal and tax on any deal of substance. Commercial due diligence wherever the value depends on growth rather than on what the business already earns. Operational and ESG due diligence scale with size. On M&A transactions between similar companies, the commercial workstream decides whether the synergies were real.
What is a red flag report?

A report listing only the issues that could change the offer or stop the deal, with no descriptive background. It costs less and arrives faster, which suits an early stage or a competitive process, and on a first look our recommendation is often exactly that.
Who pays for vendor due diligence?

The seller does, and the vendor due diligence report is then released to bidders on agreed terms. It is normal on private equity exits. On a smaller business, getting the numbers into a defensible state before anybody asks delivers most of the benefit of a full review at a fraction of the cost.
If financial due diligence was thorough, do I still need warranties?

Yes. Investigation deals with what can be found and warranties with what cannot. Covering a known problem with a warranty instead of a deduction is how a buyer ends up litigating something they could have taken off the consideration during the negotiation.
Is due diligence different in Scotland?

Financial due diligence is the same. The legal work is not. Title to property, standard securities and the rules for ending a commercial lease follow Scots law, and a purchase of Scottish land or buildings attracts Land and Buildings Transaction Tax rather than Stamp Duty Land Tax.

One conversation will tell you what a proportionate scope looks like, roughly what the review should cost, and what it is likely to find. We have no stake in the transaction happening.

Pension advisory

This page is about pensions as a company problem: what an employer still owes when cash is short, what a scheme does to a restructuring or a sale, and where it ranks when a business fails. Lancefield is not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, and we give no personal pension advice, no investment advice and no retirement planning advice to individuals.

Most of the volume behind pension advisory is people asking about their own money, and the section below says where to get that advice. If pensions have become the hardest item on your company's balance sheet, this is the right page, and it sits inside our financial advisory [link to /financial-advisory] work.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
If the pension you are worried about is your own

We will say this plainly, once. Decisions about a personal pension plan, whether to transfer benefits out of one scheme into another, when to draw a pension pot and whether to buy an annuity, are regulated advice. How the State Pension fits with the rest of your retirement belongs in the same conversation with a regulated adviser. Giving it without authorisation is a criminal offence, so we do not give it, and nothing here concerns your own pension savings.
Free guidance. MoneyHelper publishes guidance on its website, and Pension Wise is its free appointment service for people aged 50 and over with a defined contribution pension
A regulated financial adviser. The Financial Conduct Authority register lists every firm authorised to give pension advice, and its website is where you check one
Your own record. A State Pension forecast comes from the GOV.UK website
Everything below this line is about the company.
Auto-enrolment when the money is tight
[IMAGE] "Auto-enrolment when the money is tight": three cards in a row.

Automatic enrolment duties under the Pensions Act 2008 do not pause because a business is struggling. The company still enrols eligible staff, still owes the employer contributions it promised, and still has to hand over the employee contributions it deducted from wages.

The deducted money is where directors get into real trouble. It is not the company's money to use, even for a fortnight. It has to reach the scheme by the statutory deadline in the following month, and a trustee who does not receive it has to report the failure to the Pensions Regulator once it looks materially significant, so the Regulator usually hears about arrears without being told.
Enforcement escalates. A compliance notice, then a fixed penalty, then penalties accruing daily until it is put right
Inducing staff to opt out is prohibited. Persuading a worker to leave so the employer saves money is its own breach
It follows the director. Money deducted from wages and not passed on turns up in a conduct report

When the pension payment is the one that gets skipped, the problem is not the scheme, and an independent review [link to /restructuring/independent-business-review] will say how fast the company can catch up.
Defined benefit schemes and the real size of the deficit

[IMAGE] "Defined benefit schemes and the real size of the deficit": a two-bar comparison, accounting deficit against the cost of securing benefits with an insurer, with no numbers on the axis. The point is the gap, not the amount.

A legacy final salary scheme is not a trade creditor. The figure in the accounts is an accounting measure. The figure that decides a restructuring, a sale or an insolvency is what it would cost to buy the members' benefits from an insurer, and it is usually much bigger. That becomes a statutory debt on the employer when the scheme winds up or the employer fails.
The trustees are an organised creditor. They have their own actuary and covenant adviser, and they negotiate with employers for a living
Money leaving the company gets examined. Dividends and intra-group payments made while a scheme is in deficit invite questions years later
The Pension Protection Fund sits behind the scheme. If the employer fails, the scheme may enter PPF assessment and members may end up with less than they were promised at retirement

So a company that looks saleable on its trading numbers can turn out not to be, and the scheme belongs in the restructuring [link to /restructuring] conversation from the first week rather than the last.
The Pensions Regulator, transactions and sales

The Pensions Regulator's powers reach past the company that employs the members. Where a transaction leaves a defined benefit scheme worse off, it can require another group company, or a connected person, to make good the loss. There are also criminal offences aimed at conduct that avoids an employer debt or risks accrued benefits.

That changes how a deal is run rather than whether it can be run. Certain corporate events have to be notified, and clearance can be sought in advance, which binds the regulator only on the facts you actually disclose, but puts the transaction in front of it first. Design a sale or a corporate simplification [link to /restructuring/corporate-simplification] and involve the scheme afterwards and it goes badly, so the pensions workstream runs alongside the financial due diligence in our transaction support [link to /financial-advisory/due-diligence] and corporate finance [link to /financial-advisory/corporate-finance] work.

On a sale, staff who move with the business keep most of their employment rights, but occupational pension rights are treated separately and the buyer's obligation is a minimum one. Whether they transfer at all depends on the type of proceedings. In a pre-pack administration the scheme is usually left with the insolvent employer while the trade continues in the buyer's hands. That is lawful, and it is the transaction the regulator examines hardest, so the evidence on price has to exist at the time. Our administration [link to /insolvency/administration] page covers the process.
Where a scheme ranks when a company fails

[IMAGE] "Where a scheme ranks when a company fails": the strongest candidate for a visual. A ranking ladder showing the two separate claims from one scheme, one preferential and one unsecured, sitting at different heights among the other creditor classes.
One scheme produces two claims, and they rank very differently.

Employee money deducted from pay is preferential. What was taken from wages in the months before the insolvency ranks ahead of floating charge holders and ordinary unsecured creditors, provided the scheme is an occupational one. Unpaid employer contributions are not. Since contracting-out ended they rank with the ordinary unsecured creditors
The scheme's own deficit claim is not. That statutory debt ranks with the trade creditors, which on a large scheme means the trustees control the creditors' vote
The National Insurance Fund can fill part of the gap. Certain unpaid amounts are met from the fund on employees' behalf
A qualifying insolvency event starts PPF assessment. The scheme is then run with a view to whether the Pension Protection Fund takes it on

The ranking is GB-wide. The procedure around it is not: notices go in the Edinburgh Gazette, and a winding up goes to the Court of Session or to the sheriff court where paid-up share capital is £120,000 or less. If you have arrived from a winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition], the pension position is one to establish in the first week.
Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes your liquidator or your administrator, so there is no process we need to happen, and where a formal appointment is required we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] we know and trust. We are not FCA authorised, we do not arrange finance or deal in investments, and we do not act for scheme trustees.

Our work is corporate advice: what the pensions position does to the company's options, and who needs to be in the room. For actuarial and covenant work we bring in a trusted specialist firm. For anything personal, a regulated financial adviser. We work alongside your accountancy [link to /accountancy] and legal advisers, and you can contact us [link to /contact] first.
Frequently asked questions
Can you advise me about my own pension?

No. We are not FCA authorised, so that advice is not ours to give: not whether to move a scheme, and not whether to buy an annuity. We do not advise on State Pension timing either. Use MoneyHelper for free guidance, or a regulated financial adviser you have checked on the FCA register.
Can a company stop paying into the pension scheme to save cash?

Not the money already deducted from wages, which belongs to the members. The employer's own payments are a legal obligation too, and stopping them is a breach the scheme has to report. If that payment is the only thing keeping the month afloat, contingency planning [link to /restructuring/contingency-planning] is the next step.
What happens to a defined benefit scheme if the employer goes into administration?

A qualifying insolvency event puts it into a Pension Protection Fund assessment period. If the scheme cannot secure benefits at or above PPF levels, the PPF takes it on and pays compensation, which for some members is less than they were promised at retirement.
Does a scheme deficit stop me selling the business?

It changes the transaction rather than stopping it. Buyers price the risk, the trustees have a say, and the Pensions Regulator has to see the scheme was treated properly. The position needs to be understood before the business goes to market, which is part of exit planning [link to /restructuring/exit-planning].
Is any of this different in Scotland?

The rules are GB-wide, so the duties, the ranking and the Pensions Regulator's powers are the same. Procedure differs: the Edinburgh Gazette, the sheriff court or the Court of Session, and gratuitous alienations and unfair preferences where an English adviser would say transactions at an undervalue. If a director has given a personal guarantee too, Debt Help Scotland [link to /debt-help-scotland] covers that side.

Is the pension scheme the thing holding everything up?

One conversation will tell you what the scheme does to your options, who needs to be in the room, and what has to happen before anyone approaches a buyer or a lender. We take no appointments, so there is no answer we need this to have.
