/financial-advisory/capital-management
Capital management

Capital management is making sure a business has the money it needs, in the form it needs, when it needs it. Working capital management is the short cycle: cash tied up in stock, in work in progress and in customers who have not paid, set against the credit your suppliers give you. Capital structure is the long one: how much of the business is funded by borrowing, how much by its owners, and whether the mix carries the plan.

Most owners meet the subject through one unpleasant discovery. The accounts say the year went well and the bank balance says otherwise. The money is inside the business, in a form that will not pay Friday's wages.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
A profitable company can run out of money

[IMAGE] "A profitable company can run out of money": the strongest section on the page. A simple timeline showing the same order twice, once as profit recognised at the invoice date and once as cash actually moving, with the funding gap shaded between them, would carry it better than the prose does.

A business wins a bigger order than it has handled before. It buys materials, pays people to do the work, delivers and invoices. Revenue is recorded the day the invoice goes out, so the profit and loss account looks excellent. The customer pays in sixty days. The supplier wants paying in thirty, HMRC wants the VAT on an invoice nobody has settled, unless the business is on cash accounting, and the payroll runs regardless. Growth widens the gap: every order consumes money before it produces any. Overtrading is the old word for it, and it is still a common route to going into administration [link to /insolvency/administration] for a company with a full order book.

Profit and cash answer different questions. Profit says whether a period of trading was worthwhile. Cash says whether you can meet what falls due this week. The statutory cash flow test for insolvency is whether a company can pay its debts as they fall due, whatever the year looked like on paper. Profitability measures performance. Liquidity measures survival.
The cash conversion cycle

[IMAGE] "The cash conversion cycle": a horizontal bar built from stock days, work in progress and debtor days, with creditor days subtracted from the end. Label the remainder "days you fund yourself".
This is the number of days between money leaving the business and coming back for the same piece of work, and the most useful single figure in working capital management.
Stock days. How long goods sit before they sell, your money on the shelf
Work in progress. Time between doing the work and being entitled to bill for it, often the biggest block of trapped cash
Debtor days. How long customers take to pay. Not the terms you agreed, the days they take
Creditor days. How long you take to pay suppliers, the one part of the cycle that funds you
The cycle itself. Stock plus work in progress plus debtor days, less creditor days: the days you fund yourself
A business running a cycle of seventy days carries seventy days of cost before it is paid. Take a fortnight off that and cash is released permanently, with no lender involved.
Where the cash is trapped
[IMAGE] "Where the cash is trapped": five items, list rather than cards. Do not illustrate.
Late invoicing. Work finished on the fourth, billed at month end, paid sixty days after that
No credit control. Terms exist on the invoice and nowhere else, and customers pay whoever asks first
Unbilled work in progress. Jobs part done and part billed, with a milestone nobody agreed at the outset
Equipment bought from the current account. A ten year asset paid for out of this month's cash, which is what asset finance [link to /finance-and-funding/asset-finance] exists to prevent

VAT and PAYE used as an overdraft. The most dangerous of them: it works for two quarters and then stops all at once, and it is usually the point at which a VAT loans [link to /finance-and-funding/vat-loans] conversation starts

Some of that is process, fixable within weeks. Some is structural: if your customers pay in ninety days and will not move, chasing changes nothing, and invoice finance [link to /finance-and-funding/invoice-finance] may be the answer. We will also say when a facility is only interest on a problem better process would fix.
How much working capital the business needs

This should be a number rather than a feeling. A week by week cash flow across the next quarter shows the peak requirement rather than the average, and the peak is what matters: a business that averages comfortable and drops below zero for four days in October has a problem in October. An overdraft repayable on demand is not committed money, and liquidity a lender can withdraw in a phone call is not liquidity you can plan around.
Where the numbers need testing from outside, that is what an independent review [link to /restructuring/independent-business-review] is for, and lenders often ask for one.
Does the capital structure support the plan?
[IMAGE] "Does the capital structure support the plan?": four items, list.
The second half of capital management is the shape of the funding itself. A business can be solvent today and funded in a way that will not survive its own plan.
The mix. How much debt sits against owners' capital. Gearing comfortable at current trading can be uncomfortable at forecast trading
The maturity. Short term money funding long term assets is the classic error. The overdraft that bought the machine is repayable on demand. The machine is not
The conditions. Covenants are tested on dates somebody else chose. Knowing which one you would breach first is worth more than knowing your rate
The personal exposure. Directors' loans, guarantees and security over the family home turn a company decision into a household one

Where the structure has stopped fitting the business, the answer is often debt restructuring [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring]: reprofiling repayments, replacing the wrong facility, or agreeing terms with lenders before a covenant test forces it. Where the trading is the problem, turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] is the route, and contingency planning [link to /restructuring/contingency-planning] is for the owner who wants the fallback mapped before needing it.
Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes the liquidator or administrator of a company we have advised, so recommending a formal process never pays us better than fixing the business. Where one is genuinely needed, we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we know and trust.

We are not FCA authorised, and we do not arrange finance, broker facilities or take commission from any lender. Where a facility is right we introduce a trusted specialist firm, which our finance and funding [link to /finance-and-funding] section explains. Capital management sits inside our wider financial advisory [link to /financial-advisory] work, alongside corporate finance [link to /financial-advisory/corporate-finance], because how a business is funded and what it is worth are the same question at different moments.
Frequently asked questions
What is capital management?

Capital management covers the working capital a business needs day to day and the capital structure that funds it over the longer term. It answers how much cash the business needs, where the cash it has has gone, and whether the funding fits the plan.
Can a profitable company really run out of money?

Yes, and it is one of the commoner ways a sound business fails. Profit is recorded when you invoice. Cash arrives when the customer pays. Growth widens the gap, because every order consumes money before it returns any.
What is the cash conversion cycle?

Stock days plus work in progress plus debtor days, less creditor days. It is the number of days a business funds itself between paying for work and being paid for it, and the first thing to examine when liquidity is tight.
Is more borrowing the answer?

Sometimes, and often not. Borrowing works when the business is sound and cash arrives later than it leaves. It is wrong when the business is losing money: the loan buys months and adds a creditor. We earn nothing either way.
Do you arrange the funding?

No. We are not FCA authorised and we do not broker facilities. Where we refer you on, that referral is disclosed and does not affect the independence of our advice. Where a facility is right we introduce a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool.
Closing call to action
Cash problem or profit problem?
The answer changes what you do next, and the two are easy to confuse from the inside. One conversation with your last accounts and current bank position usually settles it.

/financial-advisory/commercial-arbitration
Commercial arbitration and expert determination

Most commercial disputes are an argument about money wearing a legal costume. The contract settles who is entitled to what, and the fight is about the number. Commercial arbitration decides that argument privately, in front of arbitrators the parties choose themselves, and ends in an award that binds both sides.

We are not arbitrators and we are not solicitors. What we supply is the financial expertise inside the process: the valuation, the loss calculation, and evidence that holds up when the other side's expert pulls at it. Your solicitor runs the case. We answer the money question inside it, as we do in our forensic services [link to /financial-advisory/forensic-accounting] work.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
Arbitration, expert determination, mediation or court

[IMAGE] "Arbitration, expert determination, mediation or court": the strongest candidate on the page for a four-column comparison panel, with the money question as the deciding axis rather than the legal one.
These four are not interchangeable, and choosing wrong is expensive. The useful question is whether your disagreement is about the law or about a number.
Litigation. Public and adversarial, decided by a judge in the Court of Session or the sheriff court, on an open record your customers and bank can read

Commercial arbitration. Private, governed by the arbitration agreement in your contract and decided by arbitrators appointed for their expertise. The arbitral award is final and enforceable, and the grounds of appeal are narrow

Expert determination. One expert decides the point using their own knowledge, usually on paper and in weeks not months. No hearing, no arbitral tribunal, very little room to challenge. Share valuation and earn-out clauses often name it in advance
Mediation. Nobody decides anything. A mediator helps the parties reach their own settlement, and it earns its place while the relationship still has value

Where the disagreement is really about valuation or quantum, expert determination is often quicker and cheaper than arbitration. Where it turns on what the contract means, you want a lawyer deciding it. Settling that distinction when the clause is drafted saves more than any other choice in dispute resolution.
Scotland has its own arbitration regime
[IMAGE] "Scotland has its own arbitration regime": a small map or seal vector marking the seat point would work, but only if it reads as jurisdiction rather than decoration.

Almost everything written about commercial arbitration in the UK describes the English position. Arbitration seated in Scotland runs under the Arbitration (Scotland) Act 2010, not the Arbitration Act 1996 that applies in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. The 2010 Act carries the Scottish Arbitration Rules, some mandatory, some applying only until the parties agree otherwise.

The seat decides which regime governs you, and a seat is a legal address rather than a venue. If the dispute resolution clause in your contract names London, the arbitration is seated in England: the Arbitration Act 1996 governs the procedure and the English court supervises it, usually the Commercial Court, even where every hearing is in Glasgow and the contract itself is governed by Scots law. Scottish businesses sign up to a London seat more often than they realise, because the template came from London.

Two features of the Scottish Arbitration Rules are worth knowing. Confidentiality is written in as a default, where in England it rests on case law. So is the right to appeal to the court on a point of legal error, which the parties can contract out of.
The financial questions these disputes turn on
[IMAGE] "The financial questions these disputes turn on": four cards, 2+2.
Valuation disagreements

What a company, a shareholding or a division is worth when the parties cannot agree. Maintainable earnings, minority discounts, directors' loan accounts, and the gap between what a formula produces and what the business would fetch. On a sale rather than a dispute, corporate finance [link to /financial-advisory/corporate-finance] is the page you want.
Shareholder and partnership fallings-out

Exit provisions, the buyout price, disputed drawings, and whether the accounts the price is calculated from can be relied on at all. These start as valuation arguments and become forensic ones. Owners planning an orderly separation should start at exit planning [link to /restructuring/exit-planning].
Contract and loss claims

Loss of profits from a breach, disputed variations, unpaid milestones, and the counterfactual: what would have happened had the contract been performed. That counterfactual is where claims of this kind are won and lost.
Completion accounts and earn-outs

Arguments after a deal about working capital, accounting policy and whether an earn-out target was met. The share purchase agreement usually sends these to expert determination, and that clause sets what the expert may consider. Our transaction support [link to /financial-advisory/due-diligence] page covers the deal side.
International arbitration and enforcement

International arbitration exists mainly because of enforcement. A court judgment is hard to enforce against assets held abroad, while an arbitral award travels: the New York Convention obliges the courts of the states signed up to it to recognise an arbitral award made in another signatory state. That treaty is why cross-border contracts choose arbitration at all.

International commercial arbitration usually runs under the rules of an arbitral institution such as the LCIA in London, with ad hoc arbitration under the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules as the alternative. Whichever the arbitration agreement names, the financial evidence is built the same way, although currency, tax and the applicable law can move the figure more than the facts do.
Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments, sells no financial products and audits nothing, so there is no second engagement waiting behind the opinion we give. Where a formal appointment is needed, we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] we know and trust.

Disputes and distress turn up together more often than either side expects. If the counterparty is failing, the value of winning changes, and liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] sets out what happens to a claim then. If the dispute is what threatens your own business, start with restructuring [link to /restructuring]. The rest of this section sits on the financial advisory [link to /financial-advisory] hub, and you can reach us through contact us [link to /contact].
Frequently asked questions
What is commercial arbitration?

A private process in which the parties to a commercial contract agree that a dispute between them is decided by arbitrators instead of by a court. The arbitral proceedings are private, and in Scotland confidential unless the parties agree otherwise, and they end in an award enforceable through the court like a decree.
Is arbitration cheaper than going to court?

Not always. The parties pay the arbitrators and the venue, so a small claim can cost more than it would in court. What arbitration buys is privacy, a decision maker who knows the sector, and a timetable the parties control.
Our contract says the seat is London. Does that matter?

It decides the procedural law. A London seat means the Arbitration Act 1996 and English law procedure apply, with the English court supervising, in practice usually the Commercial Court in London, even where the businesses and the evidence are entirely Scottish.
Can an arbitration award be enforced overseas?

Usually, and more easily than a court judgment. The New York Convention requires the courts of every state signed up to that treaty to recognise an arbitral award made elsewhere, apart from a limited set of grounds for refusal. It is the strongest argument for international arbitration where your counterparty's assets sit abroad.
Do we have to name an arbitral institution in the contract?

No. A contract can name an arbitral institution such as the LCIA, whose rules then administer the case for a fee, or provide for ad hoc arbitration that the parties and the arbitrators run themselves. Institutional rules cost more and remove a lot of argument about procedure.
Can you act as the arbitrator or as the deciding expert?

No. We are not arbitrators and we do not take appointments as the expert who decides. We are instructed by one party, or jointly by both, to produce the financial analysis and give evidence on it. Keeping those roles separate is what makes the evidence usable.
Closing call to action
Is the argument really about a number?

If it is, the route matters as much as the case you make, and both are easier to fix before positions harden. One conversation will tell you what the money question is and what it would take to answer.

Invoice finance

Invoice finance turns unpaid sales invoices into cash now. A provider advances most of an invoice's value within a day or two of you raising it, then releases the balance, less its charges, once the customer pays.

Factoring and discounting are not the same thing
[IMAGE] Factoring versus discounting: a simple two-column diagram, one line each, showing who invoices, who chases, and who the customer speaks to. Teal sitewide icon set, no illustration of people.
They differ in the one respect owners care about: who speaks to your customers.
Invoice factoring. The provider collects. It runs your sales ledger and chases payment, so customers know a third party is involved. For a business with no credit control, that is often a relief

Invoice discounting. You collect. The facility sits behind the scenes and your customers need never know, which is why the undisclosed version is sold as confidential invoice discounting. Providers want stronger systems and figures first, since the chasing is left to you

Scots law transfers a debt differently from English law. Since April 2025 a Scottish assignation can be completed either by intimating it to your customer or by registering it, so a Scottish ledger may be documented its own way. Ask how yours is handled.
Who it suits, and who it does not
It may suit you if

You sell to other businesses on credit terms, bill for work already delivered, and have a spread of solid customers. It is at its best when growth is the problem: every new order eats cash before it produces any. capital management [link to /financial-advisory/capital-management] covers the mechanics.
It is the wrong move if

You sell to consumers, bill in stages before work is done, lean on one customer for most of your turnover, or work under a contract barring assignment of the debt. Each of those will narrow or close it. And if the business loses money on every job, this only releases cash faster. Equipment and vehicles belong with asset finance [link to /finance-and-funding/asset-finance].
The warning nobody gives you

This is the fastest way to release trapped working capital in a business under pressure. It is also the facility most likely to be withdrawn as that pressure worsens. The provider sees your ledger weekly, so it spots the slide before your bank does. Credit notes rise, debts age, a customer fails, and the terms tighten. The cash taken back is cash you have spent.

So the timing matters more than the rate. Put in while trading is stable, it is a useful tool. Reached for in the last quarter before a crisis, it often brings the crisis forward, and one pulled at the wrong moment is a well-worn route to going into administration [link to /insolvency/administration]. /finance-and-funding/asset-finance
Asset finance

Asset finance is borrowing against things rather than against a balance sheet. It covers buying equipment on hire purchase or a lease, and refinancing assets the business already owns to release cash, which is usually called sale and leaseback or asset based lending.

It is one of the more accessible forms of business funding, because the lender's security is the asset itself rather than your trading history. That is also the thing to understand before signing: the lender's position is protected in a way an unsecured lender's is not.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
What it actually covers

Two directions. Forward-looking, it funds an acquisition: a machine, a fleet, a fit-out, spread over the asset's working life rather than paid for out of one quarter's cash. Backward-looking, it releases capital tied up in assets you have already bought and paid for, which can be the fastest source of working capital available to a business under pressure. Hire purchase ends with you owning the asset; a lease generally does not, and the difference matters for both your accounts and what happens on an insolvency.
Who it suits, and who it does not
[IMAGE] "Who it suits, and who it does not": two cards.
It may suit you if

You need equipment to grow or to replace something failing, and paying cash for it would leave the business short. Or you own unencumbered plant and need working capital faster than a bank facility could be arranged. The asset has a real second-hand value, which is what makes the lending work.
It is the wrong move if

You are refinancing assets to cover trading losses. Releasing cash from your own plant to fund a shortfall converts an owned asset into a monthly commitment and buys a few months, and it is one of the more common steps on the way to a formal insolvency. If that is the situation, our turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] page is the honest starting point.
What we see that a lender will not tell you

Assets on hire purchase or lease are not yours to sell. Directors regularly forget this, and it surfaces at the worst possible moment: an administrator arrives, and equipment the business has treated as its own for years turns out to belong to a finance company. Once a company is in administration the finance company cannot simply repossess, since it needs the administrator's consent or the court's permission, but the asset is still not the company's to sell. That changes what a business is worth to a buyer, and it changes what a pre-pack administration can actually transfer. Before any insolvency conversation, establish exactly which assets you own outright, which are financed, and what each agreement says on default. It takes an afternoon and it changes the options.

We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

If the kit is not the problem and the trading is, turning the business around [link to /restructuring/turnaround] is the work that matters, not another facility. If the issue is the shape of what you already owe, that is restructuring the debt [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring]. And if a guarantee on an existing agreement has been called, your own position [link to /debt-help-scotland] is a separate question with its own answers.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between hire purchase and leasing?

With hire purchase you are buying the asset over time and own it at the end. With a lease you are paying for use, and ownership usually stays with the lender. The distinction affects your accounts, your tax position and, importantly, what happens to the asset if the business fails.
Can I raise money against equipment I already own?
Often yes, if it is unencumbered and has a resale value. It is one of the quicker routes to working capital. Whether it is a good idea depends entirely on what the money is for.
Do you arrange the finance?
No. We are not brokers and take no commission from lenders. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and we tell you first whether borrowing is the right move at all.
What happens to financed assets if the company fails?

They generally belong to the finance company, not to the business. A liquidator cannot sell them. An administrator can, but only with the finance company's agreement or a court order, and the finance company has to be paid the asset's value out of the proceeds. Either way they are not simply yours to transfer. Our administration [link to /insolvency/administration] page explains what that means in practice.

What lenders actually look at

Three things, in this order. The property, because that is the security: what it is worth, how specialised it is, and how easily it could be sold to someone else. The income, meaning whether the business or the rent covers the payments with room to spare. And the covenants, which are the conditions you agree to keep to, typically around loan-to-value and interest cover. The covenants are where owner-managed businesses get caught, because a breach can be triggered by a valuation moving rather than by anything the business did.
Who it suits, and who it does not
[IMAGE] "Who it suits, and who it does not": two cards.
It may suit you if

You are buying premises you will occupy, or refinancing property you already own onto better terms. The income covers the payments with genuine headroom rather than exactly. You expect to hold the property for a period long enough to justify the arrangement costs.
It is the wrong move if

You need the money quickly, in which case this is the wrong instrument and bridging finance [link to /finance-and-funding/bridging-finance] is what people use, expensively. Or the business is under strain and the mortgage is being drawn to fund trading, which turns a property asset into a monthly obligation the trade already cannot support.
Enforcement in Scotland works differently
[IMAGE] "Enforcement in Scotland works differently": if any panel is used on a referral page, this is the one that earns it — a simple England and Wales vs Scotland split.

Almost everything written online about commercial mortgage enforcement describes England and Wales, where a lender appoints a receiver under the Law of Property Act 1925. That regime does not exist in Scotland. Security over Scottish property is a standard security, and a lender enforces it under the Conveyancing and Feudal Reform (Scotland) Act 1970 by serving a calling-up notice or a notice of default, then exercising its remedies. Where any part of the property is residential, including a flat above a shop, the lender needs a warrant from the sheriff before it can sell or take possession. If your property is in Scotland, the LPA guidance you will find is describing another country's law, and our LPA receivership [link to /insolvency/lpa-receivership] page sets out the contrast properly.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

If the property is sound and the business under it is not, the answer is a turnaround plan [link to /restructuring/turnaround] rather than a larger loan. If the debt itself is the problem, restructuring what you owe [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring] is the conversation. And if a guarantee has been called, your own position [link to /debt-help-scotland] is dealt with separately from the company's.
Frequently asked questions
How much can I borrow against commercial property?

It depends on the property, the income covering it and the lender, and any figure quoted without a valuation is a guess. What matters more than the maximum is the headroom: borrowing to the limit leaves no room for a valuation to move against you.
What is a covenant breach and why does it matter?

A covenant is a condition in the facility, usually about loan-to-value or interest cover. Breaching one can put the facility in default even if every payment has been made on time, which is why a falling valuation can create a problem out of nothing you did.
Is a Scottish commercial mortgage different?

The lending is the same; the security and the enforcement are not. Scottish property is secured by a standard security and enforced under the 1970 Act, not by the Law of Property Act. Use a lender and a solicitor who deal with Scottish property routinely.

Bridging finance

A bridging loan is short-term borrowing secured on property, arranged quickly and priced accordingly. It sits alongside the other options in our finance and funding [link to /finance-and-funding] section. It exists to cover a gap: a purchase that has to complete before a sale, a refinancing that has not landed yet, a development that needs finishing before it can be let or sold.

Used properly it is a useful and entirely legitimate instrument. Used to plug a hole with no clear way out, it is the single most expensive mistake a business under pressure can make, and we see the results of that more often than we see the successes.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
The exit is the whole thing
[IMAGE] The clock vector panel would fit "The exit is the whole thing" if a panel is wanted.

Every bridge is underwritten on its exit, meaning the specific event that repays it: a sale completing, a term facility drawing down, a development finishing and letting. The rate matters far less than whether that event is real and whether the timescale is honest. A bridge with a credible exit is short-term borrowing. A bridge without one is a deadline you have paid a premium to set for yourself, and when it arrives the usual answer is another bridge at a worse rate.
Who it suits, and who it does not
[IMAGE] "Who it suits, and who it does not": two cards. On this page the second card is the reason the page exists.
It may suit you if

There is a defined, evidenced event that repays the loan, and it is close enough that the cost of the bridge is proportionate. A property sale with a buyer, a refinancing with an offer, a development with a contractor and a programme. You have a margin for the exit slipping, because it usually does.
It is the wrong move if

The exit is a hope rather than a plan, or the money is being borrowed to service other debt. Borrowing expensively to keep up payments on cheaper borrowing is the most reliable route we know from a difficult position to an impossible one, and the reason is arithmetic rather than judgement. If that is where you are, debt restructuring [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring] is the conversation to have instead.
What we see afterwards

A meaningful share of the businesses that reach us in real distress have a bridge on the balance sheet, taken six or nine months earlier, whose exit did not happen. The pattern is consistent: the bridge was taken to buy time to fix something, the fix took longer than expected, and the bridge's own deadline arrived first. Because it is secured and short, the lender's options are quick, so the bridge frequently sets the timetable for everything that follows, including an administration [link to /insolvency/administration]. If you are considering one, the useful question is not what it costs but what happens on the day it falls due and the exit has not arrived.

How quickly can a bridge be arranged?
Faster than a term facility, which is the point of it and part of what you pay for. The speed is genuine, and it is also what makes it easy to commit to before thinking the exit through.
Why is bridging so expensive?
It is priced for speed, short duration and the lender's risk of the exit failing. On a genuinely short bridge the cost is proportionate. On one that rolls, it compounds quickly.
What happens if I cannot repay at the end?
The lender will look at an extension, usually at a higher rate, or at enforcing its security. That is why the exit is underwritten at the start, and why a bridge without a real one is dangerous.

Unsecured business loans

An unsecured business loan is borrowing without a charge over a specific asset. There is no property to enforce against, as there would be with a commercial mortgage [link to /finance-and-funding/commercial-mortgages], and no equipment pledged, which is why the process is quicker and why the rate is higher than secured lending.
The word unsecured does a lot of work in that sentence, and it is worth being precise about what it actually means, because for an owner-managed business it very rarely means what people assume.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
Unsecured almost always means guaranteed

For a company of any size below the corporate mid-market, an unsecured facility is normally conditional on the directors giving a personal guarantee. The loan is unsecured against the company's assets, and secured against yours. That is not a criticism of lenders, it is how the risk is priced, but it changes the decision entirely: what looks like the company borrowing is, in substance, you borrowing. A great many directors sign these without reading them, and discover the terms only when the guarantee is called.
Who it suits, and who it does not
[IMAGE] "Who it suits, and who it does not": two cards.
It may suit you if

The business needs working capital or funding for growth, has no suitable asset to secure against, and can service the repayments comfortably from trading. You have read the guarantee, you understand what it covers and for how long, and you are content to stand behind it personally.
It is the wrong move if

The company is already struggling and the loan would fund a shortfall rather than an opportunity. Taking on personally guaranteed borrowing at that point moves the risk from the company, which has limited liability, to you, who do not. It is the mechanism by which a business failure becomes a personal one.
What a guarantee does when the company fails
[IMAGE] "What a guarantee does when the company fails" is the section that matters; the shield or scales panel would suit it.

Liquidating the company does not extinguish your guarantee. The lender's claim against the company disappears into the insolvency, and its claim against you continues, reduced only by whatever the lender recovers in the liquidation, which is why a director can emerge from a creditors' voluntary liquidation owing money personally on borrowing the company took. Guarantees also hide: in bank facilities, equipment leases, commercial property leases and supplier credit applications, sometimes signed years earlier and forgotten. Before any insolvency decision, find out exactly what you have guaranteed, because it frequently changes which route is right. Where a guarantee is called and cannot be met, that becomes a personal debt problem with its own answers, covered in our Debt Help Scotland [link to /debt-help-scotland] section.

Is an unsecured business loan really unsecured?
Unsecured against the company's assets, usually. Not against yours, because most lenders require a personal guarantee from the directors. Read what you are signing: the distinction is the whole risk.
What happens to my guarantee if the company is liquidated?
It survives. Limited liability protects you from the company's debts generally; it does not protect you from a promise you personally made to a lender. The lender will look to you for the shortfall.
Can I negotiate the guarantee?

Sometimes, on the cap, the duration, or whether it is joint and several with other directors. It is worth trying before signing and almost impossible afterwards. Take advice on the wording, not just the amount.

VAT and tax loans

A VAT loan is short-term borrowing that pays a tax bill on your behalf so you can repay it over several months rather than in one payment. The same product exists for corporation tax and for self-assessment liabilities.

It is a straightforward facility and it solves a real problem for businesses whose income is lumpy. It is also, more often than the industry admits, an early warning sign, and this page is mainly about telling the two situations apart.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
What it does
[IMAGE] "Who it suits, and who it does not": two cards.

It converts a single large payment into a series of smaller ones, usually over three to twelve months, at a cost. For a business with genuinely seasonal or contract-driven income, that smoothing is exactly what it should be used for: the money is there across the year, just not on the day the bill falls due. The lender pays HMRC directly, so the liability is settled and you owe the finance company instead.
Who it suits, and who it does not
It may suit you if

Your income is lumpy for a structural reason and the bill has landed in a trough. The business is profitable and the cash arrives, just not in the right week. You are using it occasionally rather than as a matter of course.
It is the wrong move if

You need one every quarter. At that point the business is not experiencing a timing problem, it is trading beyond its working capital, and each quarter's borrowing makes the next one harder. That is a capital management [link to /financial-advisory/capital-management] question, and if the trend is downwards it is a turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] one.
Why we treat repeat tax funding as a warning

VAT is money the business has already collected on HMRC's behalf. If it is not there when the return falls due, it has been used to fund something else, usually the ordinary shortfall between what the business spends and what it collects. Borrowing to replace it fixes the symptom for a quarter. What we look at instead is why the money was not there, because that answer is the one that decides whether the business has a cash timing issue or a solvency issue. There is also a conduct dimension worth knowing: where a company later fails, an insolvency practitioner has to report on the directors' conduct, and using tax money to pay other creditors is one of the things the Insolvency Service names as unfit conduct. Our creditors' voluntary liquidation page covers that.

Is a VAT loan a good idea?
For a genuinely seasonal business facing a bill in a trough, often yes. As a regular quarterly habit, it is usually treating a symptom, and the underlying problem gets more expensive each time.
Could I use Time to Pay instead?

Possibly, and it is worth asking HMRC before borrowing. Time to Pay is a real arrangement granted on a realistic proposal, and it usually costs less than commercial borrowing, though HMRC charges interest on the arrears throughout. What it requires is that current taxes are kept up to date throughout.
Does taking a VAT loan look bad to HMRC?

Not if it clears the bill by the due date, because then it is paid in full and on time from HMRC's point of view. Pay late and HMRC's late payment penalties and interest have already started, and borrowing does not undo them. Property finance

Property finance covers two quite different things. Development finance funds a build or a conversion, drawn down in stages as the work progresses and repaid when the scheme is sold or refinanced. Investment finance is longer-term borrowing against property held to let, which is closer to a commercial mortgage [link to /finance-and-funding/commercial-mortgages].
Development is the one that gets businesses into difficulty, and it does so in a specific and predictable way that is worth understanding before you draw the first tranche.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
How development finance works
[IMAGE] "How development finance works": a simple staged-drawdown diagram would carry this better than prose if a panel is wanted.

Unlike the finance and funding [link to /finance-and-funding] products that advance in a single sum, the lender releases development money against a programme. Funds are released in stages as work is completed and signed off, usually by a monitoring surveyor acting for the lender, with interest typically rolled up and repaid at the end out of the sale or refinancing. The whole structure assumes the programme holds: that each stage completes roughly when it was said it would, at roughly the cost stated, and that the exit arrives when planned.
Who it suits, and who it does not
[IMAGE] "Who it suits, and who it does not": two cards.
It may suit you if

You have a costed scheme, a contractor, a realistic programme and a credible exit, whether that is a sale or a term refinancing. There is contingency in the numbers for the things that always happen, and you can fund a period of overrun without the scheme stopping.
It is the wrong move if

The contingency is thin, the programme is optimistic, or the exit depends on a market rather than on a buyer. Development schemes rarely fail because the buildings were wrong; they fail because time and cost ran past the funding, and the shortest route to that is a programme with no slack in it.
Where schemes actually go wrong

Cost overruns and delays turn into distress faster in development than anywhere else, because the drawdown schedule assumes the programme and the interest keeps rolling up while nothing is being sold. A three-month delay is not a three-month problem: it is three more months of rolled-up interest, a later exit, and often a contractor who now wants paying differently. The lender's security is the site, and the site is worth considerably less half-finished than finished, which shapes how a lender behaves when a scheme stalls. If yours is slipping, the time to talk to the lender is before the next drawdown request, not after it is declined, and our debt restructuring [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring] page covers what lenders will and will not agree to.

How is development finance different from a mortgage?

It is drawn in stages against build progress rather than advanced in one sum, the interest is usually rolled up rather than paid monthly, and it is repaid from a sale or refinancing rather than from income. It is short-term and it is priced accordingly.
What is a monitoring surveyor?
A surveyor appointed by the lender to check that work has actually been done before each stage is released. They act for the lender, not for you, and their view governs the drawdown.

Engineering and manufacturing finance

Engineering and manufacturing businesses have a funding profile that does not fit standard lending well. Capital equipment is expensive and long-lived, tooling for a specific contract is expensive and often worth nothing to anyone else, and there is usually a long gap between winning work and being paid for it.
The result is a sector that is frequently profitable on paper and short of cash in practice, which is a combination that catches out lenders and owners alike.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
What the sector actually needs funding for

Three things, and they behave differently. Capital equipment, which has a resale value and is therefore straightforward to fund through asset finance [link to /finance-and-funding/asset-finance]. Tooling and setup for a specific contract, which is much harder, because it is worth little outside that contract and lenders know it. And working capital across the production cycle, from raw material through work in progress to an invoice that then sits on payment terms, which is where most of the strain actually sits.
Who it suits, and who it does not
[IMAGE] "Who it suits, and who it does not": two cards.
It may suit you if

You are funding equipment with a genuine second-hand value, or bridging a working capital cycle on contracts you have won and will be paid for. The order book supports the commitment beyond the current contract.
It is the wrong move if

You are funding tooling for a single contract whose margin does not cover it, or borrowing against an order book concentrated in one customer. Both are common and both convert an operational risk into a financial one that outlives the contract.
The pattern we see in engineering failures

Engineering businesses rarely fail because they cannot do the work. They fail because a large contract absorbed working capital faster than it generated cash: materials bought, labour paid, tooling made, and payment arriving months later or in stages that lag the spend. A profitable contract can put a company under, and a growing order book can accelerate it rather than help. That is a capital management [link to /financial-advisory/capital-management] question before it is a funding one, and the honest answer is sometimes that the contract should be declined or repriced rather than financed. Where the pattern is already established, our turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] page is the more useful starting point.

/finance-and-funding/hospitality-finance
Hospitality and leisure finance

Hospitality is one of the sectors we work in most, and it has a funding profile unlike almost any other: highly seasonal, heavily fixed in its costs, exposed to energy and wage inflation, and frequently operating from leased premises on terms that leave very little room.
That combination means a hospitality business can be trading well and still hit a wall in a specific month, and the businesses that survive are usually the ones that saw that month coming.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
What the sector funds

Fit-outs and refurbishment, which are expensive and mostly worthless to a lender as security because they are specific to the site. Equipment, which does have a resale value and is straightforward through asset finance [link to /finance-and-funding/asset-finance]. Acquisitions of a lease or a freehold. And working capital across the season, which is the one that actually decides whether a business gets through the year.
Who it suits, and who it does not
[IMAGE] "Who it suits, and who it does not": two cards.
It may suit you if
[IMAGE] The clock or cycle vector panel would suit "The month that catches hospitality out" if a panel is wanted.

The trade is sound and the funding covers a known seasonal trough or an investment that will demonstrably increase trade. The lease has enough term left to justify the spend, which is a condition owners frequently overlook when funding a fit-out.
It is the wrong move if

The business is losing money in its good months. Hospitality has a thin margin for error, and funding a loss through a strong season simply means the weak season arrives with the debt already in place. If that is the position, our turnaround [link to /restructuring/turnaround] page is the honest starting point.
The month that catches hospitality out

Almost every hospitality failure we see has the same shape. Trade is strong through the busy season, the business feels comfortable, and the costs that were deferred through it, the VAT quarter, the rent, the supplier accounts stretched a little, all fall due in the quiet months when the income has gone. January and February do most of the damage in Scotland, and the decisions that determine whether a business survives them are taken the previous autumn. A fit-out funded on the back of a good summer is a decision made at the point of maximum optimism about a business whose cash position will look entirely different in twelve weeks. Where the debt has already built up but the trade is genuinely viable, a company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] can restructure it while the business keeps trading, and that is a conversation to have in October rather than in February.
How we handle it

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring [link to /restructuring] specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

Borrowing into a quiet season postpones the question rather than answering it. If the trading needs fixing, that is turning the business around [link to /restructuring/turnaround]. If the debt already in place is the weight, it is restructuring what you owe [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring]. And if a guarantee has been called, your own position [link to /debt-help-scotland] is a separate matter with its own routes.
Frequently asked questions
Can we get funding on a leased pub or restaurant?

Often, but the lease term matters a great deal. A lender will not fund a fit-out over a period longer than the lease has left, and a tied lease constrains what a business can do to improve its margin, which lenders factor in. Since 2025 a Scottish tied tenant has had a statutory route to a market-rent-only lease under the Scottish Pubs Code, which changes that calculation.
Why is hospitality funding harder than other sectors?

Because the assets are largely site-specific, the income is seasonal, and the margins are thin. Lenders price all three. Equipment with a resale value is the exception and is generally easier to fund.
We are behind on VAT and rent. Is borrowing the answer?

Sometimes, and often not. If the business is profitable across a full year and the arrears are a timing problem, funding can work. If it loses money in the good months, borrowing postpones the decision at a cost. That is worth establishing before you commit.
Do you arrange hospitality finance?
No. We are not brokers and take no commission from lenders. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and hospitality is a sector where we will often say the problem is not a funding one.

Hospitality and leisure is one of the sectors we know best, and we are not brokers or arrangers of facilities. One conversation will tell you whether funding helps or postpones.

Contractor and construction finance

Construction has a payment cycle that would put most other industries out of business. Work is done, an application for payment is made, a proportion is certified, payment arrives on extended terms, and a slice is held back as retention for a year or more after the job is finished.

A contractor can therefore be busy, profitable and insolvent at the same time, and construction records more insolvencies than any other sector, which reflects exactly that. Construction is one of the sectors we work in most.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
Where the money is tied up

In three places. In work in progress, done but not yet certified. In certified applications waiting out the payment terms. And in retentions, which are the industry's most peculiar feature: money you have earned, held by someone else, sometimes for years, and frequently difficult to recover at the end. Add plant and vehicles, which are funded through asset finance [link to /finance-and-funding/asset-finance], and the working capital demand on a growing contractor is substantial and constant.
Who it suits, and who it does not
[IMAGE] "Who it suits, and who it does not": two cards.
It may suit you if

You have certified applications or invoices and the funding bridges the payment terms. The main contractors you work for are financially sound. Growth is funded rather than absorbed, which is the distinction that decides whether a busy year helps or hurts.
It is the wrong move if

You are funding a cash gap caused by disputed work or unrecovered retentions, which is a commercial and contractual problem that money does not fix. Or your exposure is concentrated in one main contractor, in which case the funding does not reduce the risk, it increases what you lose if they fail.
When the main contractor goes under
[IMAGE] "When the main contractor goes under" is the section that matters. A simple downstream diagram would carry it.

This is the risk that defines the sector, and it runs downhill fast. When a main contractor fails, subcontractors rank as ordinary unsecured creditors for everything certified and unpaid, for work in progress, and for retentions, and unsecured creditors in an insolvency typically recover very little. The knock-on then takes out subcontractors who were themselves perfectly viable. Practical protection is limited but real: know who you are working for and check them, keep applications and certifications current rather than letting them run, resist the temptation to let one relationship dominate your order book, and take retention recovery seriously rather than treating it as an afterthought. If a main contractor above you has failed, act quickly, because our winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition] and creditors' voluntary liquidation pages describe timetables that move faster than most subcontractors expect.

When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

Where the contracts are profitable and the cash is simply arriving late, funding may help. Where they are not, turning it around [link to /restructuring/turnaround] is the real work. Where the borrowing already in place is the constraint, that is restructuring the debt [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring]. And if you have guaranteed a facility personally, personal debt options [link to /debt-help-scotland] covers your side of it.
Frequently asked questions
Can we finance retentions?

Some lenders will look at retention funding, though it is more specialised and more expensive than invoice finance against certified applications, because the money is harder to collect and the timing is uncertain.
What happens to our money if the main contractor fails?

You become an unsecured creditor for certified work, work in progress and retentions. Recovery for unsecured creditors is usually poor. That is why concentration risk matters more in construction than almost anywhere else.
Is invoice finance available to subcontractors?
Often, but lenders treat construction cautiously because of applications, certification, set-off and retentions. Some specialise in it, and the terms differ from standard invoice finance.

No. We are not brokers and take no commission. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and where the problem is a failing main contractor rather than a funding gap, that is our own work.

/finance-and-funding/care-home-finance
Care home finance

Care home funding sits between a commercial mortgage [link to /finance-and-funding/commercial-mortgages] and trading business lending, and lenders treat it as both. The building is substantial security, but its value depends heavily on continuing to operate as a care home, which depends in turn on the operator holding its registration.
That link between the regulatory position and the value of the asset is what makes this sector different from any other kind of commercial property lending.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
What lenders look at

Occupancy first, because it drives everything else in the finance and funding [link to /finance-and-funding] decision. The mix between local authority funded and privately funded residents, since fee rates differ substantially and a home weighted towards local authority rates has thinner margins. Staffing cost and agency dependence, which has been the sector's sharpest pressure. The building itself, including whether the rooms meet current expectations on ensuite provision and size. And the regulatory position, which in Scotland means the Care Inspectorate rather than the Care Quality Commission, a distinction that matters and that English-written guidance gets wrong.
Who it suits, and who it does not
[IMAGE] "Who it suits, and who it does not": two cards.
It may suit you if

You are acquiring or refinancing a home with stable occupancy and a defensible fee mix, and the funding is sized against realistic staffing costs rather than best-case ones. Your regulatory grades are sound, because a lender will look at them.
It is the wrong move if

Occupancy is falling, agency dependence is high and rising, or there is an unresolved regulatory issue. In this sector a regulatory problem becomes a financial one very quickly, because it affects admissions, and admissions drive the income that services the debt.
Why regulatory and financial distress arrive together
[IMAGE] "Why regulatory and financial distress arrive together" is a loop and would suit the cycle vector panel.

A care home in financial difficulty tends to reduce spending in ways that show up in inspection: staffing thins, agency use rises, maintenance is deferred. A poorer grade then affects new admissions, occupancy falls, and the financial position worsens. It is a loop, and by the time it is visible in the accounts it has usually been running for a while. It also constrains the options: in practice an insolvency in this sector cannot simply stop trading, because there are residents in the building. The Care Inspectorate has to be told immediately: a care service provider, and any office-holder appointed over it, must notify it of an insolvency event as soon as one happens, and administration, receivership, a creditors' voluntary liquidation and a winding up order all count. Any administration [link to /insolvency/administration] or sale then has to be run with the regulator and the placing local authorities involved from the outset. That is a materially more complex process than an ordinary business sale and it needs more notice, which is the practical reason to take advice early here rather than late.
How we handle it

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring [link to /restructuring] specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

Occupancy and grades are operational problems before they are funding ones, so fixing the trading position [link to /restructuring/turnaround] usually comes before any new facility. Where the existing debt is the constraint, renegotiating the debt [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring] is the route. And where you have signed personally, personal insolvency in Scotland [link to /debt-help-scotland] sets out what that means for you.
Frequently asked questions
Who regulates care homes in Scotland?
The Care Inspectorate. The Care Quality Commission regulates in England only, so guidance written for England names the wrong body and, in places, the wrong requirements.
How do lenders value a care home?

Largely on its trading performance rather than on bricks and mortar, because the value depends on it continuing to operate as a care home. That is why occupancy, fee mix and the regulatory position all feed into the lending decision.
Does a poor inspection grade affect funding?
It can, both on new lending and on existing facilities, because it affects admissions and therefore income. Lenders in this sector follow regulatory grades closely.
Do you arrange care home finance?
No. We are not brokers and take no commission. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and where a home is already under pressure we advise on that instead.

Sports and entertainment finance

This part of our finance and funding [link to /finance-and-funding] section covers two related things: funding for clubs, venues and promoters, and funding for individuals in sport and entertainment whose income is large but irregular and whose earning period may be short.

Both are treated cautiously by mainstream lenders, and for the same underlying reason. The income is real but it is lumpy, uncertain and, in the case of individuals, concentrated into a small number of years.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
What the sector funds

For clubs and venues: premises and their improvement, equipment, and working capital across a season whose income arrives in bursts around fixtures, events or a summer. For individuals: property and lifestyle lending underwritten against irregular earnings, which mainstream affordability assessments handle poorly. In both cases the funding challenge is not the total income but its shape.
Who it suits, and who it does not
[IMAGE] "Who it suits, and who it does not": two cards.
It may suit you if

There is a demonstrable income pattern over several seasons or years rather than one exceptional period, and the borrowing is sized against a normal year rather than a good one. For a club, there is governance capable of holding to a budget, which lenders in this sector look at closely.
It is the wrong move if

The borrowing is sized against a peak: a promotion, a cup run, a single strong season, a contract that has years left but is not guaranteed. Sport is the sector where optimism most reliably becomes debt, and the commitments made after a good season are the ones that cause the trouble two seasons later.
Why clubs get into difficulty

The pattern is consistent and it is structural rather than a matter of poor management. Costs in sport are competitive: what a club spends is driven by what its rivals spend, because the objective is relative rather than absolute. Income, meanwhile, depends on results, which are uncertain. So costs are committed in advance on the assumption of a level of success that may not arrive, and the gap between the two is filled with debt. Add the fact that a club rarely fails out of public view, because supporters, leagues and sometimes local authorities all have an interest, and you get a sector where insolvency is unusually public and unusually constrained. Where the trade is viable but the historic debt is not, a company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] is the instrument that addresses that, and our company administration [link to /insolvency/administration] page covers the alternative.
How we handle it

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring [link to /restructuring] specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

Committed costs against uncertain income is a structural problem, so fixing the trading position [link to /restructuring/turnaround] usually matters more than the facility. Where the debt itself is the constraint, that is restructuring the debt [link to /restructuring/debt-restructuring]. And where a guarantee has been called, your own position [link to /debt-help-scotland] is dealt with on its own terms.
Frequently asked questions
Why do lenders find sports clubs difficult?

Because income depends on results and results are uncertain, while costs are largely committed in advance. Add asset values that depend on continued operation and governance that varies widely, and mainstream lenders price it cautiously or decline it.
Can individuals with irregular income get funding?

Yes, through lenders who underwrite on the pattern of earnings rather than on a payslip. It is specialist lending and it is priced accordingly. The important discipline is borrowing against a normal year rather than a peak one.
What happens when a club cannot pay its debts?

The same procedures apply as to any company, but the process is more public and more constrained, and league and governing-body rules frequently impose their own consequences. Taking advice early matters more here than in most sectors.
Do you arrange this funding?
No. We are not brokers and take no commission. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and where a club or an individual is already over-committed we advise on that instead.

What a Glasgow accountant actually does for you

Most businesses need an accountant for the steady, essential work that keeps them compliant and informed. In Glasgow, as anywhere else, that means much the same set of services, and it is worth knowing what you are buying before you choose a firm.
Year-end accounts and corporation tax for your limited company, filed with Companies House and HMRC on time
Bookkeeping and VAT returns, keeping the day-to-day accounting records straight and the quarterly VAT filed correctly
Payroll, so staff and HMRC are paid the right amount on the right date
Self assessment for directors, sole traders and partners
Management accounts, the monthly or quarterly numbers that tell you how the business is actually doing rather than how it did last year
Audit, for the larger companies and charities that need one

Good accountants offer more than a filing service. They tell you what the numbers mean, flag a problem while it is still small, and answer the question before you have to ask it. That relationship is worth choosing carefully, which is why we only refer to a firm we would use ourselves.
Choosing an accountant in Glasgow
A few things separate accountants who file your accounts from those who genuinely help the business.
They explain, rather than just submit. You should understand your own numbers after a conversation with your accountant, not feel more confused
They are proactive on tax. Good advice arrives before the year end, when something can still be done, not after it when nothing can

They have experience with businesses like yours. A practice built around large corporates often serves a small owner-managed Glasgow business poorly, and the reverse is also true. The same test applies to charities, which are best served by a firm with charity experience
They tell you when something is wrong. The most valuable accountant is the one who says the difficult thing early, which is exactly the standard we hold ourselves to
Where accountancy meets the work we do

There is a point where accountancy shades into our territory, and knowing it is useful whether you are our client or not. It is the point where a business problem stops being an accounting problem and becomes a solvency one.

When a business starts missing payments, when HMRC arrears build, when new finance is hard to raise, or when a director begins worrying about personal guarantees, the question moves beyond routine accountancy. That is the crossover we specialise in. The problem a set of management accounts shows early might later call for a company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva], a formal liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation], or, where the pressure has reached the director personally, debt help in Scotland [link to /debt-help-scotland]. An unpaid tax bill that becomes a winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition] is far easier to handle months before it is filed than in the week it lands.

Many of our clients arrive through their own accountant, who recognised the warning signs and wanted a restructuring [link to /restructuring] or insolvency [link to /insolvency] specialist alongside them rather than in place of them.

We work with accountants, not against them. If your accountant refers you to us, we handle the specific insolvency or restructuring question and hand you back. If you come to us directly, we keep your accountant in the loop, because they know the business and we do not intend to replace them. For businesses and their owners we also advise in our own name on financial advisory [link to /financial-advisory] matters such as valuations, disputes and corporate finance transactions.

If you want to understand how we work before picking up the phone, our about [link to /about] page sets out who we are and the standard we hold ourselves to. When you are ready, contact us [link to /contact] and the first conversation is free.

Because we would rather do one thing properly than several things adequately. Insolvency and restructuring is where our advice carries real weight, and a specialist accountancy firm gives you a better service on the routine work than we would.

Yes, and that is exactly our work. Bring your accountant into the conversation if you can. You are not the first person to leave it too long

Most people who contact us have been carrying it alone for a long time before they say anything. People tend to wait between six and eighteen months before asking for help, and some struggle on for years. The reasons are always the same: it did not feel serious enough yet, asking might make it official, and there was a persistent hope that the next contract would fix it.

What actually happens in that period is that the options narrow. A business with six months of runway can sell a division, refinance, negotiate, restructure its debt or close in an orderly way and pay its creditors. The same business with six weeks can do almost none of that. Nothing about it changed except the time available.
So the single most useful thing on this page is this: getting advice does not commit you to anything, and it does not start a process. It tells you what your options are while you still have them.

Why the firm exists

The insolvency and debt advice market has a trust problem, and it is no secret inside the profession. Much of the advice comes from people paid out of the procedure they recommend, whether from the appointment itself or from a product carrying a commission. So the question of whether you need that procedure gets answered by someone with a stake in the answer.

The pattern is familiar. Liquidation proposed where a turnaround was still possible, or a director pushed towards a default answer before anyone has looked at what they signed personally. The harm is rarely a shortage of options. It is the absence of an unbiased read on them while there is still time to use them.
Lancefield was set up as the counterweight. We look at the whole position, business and personal together, and say what we think.
Phil Dunn

Lancefield Advisory is led by Phil Dunn, who has spent over twenty years in restructuring and recovery, gained across three of the Big Four accounting firms. That is two decades at the difficult end of this work: lenders who have run out of patience, HMRC arrears that have been rolling for a year or more, and directors who signed a personal guarantee and have not slept properly since.

Phil works as a consultant rather than as a licensed insolvency practitioner, and the distinction is deliberate rather than incidental. He is not licensed to take formal appointments and does not seek them. What he does is establish where a business or an individual actually stands, then bring in the right licensed specialist for whichever part of the problem needs one. On any given case that might be an insolvency practitioner, a solicitor, a valuer, a tax adviser or a funder. His job is to work out what is genuinely required and assemble it, not to be all of it.

He describes his own role as a trusted adviser rather than a technician, and the test he applies to it is a practical one: whether a professional contact sends him a second client after the first. Most of his work arrives that way.

A large share of what we do comes from other professionals rather than directly from the businesses themselves, and the reasons are worth stating because they explain how we work.

Accountants who cannot carry out restructuring or debt work themselves, whether for independence reasons, because the work sits outside their practice, or because the client relationship is too valuable to risk on unfamiliar ground

Distressed small and medium-sized businesses, sole traders, partners and private individuals. In practice that means companies from around £50,000 of turnover up to roughly £20 million, which is the range where the owner is still in the room and the decisions are personal as well as commercial.

What a good outcome looks like

There is a persistent misconception about why businesses fail and what happens when they get into difficulty, and it costs people time they cannot afford. Insolvency is treated as a single event with one meaning, when the reality is a range of outcomes that differ enormously.

The part that gets least attention is the positive side of a restructuring process: jobs kept, suppliers paid, a landlord dealt with properly, a business that continues in some form rather than stopping. Those outcomes are frequently available and frequently missed, because the people who could have taken them did not know they were there.
So the most satisfying work here is rarely the dramatic kind. It is the case where someone asked early enough that the good options were still on the table.

Certain roles in a formal insolvency can only be held by a licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency]: liquidator, administrator, nominee and supervisor of a company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva], and in Scotland trustee under a trust deed for creditors, or trustee in a sequestration [link to /debt-help-scotland/sequestration] where the Accountant in Bankruptcy is not acting. Where a formal appointment genuinely is needed, we bring in a licensed practitioner we know and trust, and stay alongside you rather than handing you over at the door. Because nobody here takes the appointment, we earn nothing from one happening, which leaves us free to say when a formal procedure is the wrong answer. Most firms in this market are not in a position to write that sentence.

Creditors' guides to insolvency practitioners' fees
[IMAGE - Hero] none. This is a regulatory page and should open on text, with the Mackintosh vector panel at most.
