If a company or person that owes you money has entered a formal insolvency procedure, you have a financial interest in what the office holder is paid, because it comes from the same estate your dividend does. The profession publishes a guide to fees for each procedure, and this page points you to the right one. Our fee estimates [link to /creditor-services/fee-estimates] page explains how that figure is set, and details of our work [link to /creditor-services/details-of-our-work] covers what the office holder has to report to you.

One thing first. Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here acts as liquidator, administrator or trustee, so we hold no estate and have no remuneration of our own to publish. These guides govern the licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] we bring in, and any other office holder you deal with.
[BUTTON] Book a free, confidential call
What SIP 9 asks of an office holder

SIP 9 is the Statement of Insolvency Practice on payments from an estate. The Scottish version took effect on 1 April 2021 and covers proceedings under the Insolvency Act 1986 and the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 2016. A members' voluntary liquidation is caught only if those paying the fees ask for the disclosures, and a moratorium under Part A1 of the Insolvency Act 1986 sits outside it too.

Anyone asked to approve a payment should be given enough to form a view: what work is planned and why, what it should cost, and afterwards what was done and what it came to. The office holder should also point creditors to information about their rights, in the first communication and in every later report. These guides are that information.
How the fee is calculated

Remuneration is fixed on one of three bases: a percentage of the value of the property realised or dealt with, the work reasonably undertaken by the office holder and staff, which everyone calls time cost, or a set amount. Bases can be combined across different parts of the work.

For a percentage or a set amount, the office holder should explain why it fairly reflects the work and which costs it covers. For time cost, you should see charge out rates by grade of staff. Expenses are approved separately, and any paid to an associate need approving like the fee itself.
How fees are fixed in Scotland

Scotland has its own corporate insolvency rules, so a guide written for England and Wales will send you the wrong way. In an administration [link to /insolvency/administration], the creditors' committee fixes outlays and remuneration. Where there is no committee, the creditors do it by decision procedure. If they fail to, the claim goes to the court, which must determine it.

In a creditors' voluntary liquidation, or a court winding up that began with a winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition], the liquidator submits accounts and a claim after each accounting period, and the liquidation committee may audit them and must issue a determination fixing the amount. Where no committee exists, that falls to the court.

Two rights follow. In a liquidation a creditor may appeal a committee determination to the court within 14 days, having first given the liquidator notice. And in either procedure creditors representing a quarter of the debt by value may apply for an order reducing outlays or remuneration as excessive, within eight weeks of the end of the accounting period where the case is an administration.
Finding the guide for your procedure
There is a separate guide for each procedure, with Scottish versions where the law differs. Use the one matching your appointment.
Liquidation. Covers liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation] in each form, creditor led, court led and solvent
Administration. Including a sale agreed before appointment, a pre-pack administration, which carries further disclosure under SIP 16
Company voluntary arrangement. In a company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] the nominee's and supervisor's fees usually go to creditors with the proposal

Receivership. Receivership over a Scottish company runs under Part 3 of the Insolvency Act 1986 and under the same 2018 winding up and receivership rules. A LPA receivership [link to /insolvency/lpa-receivership] is an English appointment and can be made only over property in England and Wales

Personal insolvency. A trustee's fees fall under the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 2016. In a sequestration [link to /debt-help-scotland/sequestration] the commissioners, or the Accountant in Bankruptcy [link to /debt-help-scotland/accountant-in-bankruptcy] where there are none, fix the outlays and remuneration for each accounting period. Under a protected trust deed [link to /debt-help-scotland/trust-deeds] the trustee takes a prescribed fixed fee and a percentage fee, and the fixed fee can only be increased with the approval of a majority in value of the creditors or of the Accountant in Bankruptcy
Partnerships. Where the debtor is a firm rather than a company, see partnership liquidation [link to /insolvency/partnership-liquidation]

If a practitioner we introduced is handling the appointment and the fee information does not read right, tell us. We are not paid from that estate, so we have no stake in the answer. Get in touch [link to /contact] whenever you want.
Frequently asked questions
Does Lancefield have fees to disclose here?
No, which is the point of the page. We take no appointments, so there is no estate we could be paid from and no remuneration of ours for creditors to approve.
Who approves an insolvency practitioner's fees?

It depends on the procedure. In a Scottish administration: the creditors' committee, or the creditors by decision procedure where there is none, or the court if they do not determine it. In a liquidation: the committee, or the court where none exists.
What if I think the fees are too high?

Ask the office holder for the narrative behind the figures first, because a good many objections resolve there. After that there are two routes: in a liquidation, an appeal to the court within 14 days, and in either procedure an application for a reduction by creditors holding a quarter of the debt by value.
What is the difference between remuneration and outlays?
Remuneration pays for the office holder's own work. Outlays are everything else paid from the estate that is not a distribution, from advertising in the Edinburgh Gazette to solicitors' costs.
Do the English guides apply in Scotland?
Not for the mechanics. The principles are shared, but who fixes the fee, the time limits and the court route all differ here. Use the Scottish version.
I am a creditor, and also a director of a company under pressure.

Common enough, particularly when a large customer fails. The bad debt is one problem and your own company's solvency another, and they are best looked at together. Our Debt Help Scotland [link to /debt-help-scotland] section covers the personal side.

This page covers what it should contain, who approves the fee, and how it can be challenged.

Why there is no Lancefield estimate here

We take no insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes your liquidator, administrator, receiver or trustee, so there is no estate we are paid from and no fee of ours to estimate. The estimate that matters comes from the licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] holding the appointment, and it should reach you before you are asked to approve anything.
That is easier to do honestly when none of your own income depends on appointments.
What you should be told before a fee is approved

The standard is Statement of Insolvency Practice 9 (Scotland). It covers a creditors' voluntary liquidation, an administration [link to /insolvency/administration], a pre-pack administration and a company voluntary arrangement [link to /insolvency/company-voluntary-arrangement-cva] alike, though solvent members' voluntary liquidation work sits outside it. Anyone approving a fee needs enough to judge whether it is reasonable:
The work proposed. What is intended, and why each part of it is necessary
What it will cost. And whether it benefits creditors or is simply required by statute
The rates. Where time is charged, rates by grade of staff and the time unit used
The likely return. What creditors can expect to receive
The expenses. What comes out of the estate on top of the fee, and any work sent outside
The three bases, and what the estimate binds

Remuneration is fixed on one of three bases, or a combination: a percentage of the value of the property realised or dealt with, the work reasonably undertaken, or a set amount. Different bases can apply to different parts of the work, which is common where a company later moves into company liquidation [link to /insolvency/liquidation].

An estimate is not a suggestion. In England and Wales an office holder cannot draw more than the total in it without further approval. Scotland reaches the same protection differently: outlays and remuneration are determined after the event, period by period, against what was estimated.
Outlays, expenses and disbursements
[IMAGE - "Outlays, expenses and disbursements"] a two column comparison block for category 1 against category 2, set in the brand teal and navy. No icons, no illustration.

Scottish rules say outlays for what is spent from the estate other than the fee itself. SIP 9 says expenses, and treats disbursements as a subset: payments the office holder meets first and is reimbursed for later.
Category 1. Payments to a person providing the service concerned who is not an associate of the office holder, such as advertising, insurance or storage. No prior approval needed
Category 2. Payments to an associate, or any payment carrying a shared or allocated element. These need approval before payment, in the same way the fee does
A charge calculated as a percentage of the remuneration, an administration fee on top of it, and overheads belonging inside the charge out rates are all disallowed.
Who approves the fee, and how to challenge it

In a Scottish liquidation the liquidator claims for each accounting period and the liquidation committee determines what is payable, or the court where no committee exists. In an administration the creditors' committee determines it, or the creditors by decision procedure where there is no committee, or the court if the creditors do not.

If you disagree there are two routes. A committee determination in a liquidation can be appealed to the court within 14 days by the liquidator, or by any creditor or contributory who has first given the liquidator notice of an intention to appeal. Separately, creditors representing at least 25 per cent in value can apply to have outlays or remuneration reduced as, in all the circumstances, excessive, with an eight week deadline in an administration.
Before either, ask. A request for more information is meant to be handled fairly and in proportion to the case, and one good question often does more than an application.
Frequently asked questions
Does Lancefield publish its own fee estimate?
No. Estimates come from office holders, who are paid from the estate. We take no appointments and draw nothing from any estate. Our own fees are agreed in advance, in writing.
Are the rules the same as in England and Wales?

No. Corporate insolvency law is largely shared across Great Britain, the procedural rules are not. Scottish administrations run under one 2018 instrument and Scottish liquidations under another, and they differ on how remuneration is fixed and challenged.
Can I see how the time was spent?
You can ask. Time is recorded in units of no more than six minutes for each grade of staff. Ask by work area rather than as one total, because an odd figure usually explains itself.
Does any of this apply to personal debt?

The principles carry across, the machinery differs. Trustee remuneration in a sequestration [link to /debt-help-scotland/sequestration] or under a protected trust deed [link to /debt-help-scotland/trust-deeds] runs through the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 2016, overseen by the Accountant in Bankruptcy [link to /debt-help-scotland/accountant-in-bankruptcy]. Our Debt Help Scotland [link to /debt-help-scotland] section covers it.
A creditor has petitioned. Does this page still help?

Only partly. Once a winding up petition [link to /insolvency/winding-up-petition] is live the timetable is the problem and the fee sits well down the list. Deal with that first, then creditor guides [link to /creditor-services/creditor-guides], and if you would rather talk it through, get in touch [link to /contact].

We will read it with you and say plainly what we think, with nothing of our own riding on the answer. It commits you to nothing.

Details of our work

When an office holder asks creditors to approve what they are paid, or reports on what has happened since the last time, the professional standards require more than a figure. They require a narrative: an explanation of the work actually done, why it was necessary, what it achieved, and what remains. This page explains what that narrative should contain and how to read one.

One thing to be clear about first, because it shapes everything else here. Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here acts as liquidator, administrator or trustee, so we hold no estate, we draw no remuneration from one, and we have no narrative of our own to publish. What follows describes the obligations of the licensed insolvency practitioner [link to /insolvency] we introduce where a formal appointment is needed, and of any other office holder you are dealing with.

What you should receive, and when
[IMAGE] No vector panel needed. This page should look plain and administrative, which suits its purpose.

An office holder reports to creditors at intervals through the case, and again at the end. The reports are cumulative: each one covers the period since the last, so read together they should account for the whole of the appointment.
An account of the period. What was done, by whom, and what it produced. Not a list of activities, but an explanation of what the estate got for the time spent
What has been realised. Assets recovered and money received, against what was expected at the outset
What has been paid out. Costs, expenses, and any distributions, with the office holder's remuneration shown separately
What remains. Outstanding matters, why they are outstanding, and what the office holder expects to achieve

Progress against the estimate. Where an estimate of remuneration was given, how the actual position compares to it. Our fee estimates [link to /creditor-services/fee-estimates] page explains that in Scotland the estimate is not a cap: outlays and remuneration are determined after each accounting period by the committee, the creditors or the court
The creditors' position. What has been distributed, or an honest statement of the prospects of a distribution

Where the case has moved from one procedure to another, for instance an administration [link to /insolvency/administration] ending in a creditors' voluntary liquidation, the reporting picks up in the new procedure and the earlier office holder accounts for their own period.
How to tell a useful report from a boilerplate one
[IMAGE] "How to tell a useful report from a boilerplate one": the most useful section; worth visual weight.
This is the practical part, and it is the reason a page like this is worth writing properly.

Does it explain, or does it list? "Correspondence with creditors, 14 hours" is an activity. "Dealt with 60 creditor claims, of which 11 were disputed and required adjudication" is an explanation. The second tells you what the estate bought

Does the time relate to the outcome? Significant time on an asset that realised very little should carry a reason. Sometimes there is a good one, such as a claim that had to be pursued to establish it was worthless
Are the difficulties named? Cases go wrong. A report that describes only progress, in a case that has plainly stalled, is not telling you the useful part
Does it compare to the estimate? A narrative that never mentions the original estimate is avoiding the question a creditor most wants answered
Can you tell what happens next, and when? A report that ends without a next step or a timescale has not finished its job
None of that means an office holder who writes a thin report is doing a poor job. It means you cannot tell from the document, which is precisely what the standard exists to prevent.
If the report does not answer your question

You are entitled to ask. A creditor can request further information about the office holder's remuneration and expenses, and about the work behind them. In Scotland the professional standard is that the office holder considers the request on its merits and answers fairly, in proportion to the case, rather than within a fixed statutory period. In a company voluntary arrangement charged on time there is a harder right: a written statement of the hours spent and the rates charged must be provided free of charge within a set period.

Beyond that, where the remuneration and outlays have been fixed by the committee or the creditors, creditors representing at least a quarter of the debt by value can apply to the court to have them reduced as excessive. That is a serious step and rarely the first one, but the availability of it is what gives the earlier request its weight. Where you believe the process itself has been misused rather than merely poorly reported, complain to the office holder first, and if their answer does not satisfy you the complaint route runs through the Insolvency Service's complaints gateway, which passes it to the office holder's professional body.

In our experience most unsatisfactory reports are the product of a busy case rather than an evasive office holder, and a direct question resolves them. If it does not, contact [link to /contact] us and we will tell you whether what you are being told is reasonable.
Our own fees are a different thing
Worth separating, because creditors and directors both conflate the two.

Where Lancefield advises a company on restructuring [link to /restructuring] or an individual on their own position, our fee is agreed with that client directly, before the work starts, and it is paid by them. It is not office-holder remuneration, it does not come out of an insolvent estate, and it is not subject to approval by creditors, because we are not an office holder and there is no estate involved.

If you are a creditor looking at a report and wondering which fees are which: the office holder's remuneration is the amount determined by the committee, or where there is none by the creditors or the court, and drawn from the estate. Anything we were paid for advising the company before the appointment is a pre-appointment cost like any other professional fee, and the office holder will treat it as such.
Frequently asked questions
What is the narrative of work done?

The written explanation an office holder gives creditors of the work carried out, why it was necessary, what it achieved and what remains. It accompanies the figures so that creditors can judge whether the time charged produced value, rather than simply being told the total.
How often should I receive a report?

At intervals set by the rules for the procedure, and again at the end of the case. The reports are cumulative, so together they should account for the whole appointment. If you have not received one when you expected it, ask.
Can I ask for more detail?

Yes. A creditor can request further information about the remuneration, the expenses and the work behind them. In Scotland the office holder should consider the request on its merits and answer fairly and in proportion to the case. In a company voluntary arrangement charged on time, a written statement of hours and rates must be supplied free of charge within a set period.
What if I think the fees are too high?

Raise it with the office holder first, in writing, and ask for the detail. If that does not resolve it, creditors representing at least a quarter of the debt by value can apply to the court on the ground that the remuneration or outlays are excessive. The fee estimates [link to /creditor-services/fee-estimates] page covers how remuneration is approved in the first place.
Does Lancefield publish one of these?

No, and it could not. We take no insolvency appointments, so we never hold an estate or draw remuneration from one. This page explains the obligations of the office holders we introduce and of any other you are dealing with.
